121.label: In rook endgames the player pushes a passed pawn (or shuffles the king) instead of the forcing move — almost always a rook check or checkmate — that wins outright, squandering a forced win or mate down to a draw or smaller edge.

113.label: In an endgame the player fails to play the single critical only-move—most often a capture or rescue involving a bishop—and loses material or a draw; the exact error is mixed (hangs its own bishop on ~3 boards, misses a winning/saving capture on ~6, with queen/knight/rook the decisive piece on the rest), and the SEE 'bishop/losing/hangs 100%' tags are not supported by the per-board lines.

116.label: Plays a forcing check that compels an unfavorable exchange/simplification, losing material or liquidating into a lost position (the queen is the traded piece in most lines, but every move is a check).

101.label: While winning, the player repeatedly skips the decisive tactical shot (frequently a knight fork or forcing capture) and plays a slow, routine move that squanders the advantage into equality.

129.label: The player ignores a completely undefended enemy rook that could be captured for free (e.g. Kxf3, Bxd6, Nxd2, fxe6), instead playing a slower or material-grabbing move and letting the rook escape — a pure missed-win omission, not a self-hang.

124.label: Plays a safe, passive move (often Rx-capture available) and skips a forcing combination that wins material, frequently via a fork or pin after recapture.

128.label: A move that leaves the player's own piece undefended and immediately (or within a couple moves) capturable, throwing away a winning position — the hung piece varies (queen, rook, knight, or exchange), so no single piece can be named.

118.label: In every position the player makes a slow, materially-safe move instead of the engine's decisive simplifying exchange (almost always a rook trade), squandering a winning edge or letting a drawn position slip to lost.

122.label: In critical/losing endgames the player repeatedly fails to play the engine's forcing capture (the best move is a capture in 7 of 10 boards and the player essentially never makes the right one), but the feature is genuinely mixed: ~3 boards are clean missed winning captures (dxe4, fxe5, Rxf6), ~3 are self-hangs of a piece left en prise (knight/queen/bishop), and ~3-4 are king-safety/tempo errors that weaken the king or allow mate — so no single direction or piece (bishop appears in only ~6/10) cleanly dominates.

127.label: In winning king-and-pawn (and a couple rook) endgames the player throws away or slows the win by failing to lead actively with the king — either pushing the passed pawn prematurely or sidestepping the king to a passive square instead of advancing it.

120.label: In the opening (100% of boards), the player repeatedly mishandles central pawn tension with a move-order/tempo error that squanders the advantage—usually skipping the correct capture or break (dxe4, cxd5, Bxd4, Bxd5, exd4) and occasionally making a pure positional concession or hanging a piece—so the specific material involved varies and no single piece can be named.

134.label: Plays a tempo-losing rook check that lets the enemy king escape to safety, squandering a winning advantage—frequently a forced mate—instead of the decisive move.

130.chip: Trades off bishop, squanders edge (queen recaptures)
130.label: The player captures with their bishop and is recaptured by the opponent's queen, liquidating a key (usually attacking) bishop and throwing away a winning or better position.

125.label: In a losing/holdable endgame the player gives up their only defensive bishop—usually by exchanging it for a knight or grabbing a pawn and being recaptured—collapsing into a lost pawn or bare-king ending.

132.label: The player captures/exchanges (most often a rook, but also bishop or queen) to simplify, voluntarily entering a lost pawn endgame where the surrendered active piece was the key defensive/winning resource.

131.label: The player moves a piece off a square where it was defending material or blocking a tactic, and the deserted duty is punished by a (often multi-move) refutation that wins material or collapses the position — though the piece lost varies and a few boards are walking-into-a-tactic or purely positional.

126.label: A rook operating on a central (d/e) file is the decisive piece in a queen+rook tactic on essentially all 10 boards, but the error direction is genuinely mixed: about half MISS the winning rook move (Re6, Rad1/Rfd1, Rde8, Rce8) while the rest are self-inflicted — hanging a rook by removing its defender (Qxh5, Nd1), blocking their own rook's e-file x-ray (Be6), or walking into a back-rank/king mate (Rxa7, Ke6).

97.label: In a clearly winning endgame the player makes a position-wrecking move—sometimes hanging own material to a fork/skewer/recapture, sometimes simply skipping a free capture—converting a win into a draw or loss; the lost piece varies (queen and rook both appear), so no single piece can be named.

137.label: In every position the player played a materially-safe but passive move and missed a winning queen check on h4/h5 (sometimes with a follow-up fork) that exploited the opponent's weakened, f-pawn-less kingside.

136.label: A greedy queen capture-with-check (often a Scholar's-Mate-style Qxf7) onto a defended square that loses the queen for a pawn or minor piece in the opening.

144.label: Plays an unsound Fried-Liver-style knight sacrifice on f7 (or f2) that the opponent simply takes with the king (Kxf7/Kxf2), losing a knight for a pawn in the opening.

141.label: In all 10 positions the player played a quiet/greedy move and overlooked a forcing queen shot — almost always a queen capture with check (Qxa1+/Qxc1+/Qxg8+/Qxe1+) or a queen mate — that won decisive material or forced checkmate; the captured target varies (rook, bishop, knight, or mate), so it's a missed win rather than a hung piece, with the queen consistently the delivering piece.

138.label: A quiet/developing move that ignores a forcing threat against the player's own king (typically Qxh7+, Qxf7+, or Qxh2+/Qxf2+), allowing a sacrifice or capture that exposes the king and wins material or mates.

107.chip: Slow move hangs material (skips rook trade)
107.label: In a middlegame with rook tension on an open file, the player makes a passive/slow move instead of the critical forcing rook exchange (Rxe8+/Rxe1+), allowing the opponent to win the player's own material over the next few moves.

143.label: In the opening the player plays a quiet/natural move (O-O, h3, Bb3, h6) and misses a winning tactical sacrifice—overwhelmingly Bxf7+ exploiting the uncastled king and a loose bishop on g4—squandering a near-winning advantage into equality.

133.label: A move that leaves the player's own piece hanging — to a direct capture or a follow-up fork — losing material for nothing (piece varies: queen, knight, or bishop), with one outlier walking the king into mate.

146.label: Fires on rook/queen checks in the endgame where the player reflexively checks instead of playing the direct converting move (capture the pawn, march the king), typically costing tempo or handing the enemy king a better square — but severity is genuinely mixed since ~4 of 10 flagged checks are actually best/0cp, so the only solid invariants are 'endgame' + 'check' with no material ever hung.

140.label: Plays a tactically losing move that drops its own piece to a refutation (deflection, unsound sacrifice, or removed/overloaded defender), usually a couple of moves later; the hung piece varies between knight and bishop, so it's 'a piece' rather than a specific one.

142.chip: Missed forcing tactical win (often knight fork)
142.label: In all 10 positions the player makes a quiet developing or retreating move instead of a forcing tactical shot—most often a knight fork or check, sometimes a discovered check or winning trade—that would have won material.

152.label: The player leaves their own queen en prise — almost always to an enemy knight (Nxd8/Nxf6/Nxd1/Nxf7) — by ignoring the direct attack on it while making a developing, capturing, or castling move.

150.label: Plays the queen (or removes its defender) onto a square where it is immediately captured, losing the queen for nothing or for grossly inadequate material.

147.label: In every position the player skipped a forced winning continuation—usually a check, often outright mate—commonly by grabbing material instead of delivering the decisive blow.

139.label: In a winning opening the player plays a natural developing/castling/pushing move instead of capturing a free hanging enemy piece (most often a knight, frequently on d5), squandering a full-piece advantage; a minority of boards instead overextend a pawn, hang material outright, or trade off into equality.

156.chip: King wastes tempo in pawn race
156.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, moves the king to blockade or centralize instead of advancing its own passed pawn, losing a critical tempo in the promotion race.

149.chip: Hangs own material to tactic (squanders edge)
149.label: From a winning or equal position the player makes a move—usually a greedy capture of a seemingly free piece/pawn, sometimes a king or pawn move—that loses their own material to a tactical refutation (often a discovered attack or recapture-with-check), but the material hung varies (pawn, exchange, rook) so no single piece can be named.

154.label: In a winning/already-decisive position the player passes up a forced checkmate—typically an immediate queen check—by instead playing a quiet retreat or grabbing material, throwing away the mate (2 of 10 instead hang their own piece).

155.label: A capture or piece move opens a file/diagonal or removes a defender, allowing the opponent to win the player's own rook or queen (self-inflicted major-piece loss), though 2 of the 10 boards are missed-win omissions rather than hangs.

151.label: Across these boards the engine's best move is almost always a knight capture/zwischenzug (Nxf3+/Nxf6+, occasionally N3xf4); instead the player makes some other developing/retreating move that leaves a piece — most often their own knight, occasionally a bishop — hanging to a simple capture, though a few boards (4, 5, 9) lose only a pawn or advantage via move-order/positional errors rather than dropping a clean piece.

160.chip: Hangs corner rook to Qxa1+ check
160.label: The player vacates a defender or diagonal-blocker of their a-file corner rook, allowing the enemy queen to capture it with check (Qxa1+/Qxa8+) and win a full rook.

158.chip: Hangs h-file rook, misses Rxh8+ check
158.label: In every position the player skips the winning rook capture-with-check on the open h-file (Rxh8+/Rxh1+) and instead plays a greedy or passive move, leaving their own h-file rook undefended so the opponent wins the race by capturing with check first.

135.label: The player throws away a winning or clearly better middlegame/endgame by losing or mistrading a minor piece (bishop and knight roughly evenly split), typically leaving it en prise or simplifying into an equal/lost ending.

163.chip: Allows enemy pawn to promote (passed-pawn endgame)
163.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player makes a move (often a greedy capture or stepping off the promotion file) that loses the promotion race and lets the opponent's pawn queen.

148.label: A piece move (often a greedy capture or wrong move-order) that abandons a defender and lets the player's own material fall in a forced rook-exchange / back-rank sequence — the hung piece varies (bishop, knight, rook, even mate), so no single piece is named.

162.label: A middlegame move that loses material — most often a clean hang of a rook, queen, knight, or bishop (sometimes via a greedy capture or bad trade), collapsing the position — but the set is impure: one board is actually the best move and another is a pure pawn-loss positional error.

157.label: In the opening the player plays a natural developing move that ignores an infiltrated enemy queen's threat and hangs their own material — most often the corner rook to Qxh1/Qxh8, but also bishops or a pawn.

164.label: In the opening, plays a move that leaves the player's own piece undefended, allowing a free capture — the hung piece varies (knight, bishop, or queen), and two boards are instead a greedy trade and a missed win.

159.label: Mixed material-tactics feature: the player either greedily grabs a pawn and gets punished by a larger loss (4 boards) or overlooks a free decisive capture/mate (3 boards), with a couple of tempo/move-order errors that don't fit the material theme.

145.label: The player walks into a forced checkmate—usually by greedily grabbing material or pulling a key piece off king defense—rather than addressing the mating threat.

153.chip: Missed winning capture/tactic (often quiet queen move)
153.label: In every position the player passes up a forcing winning move—usually a material-winning capture or mating tactic—in favor of a quieter, non-forcing move (most often a queen move), though in ~4 cases that move also hangs their own material, so the missed-win vs self-inflicted direction is genuinely mixed.

174.label: Across all ten boards the player skips a winning queen capture of an undefended rook on a8/a1 (Qxa8/Qxa1) along an open diagonal, playing a safe developing or recapturing move instead and throwing away a large material-winning advantage.

166.label: The player repeatedly overlooks an undefended enemy queen sitting en prise, declining the free capture and instead playing an unrelated move that allows a forced mate.

167.label: In a winning endgame (often with a passed pawn), the player makes a safe repositioning or king move instead of the decisive continuation — a promotion push, winning capture, or pawn break — though several top boards are actually harmless quiet moves rather than true blunders.

161.label: From a winning position the player squanders the advantage, most often by a bishop move in the opening that hangs material (typically Bxd4 grabbing the pawn into Qxd4, missing Nxc4) in 6-7/10 boards, while the rest are missed clean wins/zwischenzugs with other pieces.

165.label: In a won endgame, the player advances/promotes a pawn (or makes a slow king/rook move) instead of capturing or neutralizing the opponent's only active piece, squandering the cleanest win and occasionally hanging material a move or two later.

177.label: A pawn move (b6/g6/g3) played to chase away the enemy queen instead fatally weakens the king's own pawn shelter, letting the queen (or a sacrifice) crash through for a decisive attack.

169.label: In the endgame the player overlooks a forced winning resource—most often a back-rank/first-rank mate or check—and instead plays a careless king or pawn move that squanders the win.

176.label: In a won endgame, the player repeatedly declines the decisive simplifying trade/exchange (most often a queen trade into a winning pawn endgame, sometimes a rook exchange/sac), instead playing a passive king move that squanders the win — and in a few cases the chosen move even drops material a move later.

170.label: The feature fires on self-inflicted passive/prophylactic repositioning moves (most often a bishop, but also rook, king, or pawn) that vacate a square where the piece was doing critical active or defensive work; in roughly six of ten boards this directly hangs material or allows mate, while the rest are tempo/positional losses (2,3,10) or one missed tactical win (8), so the unifying thread is the passive relocation itself rather than a specific piece or material outcome.

173.label: The move initiates a capture/exchange that loses the player's own material — most often giving up the exchange (rook for a minor piece, recaptured), though sometimes hanging a knight or queen outright; the hung material varies, so it's 'a piece/material' rather than one specific piece (board 7 is near-noise, otherwise 9/10 fit).

172.label: In a winning endgame the player prematurely advances a passed pawn (or plays a tempo check) instead of the precise winning move—usually capturing hanging material or bringing the king first—squandering the win.

184.label: In the opening, plays a pawn/developing move that allows an enemy knight to leap to c7 (mirror: c2) with a royal fork — or a bishop to infiltrate c7 — losing the exchange or queen.

179.label: The move usually leaves one of the player's own pieces (most often a rook, sometimes bishop or queen) en prise in the middlegame—frequently by moving onto an attacked square or moving the wrong piece—while 2-3 of the ten are instead missed wins or positional slips.

180.label: A materially-safe move (king, rook, knight or bishop — the piece varies) that fails to play the one precise forcing resource, usually a tempo-gaining check, fork, or back-rank defense, that would win or save the position, almost always in endgames.

185.chip: Wrong king move worsens lost endgame
185.label: In an already-losing endgame the player makes the wrong king move—most often losing the tempo in a passed-pawn promotion race (sometimes letting the pawn queen with check)—and occasionally just hangs a piece outright.

168.label: A natural-looking move (develop, centralize, grab, apply pressure) that ignores the opponent's most urgent threat and gets refuted decisively — sometimes hanging own material (bishop/rook/queen/knight vary) and sometimes allowing a mating attack or breakthrough — so the specific thing lost is inconsistent and a human should review.

175.label: In winning endgames the player fires an unnecessary rook/queen check instead of the precise quiet/centralizing/king move, but the feature is mixed: it's really detecting 'gives a check in a winning endgame' — roughly half the boards (2,3,4,6) lose ~0cp and are fine, only a few (1,7,8, marginally 5) actually cost tempo or the clean conversion, and board 10 is an outlier king retreat (not a check) that throws a +680 win; materially safe throughout, so an omission rather than a hang, warranting review.

186.label: A move meant to win or grab material (capture/fork) instead abandons defense and hangs the player's own piece — the hung piece varies (queen, rook, knight, bishop) — almost always in the middlegame.

178.label: In losing/lost positions the player makes a slow pawn or king move instead of the only defensive resource (often a saving capture), most commonly allowing a forced checkmate via king-safety/back-rank collapse, though 2-3 boards instead simply hang a piece — the unifying core is failing to meet a decisive threat.

188.label: Player captures a piece (greedily, often the queen or rook) while overlooking an available forced checkmate — usually mate-in-one.

187.label: A knight move—usually a greedy grab of a central d4/e5 pawn (or centralizing on d5)—that loses the player's own material to the refutation in 6-7 boards, while 3 boards instead miss a stronger material-winning shot; the knight is the decisive piece in nearly every position.

182.label: In nearly every board (9–10/10, checks in 8) the player fires a tempting forcing move—usually a check, most often with a knight—instead of the precise winning continuation; the direction is genuinely mixed, since in roughly half the refutation simply captures the hung piece (e.g. Ne7+/Rxe7, Nf2+/Nxf2, Nf6+/Rxf6, Bxc5+/Nxc5) for clear material loss while in the other half it merely throws away a forced mate or large edge via a harmless trade (Rxg7+, Bh4+, Rxe8+, Qxf3), so this needs human review.

195.label: The played move pulls a defender (rook, king, or bishop) off the back rank/key defensive square, allowing the opponent an immediate or forced back-rank checkmate.

193.chip: Trades rook into drawn/lost pawn endgame
193.label: The player captures with the rook (usually with check), trading it for a minor piece and liquidating into a king-and-pawn endgame that squanders a winning rook-vs-minor advantage into a draw or loss.

183.label: In an already-losing position the player makes a self-inflicted move—most often a queen move that abandons a defensive post or walks into a tactic—converting a survivable loss into a forced mate or decisive material loss.

181.label: Player greedily captures with a pawn in the opening—usually fxe5/fxe4 that opens the king's diagonal to a crushing Qh4+/Qh5+ winning material—though two boards are instead missed-win/positional pawn grabs (dxc4), so direction is mixed.

192.label: Player self-inflicts a king-safety collapse—either walking the king onto a fatal square or pushing a pawn that was sheltering the king/guarding an adjacent square—turning a worse position into forced mate or decisive material loss, with the king central to nearly every refutation (outliers: one missed draw and one plain hung knight).

200.label: Fires on pawn advances/exchanges in already-losing king-and-pawn endgames; only about half actually worsen the eval while 3/10 are the engine's top move, so it tracks 'pawn move in a lost position' more than a specific mistake.

189.chip: Develops/quiet move, ignores tactic, squanders winning opening
189.label: In a winning opening (winning 100%, opening 100%, a material-winning best move available 100%), the player makes a natural developing/structural move — fianchetto, develop a piece, castle, or retreat — that ignores the board's critical tactic and squanders the advantage; the trigger is consistent but the DIRECTION is genuinely mixed: ~6 boards are self-inflicted (the quiet move lets a refutation win the player's own material, deliver mate, or wreck structure/castling over 2-3 moves — e.g. Nxc3, Nb4/Nxc2+, Nd6#, Bxc4/Qxd1+), while ~3-4 simply miss a free win (Nxe5, Bxe6), so both the punished piece and whether it's 'hung' vs 'missed' vary and a human should review.

191.label: In rook/promotion endgames the feature most often fires when the player moves or captures with a piece — usually the rook, sometimes a knight — onto a square where it's simply recaptured (boards 1,5,7,8,9), but it also catches the mirror-image error of skipping a winning king-recapture like Kxh2/Kxb3 (boards 2,4,6) plus a couple of near-zero non-blunders (3,10), so the direction is genuinely mixed around an endgame capture/recapture moment centered on the rook.

190.label: In already-losing positions (83% losing) the player makes a self-inflicted move that drops a piece outright—rook (boards 1,4,6), bishop (2,8,10), or knight (3), with no single piece dominating—while a handful of cases instead abandon king defense and walk into a forced mate (5,7,9).

201.label: In a won position the player passes up a forced winning combination — almost always a decisive rook exchange/simplification on a file — in favor of a slow positional move, throwing away the win rather than hanging material.

199.label: In the opening the player repeatedly fails to capture a free undefended central pawn with the queen (almost always Qxd4), an omission that flips an equal/winning position into a loss.

171.label: A knight move (frequently to d2, played-knight 93%) that abandons a defensive duty or vacates a guarded square, allowing the opponent a multi-move tactic—often a knight fork—that wins material; 7/10 are self-inflicted hangs (the single-ply 'safe 77%' misses the multi-move refutations), while 3/10 (castling/N-d7/Nbd2) are instead quiet knight moves that skip an available material-winning continuation.

197.label: The player delivers a tempting but purposeless check (instead of the winning quiet move) that lets the opponent's king escape and throws away a winning advantage — a 'patzer sees a check' error across all ten boards, twice even hanging the checking rook outright.

206.label: A quiet, materially-safe move that overlooks a concrete tactical shot (often a capture like Rxc6/Bxb8/Rxf8) winning a piece or the exchange, letting the opponent consolidate.

205.label: Player moves a rook to contest an open file (or the back rank) onto a square where it loses material—either captured outright or via a forced exchange sequence (frequently a back-rank tactic) that drops material.

208.label: Across all top positions the player declines an immediately available capture of the opponent's hanging/undefended piece (queen, rook, or knight, often with check) in a won endgame, squandering or delaying a decisive material win.

198.label: In an endgame, a king or rook move walks into a deflection/skewer check that wins material outright or forces a losing rook trade into a lost pawn endgame — the hung unit varies (mostly rook, once a bishop), so it's 'a piece.'

214.label: A move (usually a pawn capture or queen placement that opens/exposes a file) leaves the player's own queen on the file undefended, letting an enemy rook win it for a rook — 9 of 10 hang the queen, only board 10 hangs a rook instead.

196.label: In endgames the player repeatedly loses a rook — usually hanging it outright to a free capture or knight fork, sometimes dumping it in a disastrous trade into a lost pawn ending.

204.label: In the opening, the played move usually loses the player's own material to a short tactic—with a knight as the decisive capturing/forking piece in most refutations—though a couple of boards are pure tempo losses and one is a missed win.

194.label: A king-safety or repositioning move (usually moving the king) that ignores the position's critical demand—either skipping a winning capture or walking into a refutation—so it misses a win or hangs material; direction is genuinely mixed between missed_win and hung_own.

203.label: The player makes a tempting move—frequently a greedy capture (often by the queen)—that abandons control of a critical square guarding its own king, walking into a forced checkmate, though several boards instead hang material or, conversely, miss a forced mate.

202.label: In losing middlegame positions the played move allows or accelerates a forced checkmate, typically by vacating a key defensive square or removing a back-rank/king defender (the specific piece varies, so no single piece is named).

209.label: Mixed feature: a slim majority (~6/10) are unsound material surrenders — hanging, under-trading, or sacrificing a piece for too little (rook in #4/#5/#7, bishop in #1/#6, knight in #9) — while the rest (~3, boards #2/#3/#8) are suboptimal endgame king moves that lose tempo or squander a win, so both the piece and the mistake type are too fuzzy to commit confidently.

212.label: From a roughly equal opening, the player captures or trades with the queen to 'simplify,' but the recapture/refutation backfires — usually losing material (knight fork of the rooks, an undefended bishop, or a runaway passed pawn) or conceding a decisive positional edge.

213.label: A mostly materially-safe move that abandons the precise winning continuation (often a key file/square or tempo), collapsing a clearly winning position to equality; a few boards instead hang a piece outright, so the direction is mixed and the squandered piece varies.

210.chip: Throws away winning endgame (often hangs piece)
210.label: In a clearly winning endgame (frequently a forced mate), the player chooses a move that squanders the win — most often self-inflicted, hanging a piece that gets captured (queen in 4 boards, rook in 2), but in several cases simply missing a free capture or the mating continuation, so the unifying invariant is 'winning converted to drawn/worse' rather than one specific hung piece.

217.label: The played move loses the player's own material outright—often immediately, sometimes via a 2-3 move refutation—with the hung piece varying (knight most common) and a knight frequently part of the tactic.

211.label: Promotes a pawn to queen immediately instead of first making the necessary preparatory move (a king-safety step or intermediate check), so the rushed promotion gets the king mated or loses the brand-new queen.

222.label: Plays a quiet, retreating, or repositioning move instead of a decisive tactical strike — usually a sacrifice against the opponent's weakened kingside (Bxg6/Bxh3/Rxg6/Rxh3 type blows).

218.label: A king move that exposes the king to a decisive attack (most often a forced mating net, sometimes losing material via tempo-checks), throwing away the game instead of the available defensive queen-trade resource.

226.label: In the opening, the player leaves their own queen en prise (usually to an enemy knight), losing it outright for a minor piece.

207.label: In an already-lost position, declines the forced defensive queen trade/capture and instead plays a king move or queen sortie that either drops the queen or allows a forced mate.

215.label: The player skips a forcing, material-winning move—almost always a capture or deflection delivered with check (often Qxrook+)—and settles for a worse, non-winning continuation.

228.label: Across the boards the player makes a natural-looking capture, check, trade, or retreat and overlooks a crushing tactic — frequently a pin/trap that wins the opponent's queen — throwing away a winning advantage rather than hanging their own material.

219.chip: Loses material or king under attack (checks)
219.label: In a critical/losing middlegame the player plays a passive or greedy move that fails the only defense, letting the opponent win decisive material or mate via forcing checks; the lost material varies (king, rook, queen, pawn), so no single piece can be named.

221.label: The player chose a natural, greedy, or routine move and overlooked the one precise resource acting on the opponent's queen—usually a quiet move that traps or wins it, sometimes one forcing a favorable trade or defending against it—with the enemy queen central to the decisive line on nearly every board.

216.chip: Missed winning tactic in opening (knight capture)
216.label: In the opening the player repeatedly squanders a winning advantage by choosing a passive move (often retreating a bishop to h4/h5) instead of a forcing winning capture such as Nxf3 or Nxf6+.

220.label: A self-inflicted opening blunder that drops the player's own material to a simple recapture — most often a centralized/leaping knight, but sometimes a pawn — so the safe core is 'hangs material in the opening' rather than 'hangs a knight'.

229.label: The player repeatedly squanders a forced mate (or decisive forcing line) by grabbing material with a greedy capture instead of playing the winning continuation.

223.label: Plays a quiet, passive, or greedy move that overlooks the critical forcing continuation—sometimes skipping the player's own winning tactic (fork/free piece), sometimes walking into a decisive refutation or mate against their own king.

234.label: Player passes up a materially-safe but winning bishop capture of an undefended rook, letting the opponent rescue it with tempo.

230.chip: Trades active bishop, queen recaptures center
230.label: Needlessly captures with the bishop on d5/d4 (usually a centralized knight), letting the opponent recapture with the queen and dominate the center — surrendering an active bishop in the opening; in two cases it's outright bishop-for-pawn.

225.label: Squanders a winning/decisive position by playing a tempo-losing move (often a queen check) instead of the decisive forcing line—frequently a rook check on an open file—allowing the opponent's king to escape or castle to safety.

227.label: Across the top positions the player makes a greedy or careless move—often capturing/repositioning in the wrong order instead of first inserting a forcing check or rook exchange—that hangs their own material (a rook here, a queen there, a pawn elsewhere) or even walks into mate, so the hung unit varies and the safe call is 'a piece'.

236.label: In every opening position the player overlooked a pawn capture that would have won a hanging enemy knight for a pawn, instead playing a quiet developing or central move that let the knight escape.

235.chip: Declines opening capture, loses minor piece
235.label: In the opening the player declines the correct resolving capture (the best move is a capture in all 10 boards) and instead makes a passive or developing minor-piece move — usually a bishop, sometimes a knight — that hangs the piece, gets it trapped, or surrenders tempo/structure, losing own material in most boards.

238.label: In a clearly winning position the player throws away the decisive advantage with a non-forcing move — wasting a tempo, grabbing a side pawn, or missing a forced mate/promotion — letting the opponent escape to a draw or worse.

231.label: In losing positions the player makes a mostly-rook move that walks into a decisive enemy check — typically losing the rook to a capture/skewer or allowing forced mate; a couple of boards instead show the player wasting a tempo with a purposeless check, and one board is actually the engine's top move.

237.label: A premature queen sortie to an exposed square (a4/a5/h4/h5) in the opening is punished with tempo, losing material as the queen gets trapped or a now-undefended piece falls.

246.label: Plays a quiet, non-checking queen move when the only good resource was a forcing check — usually a saving perpetual, sometimes a winning/mating or material-gaining check sequence.

249.label: An opening move (often a greedy queen sortie or pawn overextension) that loses the player's own material to a tactical refutation, with the lost piece varying across boards.

278.label: In a winning endgame the player skips the simple capture of an undefended rook (almost always a king recapture like Kxh2/Kxg7), usually playing an aimless check or tempo move instead and throwing away the win.

363.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, plays a passive king move (or inferior pawn push) instead of the one decisive pawn break/breakthrough, throwing away the win or the draw.

361.chip: Passive king move loses tempo (pawn endgame)
361.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player repeatedly puts the king on a passive/wrong square, squandering a critical tempo or the opposition and accelerating an already-losing position (no material is hung).

364.chip: Middlegame blunder flips holdable to lost (piece varies)
364.label: Genuinely mixed: this fires on self-inflicted middlegame moves that convert an unclear/holdable position into a lost one, most often by losing material in the 2-3 move refutation (bishop on 1/9, rook on 5/10, knight on 3, pawn on 6, greedy grab on 7) but also by walking the king into a mating net (2, 8) or a forcing king attack (4) — no single piece or sub-mechanism dominates, so the original 'blunders material or king safety' read is roughly right but understates the positional-collapse cases.

365.label: In mostly-losing endgames the player makes a king move or a king-side pawn push that worsens an already-bad position—hanging material (rook/pawn), accelerating a forced mate, or occasionally squandering a win/draw—with the king consistently the decisive piece but the exact failure mode varying board to board.

368.label: The player grabs material (usually capturing a bishop) instead of attending to the decisive task, letting an enemy passed pawn promote or missing a mate, turning a win or draw into a loss.

358.label: From a winning position (75% winning) the player throws the game away with a tactical material error—most often hanging their own piece (rook on 1/6/8, knight on 5/10, queen on 9), but on several boards (2, 7, partly 1) instead playing a safe/quiet move that skips a decisive winning capture, plus a couple of king/endgame conversions (3,10); the piece and exact mechanism vary, so it's genuinely mixed around a 'squander a won position via material' core.

369.chip: Capture instead of faster forcing win
369.label: In already-winning positions the player grabs material with a rook/queen capture instead of the more forcing line (a check or mate), missing the cleaner/faster victory rather than hanging anything—though several boards are negligible inaccuracies and one (board 9) is actually the best move.

314.label: Plays a tempo-losing, pointless check that lets the king step to safety and the checking piece land passively, squandering the advantage and skipping a clearly stronger move (the check is usually delivered by a knight).

371.label: In already-winning endgames the feature fires on moves (king/pawn/knight) that fail to convert most efficiently — typically squandering a pawn, pawn-tension/structure, or a promotion/capture rather than literally hanging a piece — but it's noisy, since 3 of the top-10 are actually 0cp optimal moves and the SEE 'hung piece 100%' signal is contradicted by the multi-move refutations (which show pawn/efficiency loss, not piece hangs), so the real invariant is just 'suboptimal endgame conversion.'

366.label: In the middlegame the player loses their own queen — either moving it to a square where it is captured, capturing into a recapture, or playing another move while the queen sits en prise for little or no compensation.

373.label: In a winning/advantageous position, the player skips the decisive rook move—usually a back-rank or first-rank invasion—choosing a greedy capture or passive piece move that squanders the advantage.

370.chip: Hangs a piece for a pawn (opening sac)
370.label: In the opening, the player sacrifices a minor piece (usually a bishop on f2/f7, sometimes a knight) for a single pawn—often as a tempting check—and simply hangs it to a routine recapture.

355.label: The player plays a tempting forcing check (or check-capture) that throws away the game — on most boards it hangs a piece to the checked king's recapture (rook/bishop/queen vary), and on the rest it forces a losing trade/endgame; the harmful check is universal (100%) but the piece and the win-vs-loss outcome vary.

374.label: Plays a safe/consolidating or material-grabbing move that misses a decisive winning attack on the enemy king, frequently a rook lift to the third rank (Rf3/Re3/Rd3).

367.chip: Losing king move in endgame (misses only save)
367.label: In endgames the player plays a losing move—usually a quiet king move—that misses the sole holding/saving resource (often the only correct capture), converting a draw or a salvageable position into a clear loss; the punishment varies between a hung piece, an enemy promotion, or mate, so no single piece is named.

379.label: The player repeatedly fails to capture an undefended enemy bishop (usually on g4/g5) that could be won for a full free piece — a missed win, not a self-inflicted hang.

375.label: In 9 of 10 boards the player makes an inferior rook move (the 10th is a knight) that throws away a winning or clearly better position — variously missing a forced mate/material win (#1,6,7,9), losing tempo by abandoning an active square (#2,5,10), misplacing the rook positionally (#3), or walking it into a trap (#8) — so the consistent element is the rook in the decisive play rather than one single mistake type.

377.chip: Hangs own piece, throwing away win
377.label: In a winning position, the player makes a move (often an in-between attack or move-order error) that abandons defense of their own piece — usually the queen, sometimes a rook — leaving it to be captured and converting a win into a loss.

372.chip: Misplays pawn endgame, misses key capture
372.label: In endgames the move mishandles the pawn tension — almost always skipping the one precise pawn capture (often playing a king move instead) — and loses the pawn race to an opponent's unstoppable passed pawn.

376.chip: Missed simplifying trade into won endgame
376.label: The player keeps pieces on the board instead of making the simplifying rook/queen exchange that liquidates into a winning (or drawing) pawn endgame.

380.label: The recurring blunder is moving the queen to a square where it can be captured—almost always WITH CHECK and usually as a misguided trade offer—hanging the queen and converting a playable position into a loss or forced mate (9/10 are queen moves; one hangs a rook the same way).

388.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player moves the king instead of pushing the passed pawn to the seventh rank, squandering a forced win into a dead draw.

381.label: In every board the player chose a quiet, materially-safe king/rook move and overlooked a forcing winning tactic — almost always a knight check or fork (Nf3+, Nf6+, Nb3+, Nxe3+), with only one board (Bxg7+) using a bishop instead.

384.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player wastes a tempo on a king move or passive pawn push and misses the one critical pawn break/breakthrough (g4, h5, f5, a4, h4...), squandering a winning or holdable position rather than hanging material.

333.label: The played move ignores a decisive threat to the player's own king (often while grabbing material or chasing an enemy piece), allowing a crushing attack or back-rank mate in most positions, though a couple of boards are simply missed material wins.

391.label: In the opening, plays an undefended bishop to a square where it is immediately captured for free, losing a full piece.

382.label: The player repeatedly skips a stronger tactical move that wins material (frequently the opponent's queen) or forces mate, settling instead for a materially-safe but inferior move.

390.chip: Wastes tempo on flank pawn push
390.label: A slow flank/wing pawn advance (usually an a-, b-, or c-pawn, intended as queenside expansion) wastes a critical tempo, letting the opponent refute by winning material or seizing the initiative; the exact punishment varies across boards.

383.label: In already-lost endgames (often passed-pawn/rook situations), the player makes the decisive losing move that converts a difficult-but-fightable position into forced mate or hopelessness — by hanging the rook, trading it for a pawn, missing a saving capture, or neglecting king safety — instead of the one resilient defensive move.

386.label: In a winning position the player repeatedly fails to grab the opponent's undefended hanging rook—playing a king move, a check, or a lesser capture instead—throwing away a decisive material edge (one board the free piece is a queen, not a rook).

389.label: Plays a slow, materially-safe move (often in an endgame) that wastes the tempo needed for a decisive shot — frequently a pawn break like f5/f4/d4 but also key captures — converting a winning position into a draw.

387.chip: Squanders forced win, gives up queen
387.label: In a winning or forced-mating position the player throws away the win by giving up material — most often hanging the queen to a pawn capture (boards 1-4,9), sometimes a rook (10) or a queen trade (7) — converting a forced mate/win into merely winning, though several flagged boards (5,6,8) are actually trivial non-blunders.

378.label: From a roughly equal position the player pursues their own plan (usually advancing a pawn, sometimes a greedy capture) instead of the one move that neutralizes the opponent's decisive threat — most often an enemy passed pawn about to promote, sometimes a mating attack or an available free capture.

393.label: A slow pawn push—almost always one that kicks an enemy bishop to 'win a tempo'—ignores an immediate decisive threat, wasting the critical tempo and letting the opponent crash through with mate or winning material.

397.label: A knight move that attacks the enemy queen hoping to gain a tempo backfires when the queen repositions to a superior square (or counterattacks with check), usually costing tempo and in several cases hanging the knight outright.

400.chip: Missed Qa4+/Qa5+ check winning piece (loose bishop)
400.label: In every opening position the player passed up a winning queen check (Qa4+ or Qa5+) that forks the uncastled king and a loose bishop on b4/b5, leaving material on the board.

395.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own material hanging to immediate or near-immediate capture—the hung piece varies (knight, rook, queen, bishop, pawn), so the invariant is self-inflicted material loss, most often in the opening with a knight somewhere in the tactic.

398.label: In the opening the player repeatedly makes a quiet developing/retreating move and misses a free one-move capture of an undefended enemy piece, almost always a bishop (9/10).

392.label: The player makes a capture in the wrong move-order (or grabs the wrong piece), overlooking a refutation—usually an intermezzo, intermediate check, or left-undefended piece—that costs their own material and flips a winning position to losing/equal; the hung piece varies (queen, knight, pawn, exchange), so it's 'material' rather than one specific piece.

402.label: Voluntarily exchanges a powerfully-placed, usually centralized piece (a knight in ~8/10) for a passive enemy piece, throwing away a winning advantage by missing a far stronger tactical or positional continuation rather than actually hanging material.

405.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the king greedily captures a pawn but steps off the critical file/blockade, letting the opponent's passed pawn promote unstoppably.

407.label: In all ten positions the player had a forced checkmate available—almost always a queen capture/check leading to mate—but played a routine or materially-safe move instead, squandering the win.

399.label: An endgame move that loses or trades away material (or skips a material-winning capture), converting a defensible or winning ending into a lost one — direction and piece vary across boards.

408.label: In all 10 positions the player had a winning knight fork available (typically Nxc2+/Nxc7+/Nxf3+ against an uncastled king) but instead played a quiet/passive move, letting the opponent escape and squandering a winning advantage.

404.label: In the endgame, a king or knight move leaves the player's own knight undefended (or trades it for a pawn), self-inflicting a decisive material loss.

385.label: In a winning-or-holdable position the player chose a quiet/non-forcing move (usually a pawn push) instead of the engine's strong forcing CHECK — the best move is a check on 9 of 10 boards (Bd4+, Be6+, g5+, Bxf4+, Bf3+, Bc4+, Qf5+), most often a bishop check — though the underlying error is genuinely mixed: ~7 boards are squandered wins, while boards 8–9 actually hang the player's own queen/rook and board 10 trades into a lost ending.

406.label: A materially-safe but passive move throws away a clearly winning (or large) advantage by declining the one winning continuation—in 8/10 cases a pawn capture, often en passant—turning a won position into equal or losing.

394.label: Plays a purposeless check—almost always with the queen—that throws away the position, sometimes hanging the queen outright but just as often abandoning a key defensive square (or skipping a win) and walking into mate.

396.chip: Declines the one decisive winning move
396.label: In each top position the player had a winning/advantageous position with exactly one decisive move available (best-move-wins-material 100%) and chose a different move instead, squandering the advantage—roughly half the time the played move itself hangs material and half the time it merely skips the winning tactic, with no single piece or mechanism recurring across boards.

414.label: In winning or drawn pawn/king endgames, plays an imprecise king or pawn advance that throws away the win or draw instead of the precise winning continuation — no piece is hung, and on two boards the move is actually optimal, so the pattern is mixed.

417.label: Captures/simplifies into a losing endgame—usually trading the last active rook or queen into a lost king-and-pawn (or minor-piece) ending where the opponent's king and pawn majority decide.

413.label: Plays a forcing check (100% of boards) that throws away its own material — the hung piece varies (queen, rook, knight, or bishop) so it's just 'a piece', and two endgame cases are active-rook trades that surrender the position rather than literal hangs.

411.label: In every opening position the player fails to play the forcing queen exchange Qxd8+/Qxd1+ with check on the open d-file, instead making a developing/grabbing/retreating move that surrenders the advantage or loses material.

419.label: Player relocates a piece (usually a minor piece — bishop in 5/10, knight in 3/10) to a square where it either hangs/loses material (boards 3,4,7,9) or becomes passive/overextended (boards 1,5,6,8,10), squandering their standing; the feature is genuinely mixed between material hangs and positional misplacements rather than a clean single-piece hang.

409.label: Most positions show the player making a greedy or careless move—usually a rook capture or rook relocation—that hangs the piece or removes a key defender (back-rank/king cover) for self-inflicted material loss, with a rook featuring in the decisive play of nearly every board; however ~3 of 10 instead simply miss a winning continuation (including throwing away won endgames), so direction and the hung piece are not uniform.

423.label: A materially-safe but slow/routine move skips a forcing winning tactic — in nearly every case a knight fork (Nb5/Nd5→Nc7+/Nb6+, or Ne3+) that would win material — letting the advantage evaporate (one board is a non-knight Bxb1 combination).

418.label: In the opening the player makes a developing/retreating move that loses material—usually by abandoning a defender or ignoring an existing tactical threat (fork, hanging piece, or capture)—with the hung unit varying widely (pawn, bishop, knight, queen, rook); a minority (2/10) are instead pure tempo-losses that miss a winning tactic rather than hang material.

415.chip: Trades queens into lost position (passed pawn)
415.label: The player voluntarily trades/captures queens to simplify, but the resulting position is lost because the opponent gets a promoting passed pawn (often with check) or a winning pawn endgame.

421.chip: Hangs material by skipping rook trade
421.label: On an open file, the player avoids the saving rook exchange (the best move is almost always Rxa8/Rxc8/Rxc1/Rxb8) and instead plays a natural-looking move, allowing a tactic that costs them their own material a few moves later.

410.label: An opening move that ignores or walks into a bishop pin (Bg4/Bg5/Bb5), allowing the opponent to win the player's own material (knight, bishop, queen, or rook) within a few moves.

425.label: In (mostly pawn) endgames, a king or pawn move mishandles the structure—wrong move order, locking the position, releasing tension, or skipping a key capture—squandering the draw or worsening the loss without any material being hung.

416.label: A move that loses the player's own material—a pawn, bishop, knight, or rook depending on the board—usually to an overlooked knight tactic, with two positions being closer to pure positional/tempo errors.

424.label: Moves a piece — most often the queen — off a critical defensive square, abandoning protection of its own material (or king) and getting punished by losing material (or being mated) in the refutation.

420.label: In every position the player skips the decisive best move (usually a forcing check or capture) and instead plays a greedy material grab, tempo-waster, or passive move that squanders a winning/equal position.

429.chip: Missed free capture of enemy piece
429.label: The player repeatedly makes a passive/non-capturing move instead of grabbing an undefended enemy piece (often the queen, sometimes a rook), squandering a winning material advantage.

422.label: In already losing-or-drawn positions, the player makes an over-ambitious active move (capture, check, or aggressive centralization) that either hangs material/walks into a tactic (~half the boards) or simply loses tempo by abandoning a defensive duty (~half), with no single recurring piece or motif.

430.label: In every position the player throws away a decisive, materially-safe win—most often a forced checkmate against an exposed king—by choosing a quiet or non-forcing move instead of the crushing continuation, so the recurring mistake is an omission of a forced win rather than hanging material.

426.label: In the opening the player passes up a free capture of a hanging enemy piece (usually a queen take like Qxd5/Qxg4) and instead plays a pawn/developing move that merely attacks it, letting it escape.

433.label: The queen greedily snatches a pawn (most often b2 or d4) while behind in development, and the grab is refuted by tactics that either trap the queen or win back more material than the pawn was worth.

401.label: A quiet opening developing/prophylactic move that ignores an attack on the player's own knight, leaving it to be captured, traded for a pawn, or trapped (9/10 lose a knight; one loses a rook).

432.label: Plays a passive, tempo-losing king or pawn move in the endgame instead of the urgent capture or defense, letting the opponent consolidate, promote, or mate.

436.label: Fires on delivering a check in a winning position; in ~6/10 cases this is a missed win where a quiet capture of a hanging piece or a faster forced mate was available, but the other ~4/10 are equal-value (0cp) best-move checks, so the feature really tracks 'plays a check' rather than a clean blunder.

428.label: Fires on opening positions built around the Qb3/Bc4-vs-Qb6/Bc5 queen-bishop battery and the c3/c6 knight — a knight is the decisive tactical piece on nearly every board, but direction is mixed: ~4/10 miss the winning Na4/Na5 double-attack while ~6/10 hang material (queen, minor, or the knight itself) by mishandling the c3-knight tension.

437.chip: Hangs queen on open diagonal (bishop captures)
437.label: The played move leaves the player's own queen en prise on a fully open diagonal, where it is captured for free by the opponent's bishop in every one of the ten positions.

434.chip: Passive move ignores enemy rook (2nd/7th rank)
434.label: A slow or passive move (often a flank pawn push) that fails to challenge the opponent's dominant rook on the second/seventh rank, squandering the player's advantage and sometimes dropping material a few moves later.

427.chip: Hangs own material, blows winning position
427.label: A self-inflicted move that loses the player's own material — usually hanging a piece (frequently the queen, but also rook, bishop or a pawn in endgames) and squandering a winning or drawn position; piece is too varied to name and one board (#4) isn't even a blunder.

435.label: The player makes a rook move—usually a check—that an enemy bishop simply captures (often blocking the check), losing the rook in an already-difficult endgame; 7/10 fit this, with two boards being missed captures and one a false positive.

439.label: A materially-safe but passive queen move (occasionally a rook) that skips an available winning capture or tactic, squandering a winning or equal position; the won target varies (bishop, pawn, queen, knight, even mate) so no single piece is named.

443.label: The player grabs material with a capture (usually a rook/queen, knight or bishop doing the capturing) when a forced checkmate — or in two cases a crushing mating attack — was available, trading away the win for a 'merely winning' material edge.

447.label: In the endgame the player gives a check or grabs a pawn with the rook, and the opposing king simply captures it — hanging the rook for little or no compensation.

440.label: A critical move that throws away a winning or drawn position—most often by allowing the player's own material (queen, rook, knight, or pawn, the piece varies) to be captured within a few moves of the refutation, though several boards are pure missed wins/saves rather than direct hangs.

444.chip: Missed winning tactic, plays passive move
444.label: From a better or winning middlegame, the player passes up an available forcing tactical win (mate, fork, or intermediate check) and instead plays a slow, passive, or greedy move that squanders the advantage.

431.label: In the opening, the player repeatedly plays a passive or misdirected move instead of the correct central pawn capture/break, failing to resolve the tension and squandering a winning or equal position.

446.label: Player hangs own material by failing to neutralize the long-diagonal fianchetto bishop (usually missing the freeing ...Bxg2/Bxg7 trade), letting the opponent win a piece or the exchange along the a1-h8/h1-a8 diagonal.

445.chip: Hangs own piece in endgame (king move)
445.label: In an endgame the player makes a non-saving move (usually a king walk) that leaves their own piece — most often a rook, sometimes the queen — hanging to immediate capture next move.

442.label: While already winning, the player repeatedly fails to grab a hanging or undefended enemy piece (most often the queen), playing a quiet move instead and letting the free material—and the win—slip away.

453.label: In every position the player skips an immediate free capture of a hanging enemy piece (bishop, queen, or rook) and instead plays a routine move, letting the enemy piece escape to safety and surrendering a winning material edge.

438.label: In the opening the player throws away their own material—frequently an unsound bishop sacrifice on f7/f2, but also knights and a trapped piece—ending up down a piece with no compensation.

458.label: Promotes a pawn to a queen on a square where it is immediately captured for free, hanging the new queen in an endgame (underpromotion or king move was needed).

454.label: In an already-won endgame, plays a tempo-wasting check or pawn push instead of the cleanest winning line — usually immediate promotion — rather than hanging any material.

450.label: In a winning endgame the player throws the win away with a move that walks into a simple capture, losing their own material — but the captured unit varies (queen, rook, or an advancing pawn), so no single piece can be named.

441.label: Player consistently substitutes a slow, natural-looking move for the precise forcing continuation (often a check or correct move-order), but the result splits ~50/50 between merely squandering a win/draw and walking into a multi-move refutation that costs material (pawn, bishop, or queen, varying).

449.label: The player repeatedly avoids the strong rook capture / exchange sacrifice (most often Rxd4) that eliminates a powerful enemy knight—usually a centralized d4-knight—either skipping a clear win or, in a few cases, choosing a move that then loses material to that knight.

448.label: From a winning or clearly better position the player passes up the available winning continuation and plays an inferior move—most often an unnecessary capture/trade or premature check that relieves the opponent—throwing the advantage away (mechanism varies board-to-board: bad trade, missed tactic/mate, or move-order error, with only one true own-material hang).

452.label: The player makes a 'winning material' or 'simplifying' capture/trade that overlooks the opponent's refutation—either a recapture/zwischenzug/promotion that nets material back (boards 1,7,9,10) or a queen/rook trade that drops into a lost king-and-pawn endgame (boards 2,3,4,5)—with two outliers (a pawn push and a defender-removing rook move that allow mate/breakthrough).

455.label: Plays a backfiring queen check that loses material—most often hanging the queen outright or via a forced losing trade, though occasionally only a positional/other-piece (knight) loss results.

451.label: In every top position the player blunders away a winning or drawing position by failing to find the single best move — usually a winning capture/exchange, sometimes the one saving defense — with the piece involved varying (queen, rook, pawn, knight).

465.label: In every one of the ten positions the player had a forced back-rank checkmate available (usually a rook check on the open file/8th rank, sometimes a queen) but instead played a materially safe move that threw away the mate.

457.chip: Hangs own piece via faulty capture/sac
457.label: The player repeatedly loses their OWN material — via an unsound sacrifice (Bxh7, Bxh2) or a tempting capture/move that drops material within a move or two (Nxe5, Bxf3 hanging the queen, exd5, Nb5 fork) — but the hung unit varies (bishop, knight, pawn, even queen), so it's 'a piece' rather than one specific piece.

463.chip: Greedy hxg capture opens own h-file
463.label: Grabs a piece on g4/g5 with the h-pawn, ripping open the h-file toward its own castled king and inviting a devastating attack.

459.label: The player ignores an immediate threat (usually an enemy bishop, often fianchettoed, attacking a rook) and plays elsewhere, dropping own material — most often the exchange/rook, sometimes a minor piece — for nothing.

468.label: A queen lands on d4/d5 (usually grabbing a knight) on the open d-file in the opening and is simply recaptured, losing the queen for a minor piece.

466.chip: Squanders won middlegame, misses only move (queen)
466.label: In a winning middlegame the player makes a natural-looking active rook/queen move that throws away the advantage by missing the single saving continuation (most often a queen reposition such as Qh2/Qa4/Qh3+), with the move outright hanging material in about 3/10 cases.

462.label: In a better/winning position the player abandons the decisive continuation and plays an inferior move that throws the advantage away — with the queen central to the decisive play (it's the moved piece in 6/10 and the key attacking/defending piece in ~9/10) — but the refutation is genuinely mixed between missed wins (Rxf4, Qxd2, Rxe2, Rc1, Rxa4/Rxc3) and self-inflicted losses (king-weakening allowing mate, hung e6-rook, queen-for-rook trade), so no single 'Missed X' or 'Hangs X' direction holds.

460.label: In nearly every board the player makes an inferior rook move when the engine wanted the classic rook-doubling/seventh-rank maneuver, but the outcome splits roughly evenly between outright hanging material (loose pieces, back-rank/mate) and merely forfeiting the stronger rook plan, so a human should confirm direction.

470.label: The player makes a plausible-but-irrelevant move (centralizing, fleeing, developing, advancing a pawn, or grabbing material) while ignoring the opponent's immediate decisive threat, self-inflicting the loss — most often by neglecting its own king and walking into a forced mate (6/10), otherwise by leaving material hanging (4/10).

464.label: Plays a materially-safe but passive/retreating move that overlooks the engine's best active continuation — usually a forcing check that wins or saves the game.

456.label: In already-losing/difficult middlegames the player makes a passive, non-forcing move (often a pawn push on the wrong wing) that ignores the single critical resource — a saving capture (exf6, Qxf6), essential counterplay (bxa3, bxa4), or a needed defense — but the resulting damage is genuinely mixed: forced mate by removing a king defender (boards 1,8,10), outright material loss (3,5,6), positional/endgame omission (4,7,9), and one near-equivalent non-blunder (board 2), so no single error type or piece dominates and it needs human review.

461.chip: Hangs major piece taking passed pawn

478.label: In an endgame, the player leaves a piece en prise—most often a bishop (with a rook and knight among the cases)—either by a move-order slip, an unsound capture/trade, or putting the piece on a square covered by the enemy king/knight, losing material for nothing and turning a tenable position into a lost one.

484.chip: Imprecise king play in won endgame
484.label: In winning endgames (mostly king-and-pawn), the player makes a tempo-losing or imprecise move — usually a suboptimal king advance or a pawn push instead of correct king activity ('king-first'/keeping the king near the key pawn) — and while a couple of cases throw the win toward a draw (boards 1, 10), most flagged moves are only minor inaccuracies or even 0cp non-mistakes, so the feature is a mixed 'winning-endgame imprecision' detector with the king central to nearly every board.

477.label: In an already-lost middlegame (100% losing before the move), the player makes a self-destructive move that hastens defeat — most often giving away a piece (knight, bishop, rook, or queen, frequently the last defender) for a pawn or an empty check, with the remaining cases being king-weakening pawn pushes (g4) or simplifications that simply allow a forced mate.

481.label: Plays a passive or tempo-wasting move that fails to resolve the central pawn tension, letting the opponent strike with a favorable central break (usually ...fxe5/...fxe4) that wins material or rips open lines toward the king.

492.label: From a winning position the player plays a slow/routine move and overlooks a forcing tactical shot — frequently a check or fork — that would have won material outright.

490.label: Fires on winning endgame positions (often king-centralization or queen-check maneuvers), but the 'mistake' is inconsistent — one bad check loses the win, two lose only mate-efficiency, two are actually optimal moves, and one hangs the exchange, so there is no single clean recurring error.

486.label: In a winning middlegame the player makes a quiet/positional move and overlooks a simple winning capture — almost always a pawn grabbing a hanging enemy piece (most often the queen) — squandering a decisive material advantage.

493.label: In every position the player chose a quiet pawn push or a greedy capture instead of an available forcing check (a winning attack/mate or a saving perpetual), squandering the critical tempo.

483.label: In king-and-pawn / passed-pawn endgames the player routes the king to the wrong square (or pushes a pawn out of order), failing to catch the opponent's passer or escort its own — though several boards show only negligible cp loss in already-decided positions.

496.label: Captures a pawn (usually on a2) for material instead of playing the available forced mate or winning continuation, throwing away the win.

494.label: In tense/losing positions the player has a bishop that can capture the enemy queen (typically a forced Bxd8/Bxe8 trade) but instead repositions the queen or another piece, both declining the capture and leaving the bishop hanging, losing material.

488.chip: Quiet move skips decisive bishop play
488.label: In winning/balanced opening positions the player plays a natural quiet move (pawn push, king/rook shuffle, developing move) instead of the one concrete move the position demanded — almost always a bishop capture or trade — either missing a winning bishop capture (Bxb5/Bxb4) or skipping a forced defensive bishop exchange (Bxd5/Bxg5), so direction is mixed and a human should confirm.

499.label: Instead of the only resolving pawn capture/exchange, the player makes a passive king or bishop move and lets the opponent create a decisive passed pawn.

489.label: In 8/10 positions the player chooses a natural, greedy, or pointless-check move instead of the one precise tactical shot that wins or traps the opponent's queen, squandering a winning advantage; the queen is the tactical target in nearly every board, but two cases (Kd8, Bg4) instead simply hang the player's own piece, so the boards aren't a clean single-mistake set.

500.chip: Hangs material with own pawn break
500.label: A premature pawn advance that wrecks the player's own structure/center and loses their own material by force over the next few moves (the lost material varies — usually a pawn, sometimes a rook or the exchange).

487.label: On nearly every board the player overlooked the critical forcing line — usually a forced mate or decisive king-side tactic — either failing to deliver the win or, by weakening their own king's shelter (often with f3), walking straight into checkmate; the direction is mixed (offense vs. defense) so it warrants review.

501.label: On all 10 boards the player passed up an immediately available material-winning capture (usually winning the exchange) — playing a pawn-grab, a check, or a slow move that let the attacked enemy piece escape — and in every case the winning capture is made by a knight.

491.label: In a winning (occasionally equal) position the player picks a tempting check, greedy/lesser capture, or pawn push instead of the clean material-winning move — often ignoring an outright hanging enemy piece (Nxf7, Bxb7, Rxh6, Qxd8, Bxb2, Rxg2) — and ends up hanging its own material within 1-3 moves (8/10 boards), with the rest being a safe move that skips a forced win.

495.chip: Abandons passed pawn, squanders won endgame
495.label: In a winning rook endgame, the player abandons or fails to support a decisive passed pawn (often by greedily grabbing a different pawn), throwing away the win.

497.label: The player makes a capture (often Bxf6/Nxc3) that removes a defender or ignores a threat, losing their own queen in ~6 boards and allowing mate/king collapse in the rest.

502.label: In winning positions the player skips the available decisive/forcing winning move for a quiet or routine one, throwing away the advantage — about half the time the opponent's refutation then wins material back (queen/exchange/pawn/knight, no consistent piece), the rest are simply missed winning shots, and one board (#10) isn't even a blunder, so the feature is mixed between 'missed win' and 'hangs material in the refutation.'

510.label: Player moves a knight (often from a strong outpost) onto a square covered by an enemy piece, losing a full piece for nothing—or in a couple cases trading the key knight away to its ruin.

509.label: Plays a materially-safe but non-winning move, missing an available forcing check that wins material (often a fork) in the endgame.

498.label: In the endgame, the player captures a passed pawn but allows an immediate recapture that wins back the capturing piece, throwing away a winning or drawn position.

506.label: Plays a slow, non-forcing move and overlooks an available forcing resource—frequently a check or back-rank sacrifice—that would have won or saved the game.

503.label: The player repeatedly throws away a forced winning tactic (often a back-rank mate or queen sacrifice) by grabbing a natural capture or simplifying trade instead.

504.label: From a winning/favorable middlegame the player throws away the advantage—most often (7/10) by hanging a piece to a tactical refutation, usually the queen but sometimes a rook, with the remaining boards instead missing a winning capture or playing an inaccuracy that allows unfavorable simplification.

514.chip: Missed forced win (often mate via check)
514.label: The player makes a materially-safe but slow/greedy move that throws away a decisive winning continuation — most often a forced checkmate available via a forcing check — rather than hanging their own material.

517.label: A move (usually a fianchetto pawn push) clears a long diagonal, leaving an undefended corner rook to be captured for free by the enemy bishop (queen in one case).

508.chip: Slow move loses to tactic (missed queen trade)
508.label: Plays a slow, non-forcing move — frequently skipping the critical queen trade (Qxd1+/Qxd8+/Qxe2) — instead of the forcing line, allowing a multi-move refutation that wins material (or, in one case, mates), so the boards share the 'tempo-losing move punished tactically' pattern but vary in which piece falls.

469.label: An opening move that self-inflicts material loss—hanging a piece outright or via an open-diagonal queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+) that forks king and rook—though the specific piece varies (bishop/knight) and two boards are instead positional or a missed win.

505.label: A king-safety blunder: the played move removes a critical defender (often the king itself), exposing the king to a decisive attack—frequently forced checkmate—or losing material to the resulting invasion.

515.label: The played move loses the player's own material to a simple recapture or short tactic — a piece (knight, rook, or bishop, varying by board) hangs, almost always in the middlegame.

511.label: A move that throws away the player's own material or winning advantage — typically hanging a piece or botching a trade/capture (a rook most often, but the piece varies), self-inflicted across nearly all boards.

519.chip: Hangs own piece in opening (unsound sac)
519.label: In the opening the player loses their own material via an unsound sacrifice or illusory fork (often Bxf7+) that the opponent simply captures — the hung unit varies (bishop/knight/pawn), so it's 'a piece', not a specific one.

516.label: From a winning/better position the player makes a move that self-inflicts material loss to a simple refutation (and twice walks into mate); the hung unit varies across boards (pawn, knight, bishop, rook), so it's 'a piece/material' rather than any specific piece.

523.label: In the opening, the player makes a move that abandons or exposes their own material (bishop, knight, queen, or rook depending on the board) — leaving it hanging to an immediate or near-immediate capture and losing a near-equal position.

512.label: In a winning/mating position the player chooses an inferior move (a king walk, greedy capture, or quiet move) that squanders a forced win — most often a forced mate, sometimes a queen or exchange — instead of the available forcing continuation.

529.label: The player moves or leaves a rook on an undefended square where an enemy minor piece captures it for free, throwing away a winning (mostly endgame) position by hanging the rook.

527.label: An aggressive rook move (almost always a check) that throws away the rook for little or nothing, frequently captured/refuted by an enemy knight.

521.label: The feature fires on middlegame moves that overlook a hanging-piece tactic, but the direction is genuinely mixed: in ~6/10 boards the move self-inflicts the loss by moving a defender or opening a line so the player's own piece/pawn hangs (e.g. d5 unguards e5, Nxg4 opens Bxe6+, Qc5 exposes the f8 rook to a skewer, Bh6/f4 leave a piece undefended), while in ~4/10 it's an omission that fails to grab the opponent's hanging piece or resolve tension (Qxc5, Qxc3, Qxd6, Bxd3 missed).

518.label: The played move (developing, pushing, capturing, or castling) overlooks an opponent pawn break/lever — e4, d4/d5, a5, c4, or b4 — that punishes by winning material or seizing decisive initiative; a pawn is the decisive instrument in 9 of 10 refutations, though the player's own error type is mixed (missed win, hung piece, positional/king-safety slip).

526.label: From a winning position the player makes a self-inflicting move that squanders the advantage—most often a king move walking into a forced mate, but also moves that hang material to a fork, discovered attack, back-rank mate, or simply lose tempo—with the mechanism and piece varying board to board (and one board a false positive).

513.label: In the opening the player makes a slow/passive move (flank pawn, premature queen, or passive development) instead of the thematic central break ...d5 (or e5), surrendering the center and the advantage; ~7/10 boards fit this, while two are unrelated knight hangs (Nh5, Nd5).

530.label: Plays a quiet, non-forcing move that throws away an available forced checkmate or decisive winning line — almost always a rook check (frequently a rook landing on the 7th/back rank) was the move that should have been played.

531.label: The player makes a move that leaves one of their own pieces (knight, bishop, or rook — it varies) undefended, allowing the opponent's queen to capture it for free (often with check), losing material mostly in the opening.

507.label: A materially-safe but passive move that skips a forced win — overwhelmingly a checkmate or mating queen-check (often mate-in-one) — instead of delivering it.

525.label: In each already-lost position the only defense was a forced queen trade/capture, but the player declined it (king/queen/knight move) and walked into forced checkmate (once simply hanging the queen).

533.label: The player blunders a piece—a knight in 9 of 10 cases, typically jumping to an undefended d4 (or d5) square—where the opponent's queen simply captures it for free in the opening.

536.chip: King to wrong side, abandons zone
536.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the king walks to the wrong side—usually to grab a distant peripheral pawn—abandoning the critical zone and converting a win into a draw or a draw into a loss; two of the ten boards are false positives where the chosen king move was actually optimal.

532.label: Across nearly all positions the player fails to push or directly support the decisive passed pawn, instead playing a slower king/rook move or grabbing a lesser pawn, squandering the win.

528.label: In positions where a decisive material-winning move existed (SEE floor 100%, often endgames), the player instead either hangs a piece/pawn (boards 3,4,6,9, plus trade-downs 2,10) or skips the winning capture/promotion/tempo move (boards 1,5,7,8) — it fires on both hung-material and missed-win cases rather than one clean direction or piece.

538.chip: Missed faster win in won endgame
538.label: In a clearly winning endgame, the player chooses a slow/quiet move (with various pieces) instead of the forcing, often checking continuation that wins fastest — though two boards are actually optimal and two involve hanging a piece, so the pattern is mixed.

534.label: The move moves or trades away a piece performing a critical defensive/blockading role, leaving own material hanging or letting a passed pawn promote — the specific piece varies (rook most often involved), and 2 of 10 are instead pure missed wins (mate/fork).

535.label: An aggressive or careless move (often a queen sortie or rook invasion that abandons a defender) walks into a refutation costing the player's OWN material over 1-3 moves — but the lost unit varies (knight, bishop, rook, or exchange), so it's just 'a piece'; ~2 of 10 are instead a missed win/positional misplacement rather than a hang.

522.label: A passive/misplaced queen move in the opening (most often leaving d5 instead of the resolving tactic Bxf3) squanders equality and loses tempo, usually punished by White's d5 break with tempo on the c6-knight.

543.label: A (usually king) move that abandons control/blockade of the opponent's passed pawn, letting it run to promotion in the endgame.

549.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player moves the king to the wrong square, surrendering the opposition/blockade and converting a dead draw into a lost (usually mating) position.

542.label: An opening move that fails to contest the center, letting the opponent's central pawn break (d4/d5/e4) seize space or win material — the punished piece and mechanism vary too much to name one piece.

524.label: In a winning middlegame the player plays an inferior, often greedy or non-forcing move that throws away the advantage—frequently allowing a back-rank/king-safety mate or a material-recovering fork, or simply missing the forcing win.

520.label: Develops the bishop (usually ...Bg4) to harass the enemy queen, but it sits undefended and is won by a knight-check zwischenzug (Nxf6+/Nxf3+ then Qxg4/Qxg5) — occasionally dropping the b7 pawn instead.

548.label: A move that leaves one of the player's own pieces undefended—usually by removing its defender or stepping into a tactic—handing material to the opponent; a knight features in nearly every position, though the hung piece itself varies (knight, bishop, queen).

537.label: An opening move (often a tempo-grabbing pawn push or development) that opens a line or undefends a square, letting the enemy queen win material or deliver mate — the hung piece varies (rook/bishop/pawn/king), but the queen is always the punisher.
