544.label: Across all ten boards the saving line was a forced queen trade (Qxd4/Qxc5/Qxd5/Qxf7 etc.) which the player declined, and the chosen move instead leaves their own queen hanging or walks into a mating net — but since a couple of cases are bishop-hangs or pure checkmates rather than literal queen captures, the exact piece is fuzzy and warrants review.

550.label: In a losing position the player fires a reflexive rook check that, in most cases, simply hands the rook over for free (Kxrook → mate) and otherwise just wastes a tempo and improves the enemy king.

553.label: A check (frequently a speculative Bxf7+/Greek-Gift sacrifice) that loses the player's own piece for little or no compensation, where the simple recapture/quiet move was correct.

541.label: In mostly-losing/tense middlegames the player plays a slow, greedy, or non-forcing move that ignores a decisive opponent threat — skipping the required forcing/defensive resource — and is punished by forced mate (1,2,8,9), a hung queen (5,6), or major material loss (3,4,10), with the queen central as mater, victim, or missed savior on nearly every board (board 7 is a milder tempo-loss outlier).

546.label: A purposeless/passive rook move that wastes a tempo and parks the rook on a useless square (a-file, h1, or the 7th rank) in a rook endgame, failing the critical defensive or active task the position demanded.

540.label: Player makes a tempting but losing capture of an enemy centrally-posted piece (a knight in ~8/10, captured with the bishop in most), giving up a key piece or walking into a refutation that backfires into material loss, a winning tactic for the opponent, or positional collapse.

561.label: In the opening the player skips a crushing queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+) that exploits the diagonal opened by a missing f-pawn, throwing away a winning advantage.

551.label: Plays a tempting rook move — frequently a check or grab — that voluntarily sacrifices or hangs the rook for inadequate compensation, losing material.

554.label: In a queen-on-b6 opening, White plays a quiet developing move (usually Be3, vacating c1) that abandons defense and loses own material—most often the b2 pawn—instead of the resolving dxc5 break.

539.chip: Missed queen trade on open d-file
539.label: In every opening position the player fails to resolve the queen confrontation on the open d-file with the forcing Qxd1+/Qxd8+ exchange, instead developing or pushing a pawn — squandering the castling/tempo advantage and often hanging a pawn (or bishop) in the resulting refutation.

559.label: In most positions the player passes up a decisive forcing continuation—frequently a rook check/mate or rook penetration that wins material or mates—and instead plays a slow, non-forcing move (two of ten boards instead simply hang the player's own knight).

555.chip: Premature pawn push over king play
555.label: In pawn endgames the player makes a tempo-losing or structurally premature pawn/king move (commonly advancing a pawn that blocks its own king instead of centralizing or timing a break), losing eval without hanging material — though ~3 of the flagged king moves are actually optimal.

558.label: An inaccurate endgame move — often a tempo-wasting check or a bad trade — that throws away a winning or drawing position, with the specific mechanism (tempo loss, wrong trade, hung rook, missed mate) varying board to board.

556.label: In a winning endgame the player gives a purposeless check (usually with the rook) that only lets the opponent's king centralize or escape, squandering tempo and conversion instead of promoting or advancing the passed pawn.

557.label: A materially-safe move that skips a forced checkmate or decisive king attack — frequently grabbing a pawn/piece instead of delivering the winning blow.

565.label: In a winning position the player repeatedly skips the one forcing capture of the opponent's centralized knight on d4/d5 (almost always Nxd4), playing a safe but inferior move and squandering the advantage.

560.label: A queen move that offers or initiates a queen trade (or challenges the enemy queen) which backfires — usually losing material to a follow-up tactic, sometimes surrendering counterplay or even allowing mate.

564.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a result-losing move—usually misplacing the king or choosing the wrong pawn break/trade—that converts a won or drawn position into a draw or loss, with no material actually hung.

566.label: Across the top positions the player repeatedly fails to play a material-winning queen grab of a loose pawn (most often Qxg2, also Qxb7/Qxg7) and instead chooses a quiet developing/structural move — though in a few boards the played move actually hangs the player's own piece, making the direction somewhat mixed.

563.label: A move that loses the player's own material to a tactical refutation; the hung piece varies across positions (rook, knight, queen, bishop), and two of the ten boards are actually missed wins rather than hangs.

568.label: In winning opening positions White plays a natural developing/castling move and misses the crushing queen centralization (usually Qd5) that exploits the weak f7 square via a double attack.

562.label: From a better/critical position the player picks a tempting but inferior move (often a capture or a queen/knight centralization) that throws away the edge; the mechanism is genuinely mixed — roughly 6/10 lose material to a tactic in the refutation (knight, queen, pawn, or exchange, with the queen most frequently the piece that ends up lost or misplaced) and roughly 4/10 simply lose tempo and let the opponent castle or consolidate, so no single 'Hangs X' or position-state cleanly fits.

574.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player repeatedly makes a natural king-walk or pawn-push instead of the single precise resource (a capture, knight relocation like Na4, or promotion tactic) needed to win or hold, squandering the advantage rather than hanging material.

547.label: The player captures to simplify (usually trading a rook or queen) into an endgame that is actually worse or outright lost, converting winning/drawn positions into draws or losses — most often by swapping into a lost king-and-pawn endgame.

567.label: In the opening the player repeatedly overlooks a free enemy queen left en prise (a hanging bishop in one case) and plays a quiet developing move instead of the winning capture, throwing away a decisive material advantage.

577.label: The player had a forced checkmate available (almost always a back-rank mate) but played a materially-safe capture or developing move instead, squandering the immediate knockout while staying winning.

552.label: In winning positions the player repeatedly fails to grab a hanging enemy piece—most often a free queen—playing a quiet developing move instead; 2/10 are instead pure self-hangs, so direction is slightly mixed but the dominant event is a missed winning capture.

571.chip: Loses own material on tempting check/capture
571.label: An aggressive-looking check or capture that costs the player their own material — hung, trapped, or badly traded — though the piece varies (knight/queen/bishop) and two of the ten instead miss a winning capture.

576.label: In every position (all opening), the player makes a move that loses their own material—most often a bishop, but also a knight, queen, or pawn—either hanging it outright or dropping it within 2-3 moves of the refutation; since the hung piece varies, it's 'a piece/material' rather than one specific piece.

570.chip: Active move neglects defense, loses to tactic
570.label: A seemingly active rook or queen move that abandons a defensive duty and loses material or the king to a multi-move tactic in 7/10 boards, though 3 boards are instead missed winning shots (Nef3+, Ne4 fork, Nxg4) and the hung/missed target varies, so the feature is partly mixed between defensive oversight and missed wins.

581.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (often knight)
581.label: An unsound aggressive move (frequently a knight check) drops the player's own undefended piece for no compensation in the opening, where the simple recapture refutes it.

583.chip: Hangs own piece via greedy capture
583.label: A capture (or infiltration) that self-inflicts material loss — most often the queen, recaptured or won after the moved piece abandons a defensive/blocking duty (twice this removal even allows mate).

584.label: In every position the player skips a winning tactic—in 8/10 a knight fork that wins material (exchange/piece)—by choosing a natural-looking trade, capture, or developing move, squandering a winning advantage.

586.label: Plays a natural-looking developing/flank move instead of the winning central pawn break d5 (or d4 for White), which would challenge the c4-bishop or open lines to win material.

569.chip: Trades last defender into lost endgame
569.label: In the endgame, surrenders the player's last defending piece (usually a rook, sometimes the queen) via a losing capture/trade or outright hang, converting a drawable or merely-difficult position into a lost one.

573.label: In a winning middlegame the player overlooks a forcing tactical shot — most often a bishop capture/check exploiting king-queen alignment — and instead plays a weaker queen or pawn move that squanders much of the advantage.

575.label: Mostly loses own material—typically a bishop or central pawn—by mishandling the unresolved central pawn tension (cxd5/dxe4-type exchanges), though 2-3 boards are instead missed captures of an undefended queen in an already-winning position.

582.chip: Move loses material or exposes king
582.label: In most of these middlegame positions the played move is self-inflicted — either directly hanging the player's own material (often a knight) or fatally exposing the king to a decisive attack/mate — but the specific failing (hung piece vs. king-safety collapse) and the piece involved vary too much to name one clean invariant.

588.label: The move leaves the player's own bishop undefended, allowing an enemy knight to capture it for free.

579.label: Pushes a pawn (usually racing a passed pawn or rushing promotion) instead of the correct move, ignoring the opponent's reply and either hanging own material or squandering the winning advantage.

578.label: Mostly hangs own material—dropping a pawn via a wrong-way king move in pawn endgames or leaving a knight undefended in the opening—though 3 of 10 are instead missed material-winning tactics (fork, free pawn, promoting intermezzo).

590.label: In winning or equal positions the player declines an available capture of material—usually by throwing in a pointless tempo check—forfeiting or badly diluting the win.

572.label: In a winning endgame the player gives a check or promotes with check that leaves the queen on a square next to the enemy king, who captures it for free or for far less material, throwing away the win or a forced mate.

589.label: In a winning or advantageous position the player plays a natural recapture or quiet move and lets the win slip, missing the one precise decisive continuation — but the missed idea varies by board (promotion, sacrifice, tempo move, defense, or forced mate) and one case actually hangs the queen, so no single piece or motif holds across all ten.

595.label: In endgames the player makes an inaccurate move (king move, wrong check or wrong promotion) that throws away the optimal result — letting a win slip to a draw/perpetual/fortress or missing a saving stalemate, and occasionally hanging the queen outright.

597.chip: Hastens own mate in lost position (king safety)
597.label: In already-losing middlegames, the player makes a passive or king-exposing move (often a king walk to the rim) that fails to mount the best defense and accelerates the opponent's attack/checkmate against their own king.

598.label: An aggressive 'with tempo' attack or repositioning move (often a knight to b5 chasing the enemy queen) backfires — most often leaving the player's own piece undefended and lost immediately or in a short forcing sequence (hung material varies: pawn, knight, bishop, rook), and in a few cases merely squandering tempo for a worse position rather than dropping material outright.

594.label: A move—usually a capture or pawn grab—that opens the player's own king (typically the f7/f2 square or a key diagonal/file), letting the opponent refute with a tactic that wins back material or mates, in the opening.

602.label: An unsound knight sacrifice in the opening (almost always Nxf7) that simply hangs the knight, since the king captures it for free with no real attacking compensation.

580.label: A passive or mistimed opening move that loses the player's own material — most often a bishop on the b4/a5 diagonal trapped by b4, but also a queen (board 5), a pawn (board 8), or a missed winning capture (boards 6, 10) — so the specific piece hung varies rather than being consistently one piece.

601.label: A slow/passive opening move that squanders a winning advantage by failing to play the decisive central pawn break (usually e5 or d5).

606.label: A materially-safe quiet/developing move is played instead of the winning central pawn break (e5/d5/f4/e4/cxd5), most often one that exploits a pin or attacks a piece — an omission that squanders a near-winning advantage rather than hanging own material.

603.label: In rook endgames the player skips a forcing rook check (often a forced mate, sometimes a piece-winning sequence), instead grabbing a pawn or playing a passive/quiet move and squandering the win.

587.label: Black repeatedly fails to neutralize White's Qh5+Bc4 battery against f7 (the correct ...g6 is always available), walking into Scholar's Mate or decisive material loss — a self-inflicted king-safety collapse where the falling target varies (king, knight, bishop) so no single piece is named.

591.label: In the opening, instead of resolving the central tension with the indicated capture (almost always ...exd4 / cxd5 / exd5), the player makes a slow non-central pawn or piece move that self-inflicts the loss of a central pawn or other material.

600.label: A move that loses the player's own material—usually hanging a piece, either immediately or to a tactic/fork a couple moves later (piece type varies: knight, bishop, or rook)—with a couple of boards instead being king-safety/mate collapses.

610.label: Player repeatedly skips a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (bishop/rook/queen/knight all appear), squandering a clearly winning position into a draw or worse.

607.label: In queen endgames the player plays a slower or non-forcing move—usually a check—instead of the decisive continuation, missing a forced mate or material-winning line and letting the enemy king escape.

608.label: An opening move — usually a pawn advance that abandons support of a central or queenside pawn — that loses the player's own material (most often a pawn, occasionally escalating to a piece/queen via the refutation).

605.label: A bishop moves deep into enemy territory (usually grabbing a pawn on c7/c2/b7) where it is undefended and immediately captured for free, losing a full piece in the opening.

592.label: Mostly fires on self-inflicted moves—often a greedy queen/rook pawn-grab, but also king walks, pawn pushes and an ignored mate threat—that abandon a defender or expose the player's own king to a decisive attack or mate (7/10), with two boards being pure hung material and one an endgame tempo loss, so no single piece/theme cleanly fits all ten.

612.label: An unsound Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice in the opening that simply hangs the bishop for a single pawn after the king recaptures with Kxf7.

604.label: A passive move (usually a queen retreat) in the opening that declines an available winning capture of material — varying among rook, bishop, knight-fork, and pawn — with one outlier case actively hanging the queen instead.

599.label: In the opening the player makes a quiet/developing move that ignores a concrete tactic; ~6/10 hang their own piece (most often a knight already attacked by a pawn) while ~4/10 skip a forced material-winning capture, with a knight in the decisive play of roughly 8/10 boards but the direction genuinely mixed between hanging and missing material.

585.label: The feature plays a pointless queen check that drives the opponent's king to a safer/more active square, squandering tempo and often a winning position or forced mate rather than playing the quiet improving move or capture.

596.label: In endgames the player abandons the blockade/stopping of an opponent's passed pawn — usually drifting a bishop to a 'more active' square — allowing that pawn to promote by force.

616.chip: Hangs a piece on greedy capture
616.label: A short-sighted material grab (usually capturing a pawn) that ends up losing the player's own piece — most often a bishop (7/10) — though a couple of boards are queen-for-pawn trades or a missed mate, so the piece isn't uniform enough to name.

624.chip: Hangs bishop on faulty h3/h6 sac
624.label: Plays an unsound Greek-Gift-style bishop sacrifice on h3 or h6 to rip open the enemy king's pawn cover, but the attack is toothless and simply loses a full bishop for one or two pawns.

619.label: In a completely won king-and-pawn endgame, the player mishandles the conversion—pushing the passed pawn too early or making the wrong king move instead of the precise winning king maneuver—throwing away the win and drawing a won game (no material is hung; it's pure endgame technique).

622.label: In a winning or advantageous middlegame the player chooses a slow, non-forcing move (a tempo-loser or preparatory move) instead of the decisive continuation — a forced mate, a free piece, or a passed-pawn push — throwing away most of the advantage; the materially safe move is an omission rather than a self-hung piece, and the squandered resource varies (mate, material, passed pawn) so no single piece is named.

620.label: Fires on king-safety mishandling: usually a self-weakening or defense-neglecting move that exposes the player's own king to a decisive attack/mate (often the Nxe4→Qh4+ motif against an uncastled Ke1), though ~2 of 10 instead miss that same shot against the enemy's exposed king.

611.chip: Hangs a pawn, blows winning endgame
611.label: The move abandons the defense of (or removes) a pawn—usually by stepping a king or swinging a rook off its guard—so the opponent grabs it cleanly, often with check, converting a clearly winning (mostly endgame) position into a draw.

613.label: In a critical (usually winning) position the player skips a decisive forcing tactic—most often a forced mate, frequently by greedily grabbing material instead—though a couple of already-losing boards simply hang a piece or blunder into a lost ending.

617.chip: Trades major piece for a pawn (endgame)
617.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player gives up a major piece (rook in ~6 boards, a newly-promoted/existing queen in the rest) to grab or stop a passed pawn, but it is immediately recaptured, converting a winning or drawn position into a worse/lost pawn endgame.

627.label: Captures with the queen to force a queen trade—almost always with check—simplifying away the active queen and converting a winning or drawn position into a worse or lost endgame.

626.label: The player greedily grabs material (usually a pawn) instead of the decisive winning move, missing a forced mate or game-winning tactic in nearly every position.

614.chip: Hangs material, skips forced rook capture/trade
614.label: The player declines a forced/only rook capture or exchange and instead plays a self-inflicting move that loses their own rook or walks into a back-rank checkmate.

623.label: A knight greedily captures a central pawn (e4/d4/d5) in the opening and is then trapped or won by a recapture/fork, losing the knight for a pawn.

621.label: The player gives up their rook—either by moving it directly into capture or by allowing a forced exchange—surrendering their last active piece and collapsing into a trivially lost (usually pawn) endgame.

628.label: In an endgame, the player declines to capture the opponent's completely undefended major piece — the hanging queen in 8 of 10 boards (a hanging rook in the other 2) — throwing away a won position by leaving the free capture on the board.

618.label: The feature fires on quiet, non-forcing moves (mostly pawn pushes ~38% and queen retreats ~35%) that fail the position's tactical demand — usually a weakening move that lets the opponent strike for material or mate (8/10: e.g. f6/g5 removing a defender, Kg8 into a discovered check, Na6/Ne2 allowing a fork/attack), but in 2/10 it's a safe queen retreat that skips a winning capture (Qf2 missing Qxg4, Qd8 missing Qxb5), and the dropped material varies (pawn, bishop, exchange, or full piece), so only 'a passive move that hangs material or misses a win' can be named, not a specific piece.

632.label: The player moves the queen out early and hangs it — usually grabbing a defended pawn — losing the queen to a simple recapture in the opening.

631.chip: Premature pawn trade draws won endgame
631.label: In a winning pawn endgame, advances/exchanges a pawn that liquidates into a theoretically drawn (or worse) king-and-pawn ending, throwing away the win rather than improving the king first.

634.label: In a winning position the player chose a quiet king/piece move instead of a forcing check (frequently a knight fork) that wins material, squandering the advantage.

629.chip: Squanders win with flashy forcing move
629.label: The feature fires on positions where the player has a winning or clearly better position and throws it away with a tempting forcing move—usually a flashy check or greedy capture—that most often hangs the player's own material (the dropped piece varies across bishop/rook/knight/queen), though in roughly a third of boards the move instead skips a cleaner win or mate without losing material, so the direction is genuinely mixed.

640.label: In winning endgames the player skips the immediate (often checking) pawn promotion in favor of a king/rook move or extra pawn push, squandering a forced win or mate.

641.label: Plays a safe, quiet, or retreating move instead of an available winning blow—free material (Qxh8, Qxd3, Qxg6) or a forcing tactic/fork (Nxf7, Ndb4, Bxg8)—squandering a winning advantage into equality.

635.chip: Gives up material, blows won game
635.label: From a clearly winning position the player throws it away by surrendering material — most often hanging a piece outright via a flashy but refuted check (Nxd4/Nxf5/Rxf3/Nxd3/Nxb1), and in several cases through a losing 'simplifying' trade — and the piece involved genuinely varies (rook, knight, bishop, queen), so no single piece can be named.

637.label: The player prematurely captures or advances a central pawn, releasing the tension or surrendering a strong advanced pawn, and squanders a winning or advantageous position (direction varies: a few are greedy grabs, one hangs a piece, one misses a free capture).

636.label: The player consistently skips an available forcing queen check (Qh5+/Qh6+/Qg6+/Qxg3+/Qxc3+ etc. delivering perpetual, mate, or won material) in favor of a slower or wrong-move-order move, throwing away the draw or win.

630.label: In the opening—with a knight as the decisive piece on essentially every board—the player squanders an advantage by playing a safe-looking move that skips the right idea: most often missing a winning capture or tactic (frequently a hanging enemy knight on f4/e4, or a knight fork), and sometimes mishandling their own knight (moving it off a key square or capturing with the wrong one) so material is lost over the next few moves.

638.label: A self-inflicted move—often a greedy capture that removes its own blockader/defender or a forcing line that loses material—that throws away the player's position, frequently by letting an enemy passed pawn promote; the lost piece varies (knight, rook, bishop, queen+rook), so it's 'a piece,' not one specific piece.

644.label: Across all 10 boards the player passes up a materially-winning bishop capture that removes a key defender (Bxf3 in 8/10, Bxc3 and Bxb3 in the others), playing a safe-but-passive move that throws away a winning advantage rather than hanging their own piece.

633.label: A self-inflicted middlegame blunder that strips away a critical defender — of the back rank, king-shelter, or a piece — and is refuted by immediate checkmate or decisive material loss, with the exposed piece varying across positions.

625.label: In almost every position there is a hanging piece on the board—most often the enemy queen (boards 1,2,3,6)—and the player makes a quiet, king, or pawn move instead of the available capture, walking into a forced mate; because the missed/ignored piece varies (queen, rook on board 4, bishop on board 5) and one case is failing to save the player's OWN hanging queen (board 7), it's labeled at piece-level rather than as 'queen' specifically.

647.label: A clear winning move is available — frequently a forced mate on h2/h7 or a decisive material-winning capture/fork — but the player instead plays a quiet developing, consolidating, or wrong-capture move, throwing away the win.

648.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a passive or wrong king move (retreating to the corner/back rank instead of seizing the opposition, holding the blockade, or defending the key pawn), throwing away a held draw or the only active defense — a positional/endgame king-placement error, not a hung piece.

645.label: Throws away a winning position by playing a slow, non-forcing move (often a tempo-losing pawn push) instead of the decisive continuation, letting the opponent equalize or escape.

639.label: Repeatedly missed a forced win—most often a forced checkmate—by playing a routine material-grabbing capture instead of the decisive blow.

593.chip: Overlooks threat: hangs piece or mate
593.label: A self-inflicted blunder that ignores the opponent's immediate refutation — a routine or greedy move (often a castle or a capture) that either leaves the player's own piece hanging or removes a defender and allows a forced mate.

653.label: Plays a passive, tempo-wasting move that squanders a forced win — frequently a forced mate — instead of the available forcing continuation, while the move itself stays materially safe (own material isn't hung).

652.label: Most boards leave an own undefended piece — usually a bishop on a5/b5/b6, sometimes the queen or rook — hanging early and lose it to the refutation, but 3 of 10 are instead materially-safe moves that just miss a winning tactic, so the feature is mixed.

649.chip: Abandons king defense, allows mate (queen often)
649.label: A move — frequently a greedy capture or queen excursion — that pulls a defender off the player's own king (or walks the king into the open), allowing a forced checkmate against the mover.

656.label: In an already-winning endgame, plays a slow tempo-wasting move that throws away the forced win or mate, letting the opponent draw or escape.

646.label: A quiet/passive piece move (usually a knight, sometimes queen/rook) abandons the position's key forcing resource — perpetual, fork, or winning check — but the result splits ~5/5 between directly hanging own material (boards 3,6,7,8,9) and merely forgoing a winning/saving tactic (boards 1,2,4,5,10), so the hung-vs-missed direction is genuinely mixed.

650.label: In a pawn-promotion/passed-pawn endgame, plays a move that turns a draw or holdable position into a loss — sometimes hanging a piece (knight, rook, queen, or bishop), sometimes mishandling the pawn race itself.

654.label: Player advances or captures with a passed pawn one move too early (c3→b2, f6→g7, c6→b7, b3→b2) instead of first inserting a deflection, check, or queen trade, so the opponent simply recaptures (often Bxb2 onto the long diagonal) and neutralizes the pawn.

655.label: In endgames (mostly rook/queen vs rook), plays a passive piece move or pawn push instead of the active tempo-gaining check, allowing the opponent's intermezzo check to win tempo, the promotion race, or the rook outright.

661.label: A move that squanders a winning position (often a forced mate), most commonly a king move that walks into perpetual check or a greedy capture that abandons the attack — the punishment is usually the opponent escaping via checks rather than the player hanging material outright.

643.label: A self-inflicted blunder that loses the player's own material (piece, pawn, or queen) or fatally exposes their king to a decisive attack, with the precise weakness varying across positions.

660.label: In a favorable (usually winning) opening position the player makes a quiet, non-capturing 'safe' move that throws away the advantage—most often failing to grab a hanging enemy knight or pawn (boards 1-5,7)—while a minority instead hang their own king safety/queen or lose a decisive endgame tempo (boards 6,8,9,10), so the core is missing the best material-winning move rather than any single piece.

663.label: A self-inflicted material loss in the middlegame: the player (usually moving a rook) either walks the piece into a capture or abandons a defensive duty, hanging material — most often a rook, sometimes triggering a back-rank mate.

642.label: In sharp (mostly opening) positions the player chooses a natural quiet move—castling, Qe2/Bd2 development, a bishop or pawn move—instead of the one forcing best move, repeatedly missing a winning tactical shot, frequently the axb4 capture of a bishop on b4.

662.label: A superficially active or natural-looking move—centralizing a piece, doubling rooks, or firing off a check—that throws away the player's position, in ~7/10 boards by giving the opponent tempo/counterplay or opening lines (positional/tempo squander) rather than by hanging material, with 3 boards instead dropping a pawn/piece/rook outright; the moved piece (rook 5/10, also bishop/knight/king/queen) and the pre-move state (winning, equal, and losing all appear) vary too much to pin a single piece or position-state.

667.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player fails to stop or capture the opponent's passed pawn, allowing it to advance and promote, though two of the ten boards (a missed knight capture and an opening sacrifice) break the pattern.

664.chip: Missed fastest win in passed-pawn endgame
664.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player picks a materially-safe but suboptimal move — a premature/wrong pawn push or a slow king/knight move (and once a skipped free capture) — instead of the decisive move, throwing away a forced win for a slower or merely-better position.

668.label: The player repeatedly chooses a quiet, natural developing/recapturing move and overlooks a winning knight-capture tactic (almost always Nxe4/Nxe5-type) that wins material or saves the position.

665.label: In nearly every position the player had a decisive winning continuation — very often a forced checkmate — but chose an inferior, materially-safe move that threw away the win (one board instead just hangs a knight).

666.label: The player's move walks into or fails to prevent a forced mate against its own king — overwhelmingly an immediate back-rank checkmate (e.g. Rh1#/Rb1#), whether by moving the king to a fatal square, blocking its own escape, or pulling a defender (often a rook) off the back rank, sometimes while greedily grabbing material.

669.label: An over-aggressive opening move—typically a greedy grab (Nxf2, Qxh7) or unsound sacrifice—that loses the player's own material with no compensation; usually a piece (knight, bishop, queen), occasionally a pawn, so the specific unit varies.

671.label: In every position the player passed up an immediate winning bishop capture (most often grabbing an undefended rook for the exchange on the long diagonal) in favor of a quiet move, throwing away free material.

670.chip: Passive endgame move, no king activation
670.label: In endgames the player makes a passive or wrong-direction move (usually failing to centralize/activate the king, sometimes a non-urgent pawn push) that squanders a winning or drawable position rather than pursuing the active king march.

651.label: In the endgame the player makes a losing move — usually pushing a flank pawn or a passive king move — that fails to address the critical passed-pawn/promotion race (or skips the only saving capture), turning a drawn or holdable position into a loss.

657.label: Across the boards the played move vacates the sole defender of a critical square or piece, self-inflicting a decisive blow—most often an immediate checkmate (boards 2,4,7,8,9), sometimes a forced material win (1,3,5,10)—with one outlier being a tempo-wasting check that squanders a win (6).

659.label: The player chooses an intuitive material-grabbing or routine move (often a capture/recapture) and overlooks the position's forcing resource — sometimes hanging its own rook/queen/knight to a refutation, sometimes squandering a forced win, fork, or mate — with the decisive piece and the direction (hung vs. missed) varying board to board.

678.label: The player makes a move that opens or fails to defend a long diagonal, allowing the opponent's bishop to capture an undefended rook and win the exchange.

680.label: While already winning, the player skips a decisive shot — usually a free enemy piece hanging for capture (rook, bishop, pawn) and sometimes a forced mate — settling for a lesser advantage instead of the clear win.

672.label: The player neglects the position's thematic central break or capture (d5/e5/f5/d4/Nxe5) in favor of a passive, prophylactic, or wing move — squandering an equal-or-winning position; on ~4 boards this takes the concrete form of an unsound Bxf7+/Bf5 that simply hangs a bishop.

673.label: In nearly all positions the played move self-inflicts material loss, hanging a piece (bishop most often, but also queen/exchange) to a 2-3 move tactical refutation that usually features an enemy knight capturing with check (Nxf3+, Nxd3+, Nxh6, Nxd6+, Nxf6+).

674.label: In endgames (frequently with passed pawns), the player makes a natural-looking move that fails to find the single precise resource — throwing away a win in some cases and a draw in others — rather than hanging material outright.

683.label: Plays a slow, materially-safe move (king/rook shuffle) that throws away a winning position by ignoring the one decisive shot — a pawn or knight fork, a promotion, or a rook invasion — with the winning piece varying across boards.

682.label: In every position the player overlooks a knight-fork check (Nf2+/Ne2+/Nf3+/etc.) that simultaneously attacks the king and wins the queen, instead playing a passive or routine move that throws away the win.

679.label: Player repeatedly fails to grab the opponent's undefended queen, passing up a free winning capture (8/10 are a hanging queen; the other two miss a back-rank mate and a hanging bishop).

675.label: In a winning endgame the player rushes their own passed pawn one square toward promotion instead of the prophylactic blockading/winning move, allowing the opponent to promote with tempo or mate and squandering the win.

681.label: Player moves the queen to a square where the opponent can force an unfavorable queen trade, dissolving the player's attack or advantage.

684.label: In queen endgames the feature nominally fires when the player skips a forcing queen check/capture that mates faster or wins outright (boards 1, 2, 7, 10 — e.g. Qxh5+/Qh5+/Qa5+, or keeping the queen on its blockading square), but roughly six of ten boards are 0cp non-blunders where the chosen queen move is in fact a joint-best move, so the feature is genuinely mixed and detects 'queen-endgame positions with a forcing-check option' more than a consistent error.

687.label: In a winning endgame the player skips the immediate, often check-giving pawn promotion (playing a king/pawn/capture move instead) and lets the forced win slip to a draw or worse.

688.chip: Missed capturing hanging enemy piece (often rook)
688.label: The player repeatedly overlooks an elementary free capture of an undefended enemy piece (usually a hanging rook), throwing away a winning position by playing a passive/repositioning move instead.

676.label: Player makes a capture (almost always on b4/b5) that the opponent answers with a recapture or pawn-grab delivering check against the uncastled king on e1/e8, costing material or a winning advantage.

695.label: In every position the player overlooked a simple capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away a winning position by playing an unrelated move instead.

658.label: A move that abandons the defense of, or directly exposes, the player's own piece—self-inflicting decisive material loss, with the queen most frequently the piece hung and a queen involved in nearly every position.

691.label: Across all 10 boards the player makes a materially-safe but soft/preparatory move and overlooks the concrete winning continuation (a capture or forcing tactic) that wins material or preserves a near-winning advantage; the specific winning piece varies (queen, rook, knight, bishop), so this is a piece-agnostic omission rather than a self-inflicted hang.

693.chip: Weakening pawn push hangs material (chasing queen)
693.label: A pawn push—usually intended to chase away the enemy queen—opens a line or strips a defender around the player's own king, and the refutation wins material (or mates) within a couple of moves.

690.label: In every position the player had a decisive winning continuation (often a forced mate) but threw it away with a greedy capture or a slow, non-forcing move.

685.chip: Hangs piece to f7 knight fork (opening)
685.label: In the opening the player ignores a knight fork on f7 (failing to play Kxf7), hanging material — usually the queen to Nxd8, sometimes the d5 knight after retreating the queen.

696.label: The player ignores an immediately capturable undefended enemy rook (taken by the queen, often with check) and instead plays a slow move, squandering a winning advantage.

689.label: Player plays a passive or inferior quiet move that declines an available material-winning move—usually a direct capture in 7/10 boards (gxh3, Rxe2, axb6, Bxf4, Bxd4, hxg5, Qxf3)—with a minority (~2/10) where the chosen move instead hangs a piece outright.

677.label: Player moves the queen onto (or leaves it on) a square where it is immediately captured by a rook—often while greedily grabbing a pawn—throwing away a winning queen-vs-rook or mating advantage.

697.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight involved)
697.label: In the opening the player makes a move (often a premature knight sortie like Ng5 instead of Nxe5) that loses their own material; the lost piece varies (knight, bishop, or d4 pawn), so it's 'a piece', with a knight involved in nearly every position.

694.label: Pushing or capturing with the f-pawn in the opening weakens king safety and loses material, typically to a forcing queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+) along the freshly-opened diagonal.

700.label: Self-inflicted material loss: the player hangs their own piece — usually by greedily capturing a defended pawn (mostly a bishop, but knight/queen vary, so 'a piece'), occasionally throwing away a forced mate while doing so.

703.label: In a (usually winning) middlegame the player overlooks an immediate material-winning capture — most often grabbing an undefended enemy rook — and instead plays a passive non-capturing move (king walk, pawn push, passive rook), throwing the win away; a few boards instead show a bad trade, wrong-piece recapture, or greedy/defensive misstep.

701.label: Player needlessly trades queens, simplifying away a winning or favorable position when keeping the queen (often to grab a free piece/pawn or sustain an attack) was far stronger.

702.label: A self-inflicted move that ignores the opponent's threat and walks into a forced refutation, losing the player's own material or king — but the punished asset varies (knight, bishop, rook, pawn promotion, and several lines end in checkmate), so no single piece can be named.

699.label: An overoptimistic opening capture/sacrifice — most often an unsound Nxf7 fork attempt — that simply hangs the player's own piece, since the opponent quietly recaptures and emerges up material.

705.label: The player makes a self-inflicting move that hangs their own piece — most often the queen left on an aggressive square (h4/h5/e5) where it's captured for free — though two positions instead skip a forced winning tactic, so the core invariant is 'a piece hangs' rather than any single piece.

707.label: In an already-lost position, plays a move that shortens the path to the opponent's forced mate, most often by walking the king into a mating net.

704.label: From a winning, equal, or already-favorable-side position the player makes a careless move (often a greedy capture) that squanders the advantage — most commonly by hanging own material or exposing the king, but a sizeable minority instead simply miss a forced win/zwischenzug — and the decisive piece and position-state vary, so the feature is genuinely mixed.

710.label: Player loses the exchange by capturing a centralized enemy minor piece with a rook that is simply recaptured by a pawn, dropping rook-for-minor with no compensation.

698.label: In middlegame positions the player repeatedly loses its own material — leaving a piece en prise or trading/sacrificing it for inadequate compensation (most often a bishop, but the hung piece varies).

712.label: The bishop snatches a seemingly free edge pawn (usually Bxa7, also Bxa2/Bxh2) but gets trapped and lost over the next few moves, sacrificing a full piece for a single pawn.

713.label: In every one of the top-10 opening positions the player loses a bishop for free—either by moving it onto an undefended square on a long diagonal (g7/b7/b2/f5/f4) or by failing to defend an already-fianchettoed bishop—so the recurring mistake is hanging a bishop.

706.label: Against White's queen-on-h5 + knight-on-g6 battery, Black fails to play the only defense ...Nf6, instead playing a move (hxg6, Kd7/Kd8, Nxc3, Nc6) that self-inflicts loss — either Qxh8/Nxh8 winning the h8 rook or a Ne5+/Qf7 discovered-check mate.

692.label: Fires on natural-looking developing/positional moves (castling, piece development, pawn pushes, prophylaxis) that ignore a live material tactic — ~6/10 hang the player's own piece or the exchange in the refutation, ~4/10 instead miss a winning/equalizing capture; the piece varies (knight, bishop, pawn, exchange) so only 'ignores material' is invariant, and direction is mixed.

720.label: Plays a tempo/pawn check that lets the enemy king flee to safety, squandering a forced checkmate (8/10) or otherwise decisive win that the player should have delivered instead.

711.label: In a winning middlegame the player plays a slow or inferior move that throws away the decisive advantage—failing to execute the forcing winning continuation (often the fxg6 pawn break or a forced mate), though in ~2 cases the inferior move actually hangs material.

709.chip: Hangs material chasing a piece (pawn lunge)
709.label: A premature flank pawn lunge intended to chase an enemy piece (almost always a knight) backfires, costing the player their own material or fatally exposing their king.

715.label: A king-safety blunder—walking the king into a mating net or removing the back-rank defender—that allows a forced checkmate, almost always delivered by an enemy rook.

686.label: The player passes up an available forcing move — almost always a rook exchange, rook capture, or check (frequently on an open file) — in favor of a slow or unsound move that either hangs material or squanders a winning/equal position.

719.label: In the opening, the player loses material by declining the correct Nxe5 capture/recapture and instead hanging a piece (a bishop on f2 in several, a knight or other piece elsewhere), with a knight on e5 the recurring tactical element rather than the consistently-hung piece.

708.label: Genuinely mixed: in an endgame the player chooses a tempting forcing move — a capture (1,2,4,6,8) or a flashy/spite check (3,5,9) — instead of the correct continuation, which hangs a piece in ~4 cases (Q/B/N, no single dominant piece), misses a forced mate or perpetual in ~4 cases, and ruins a winning plan with a quiet move in ~2 cases (Ra1, g4); position-state is also split (≈4 winning, 2 drawn, 4 already losing), so the SEE 'winning/hung/capture 100%' signature overstates a single direction.

722.label: In an endgame the player makes a slow/passive move—most often a king move—that skips the decisive pawn break or material-winning capture, throwing away the win or worsening a lost position (no own piece hung).

716.label: Across these positions the player self-inflicts a material/positional loss by making a faulty capture or simplifying trade (often missing a stronger zwischenzug, alternative capture, or saving resource), or by leaving an attacked piece hanging — but the piece involved varies (rook, bishop, knight, pawn) and the mechanism alternates between bad trades and outright hangs, so it is 'a piece' rather than any single type.

718.chip: Misses the only good move (king safety)
718.label: In each position the player overlooks the single critical move — usually a forcing queen check, capture, or precise defensive resource — and instead plays a quiet, slow, or greedy alternative that lets the position collapse (most often into a mating attack on their own king, but sometimes losing material or surrendering a saving perpetual).

714.label: A queen or rook moves off a critical square—directly hanging itself, dropping support from another piece, or abandoning a defensive/back-rank duty—losing material or allowing a decisive tactic/mate, though 2-3 boards are instead missed wins (safe move skips a winning tactic) or near-perfect.

726.chip: Misses fastest win in won endgame
726.label: In winning/clearly-better endgames the move keeps own material safe but throws away the fastest or even forced win — typically through underpromotion, a wrong recapture, or decentralizing technique — though 2/10 boards aren't mistakes at all and one is an exchange-losing trade, so it's a somewhat mixed 'missed win' rather than a hang.

725.label: Mixed feature firing on endgame positions where the player picks an inferior move that squanders the position — about half mishandle a passed pawn/promotion (1,2,5,6,10), three miss a free capture (Qxb6, Rxa3, Rxd4), and two walk into mate (g3, Re3) — with no single piece or position-state common.

724.label: In a winning or roughly equal position the player chooses a natural-looking move that throws the advantage away — most often by skipping a forcing winning continuation (frequently a tempo-gaining check like Re1+/Bc5+/Bxc4+/Bb2+, ~6/10 boards), but in the remainder by hanging material outright (Bc7, Qb4) or making a bad sac/greedy grab — so direction is mixed (missed-win dominant, ~7/10; hangs ~2-3/10).

733.label: Plays a passive or routine move, missing a winning bishop sacrifice against the enemy king (consistently Bxf2+/Bxh7+/Bxf7+/Bxh2+).

717.chip: Hangs material via pawn push (tempo grab)
717.label: A pawn move — typically a push to gain tempo on the enemy queen or open lines — hangs the player's own material (usually a pawn, sometimes a piece falling over 2-3 moves), often punished by a capture-with-check against an uncastled king.

732.chip: Hangs a piece with an unsound check
732.label: Plays a forcing check that sacrifices/hangs the player's own material unsoundly (most often a rook, but bishops and queens too), losing material rather than achieving the hoped-for attack.

727.chip: Passive blockade misses active save (passed pawn)
727.label: Repeatedly chooses a passive blockading/quiet move—most often parking the queen on a1/a8 in front of a passed pawn—instead of the active forcing resource (usually a perpetual check or a saving king move), throwing away the draw or win.

723.chip: Hangs a piece in the opening
723.label: In the opening the player makes an unsound move that loses their own material — most often a refuted bishop sacrifice on f7/f2, sometimes a knight grabbed or trapped in the tactic — so the piece type varies (bishop ~6/10, knight ~4/10), making the invariant simply 'hangs a piece'.

728.label: In winning/equal endgames the player makes a passive king or rook move instead of the one precise pawn break (usually d4 or e6), squandering the advantage.

721.chip: Hangs a piece via quiet move (knight tactic)
721.label: Instead of the forcing tactical capture demanded by the position (most often Nxf3+), the player makes a quiet developing/castling move that fails to resolve the tactical tension, hanging a piece within two or three moves (a knight is the pivotal piece in nearly every line).

737.label: In every one of the top-10 positions the player passed up a winning knight fork (Nc2+/Nc7+) that checks the exposed king on e1/e8 and wins the rook (the exchange), instead playing a quiet developing/castling or material-grabbing move that lets the opponent cover the fork square.

731.label: Player moves or leaves the queen on a vulnerable, often open-file square where it is won — frequently after an intermezzo check or discovered attack that deflects its defending king — though in a couple of boards a different piece falls or the queen is merely hounded off.

729.label: In winning (or occasionally drawn-but-savable) middlegames the player chooses a non-forcing repositioning move—most often a queen retreat/sidestep, sometimes a bishop, king or pawn—that abandons a key square or defensive duty and squanders the advantage by skipping a forced tactical sequence, with about 3/10 boards where the move directly hangs material or allows mate.

735.label: Plays a slow developing/expanding move that ignores an active opponent threat, hanging the player's own material (piece varies — knight, bishop, rook; often king-safety related).

743.label: The player overlooks a forcing queen move — almost always a check, frequently Qxc6+ — that wins material by force, instead playing a quiet, safe, or developing move.

740.label: In an endgame the player makes a faulty pawn advance or premature promotion that throws away a drawn or winning position — sometimes hanging the newly-promoted queen (boards 3,6,10), more often a tempo/structure loss (boards 1,2,4,5,8) or a missed saving resource (7,9).

738.label: A piece/pawn is moved off the square where it was defending material, supporting a pawn, or attacking a key piece — but the result is inconsistent: ~5 boards hang own material (queen, bishop, rook) while the rest merely miss a faster win/draw or allow decisive passed pawns, so the feature is mixed.

736.chip: Declines saving queen trade, hangs piece
736.label: In a losing or inferior position the player passes up the forced queen trade that was the only way to limit damage, instead playing another move (usually a king move) that leaves their own piece — most often the queen, but sometimes a rook — hanging.

734.label: Mostly fires on moves that throw away material (hung pawn/piece or losing trade, sometimes only in the multi-move refutation) with the piece varying across bishop/knight/queen, but ~2-3 boards instead miss a forced win/mate and one is purely positional, so the core is only loosely shared.

741.label: In the opening the player passes up a winning tactic that punishes the opponent's exposed queen on f3/c3 (frequently a knight fork or ...Nd4), playing a quiet developing move instead and squandering a winning advantage into equality.

745.label: The move leaves the player's own piece en prise (usually a bishop or queen, hung directly or via a short 2-3 move tactic), though ~2/10 boards are instead missed wins rather than self-inflicted hangs.

750.chip: Hangs a piece grabbing central pawn
750.label: In the opening, captures a defended central pawn (almost always d4), hanging its own piece — a bishop or knight depending on the position — for just one pawn.

739.chip: Misses critical tempo move in endgame (often a check)
739.label: In a rook endgame, plays a slow move—frequently failing the one saving/winning check—that surrenders critical tempo, letting the opponent's passed pawn promote or a back-rank mate land.

744.label: In winning endgames the player fails to capture the opponent's only remaining active piece (knight or bishop), letting it escape and converting a win or forced mate into mere advantage; one outlier instead hangs its own queen.

742.label: In a winning or clearly advantageous position the player repeatedly throws away the win by choosing a routine/materialistic capture or passive move instead of the precise forcing continuation—mechanism varies (missed tactic, missed mate, bad trade, even a self-inflicted hang), so no single piece or capture is the true invariant beyond 'squandered advantage'.

753.label: In a won position the player passes up a free winning capture (most often the opponent's completely undefended queen) and instead plays a pointless forcing check, throwing away mate or a decisive material edge.

752.label: In nearly every position the player skipped a forced win — frequently a forced checkmate (Ne7#, Rd1#, Qh7#, mate-in-3/6) or a decisive tactic like Ne2+ or Nxf2 — and instead played a materially-safe but inferior capture/positional move, throwing away the advantage.

748.label: Across all 10 boards the played move allows a one-move checkmate (usually Qxg7# or Qxg2#, occasionally Qxh2#/Qxb2#), either by greedily capturing a piece that was the king's last defender or by ignoring an already-present mating threat — a self-inflicted king-safety collapse rather than a missed win.

747.label: The feature fires on moves that fail to neutralize a concrete threat — most walk into a decisive loss of the player's own material (queen on 3/4, rook on 2) or a forced mate (back-rank on 1, mating net on 8/10), though a few boards (5, 9) are softer positional/tempo losses and one (7) is a missed-win that throws away a draw.

751.label: A developing/repositioning move in the opening—often skipping the necessary Nxd4—that hangs material to a knight capture, frequently with check (Nxf3+/Nxe2+/Nxe3), though two boards are missed free captures and one is a king-safety lapse refuted by a bishop check instead.

746.label: In a (usually winning) position the player passes up the decisive continuation—frequently a forced mate or a crushing attacking/material-winning shot—in favor of a quieter developing, retreating, or simplifying move, though in a few boards (Nf4, Nf3, Qxb7) the chosen move also outright hangs the player's own piece, so the direction is mixed and the hung piece is not consistent enough to name.

754.label: In each top position the player passes up the single precise best move—frequently a promotion-with-check, but elsewhere a key capture or equalizing resource—playing a passive king/piece move instead; the mistake is an omission of a win/save, not a self-hung piece.

760.chip: Missed winning attack on king (queen check)
760.label: A materially-safe move that skips a forced mate or decisive attack against the exposed enemy king, typically a forcing queen check (Qxg3+/Qxb6+/Qg6+).

749.label: A tempting bishop check (always a bishop, always a check) that backfires—most often the bishop itself gets trapped or captured a move or two later, though in a few boards it's instead a wrong-capture/bad-trade that squanders a bigger win.

758.label: In every position the player chose a quiet developing/retreating move and overlooked a forcing winning shot — often a checkmate, usually delivered by a bishop check (Bb5+/Bh5+/Bxe6#) — squandering a clearly winning tactic.

757.label: In the opening, the player abandons an advanced/infiltrating bishop by playing a routine developing move instead of capturing or trading it, letting the opponent win the piece for free (9/10 bishop, 1/10 knight).

762.label: In all 10 positions the player plays a safe quiet move (developing, castling, or a pawn push) and overlooks a forcing capture-with-check that wins material against the exposed/uncastled enemy king — the check is delivered by the queen in 9/10 (most often Qxc3+), so the win is omitted rather than any own piece hung.

755.label: In the opening the player repeatedly grabs the knight fork Nxf7 instead of the correct Bxf7+, and the refutations show this loses material a couple moves later (knight gets trapped on h8, or a rook/bishop falls, or the king is mated) — the hung piece varies, so the certain core is 'hangs material via Nxf7 over Bxf7+'.

761.label: Player drifts the queen to a passive square, missing a forcing material-winning queen capture of a rook (often an exchange/queen sacrifice such as Qxe1).

764.chip: King to wrong square in endgame
764.label: In an endgame the player walks the king to the wrong square — declining a key capture or losing the opposition/defensive zone — turning a draw or holdable position into a loss.

768.label: Player inserts a flashy 'check first' move (zwischenzug) instead of the clean winning capture, hanging the checking piece — bishop, knight, rook or queen — for far less than it was worth.

759.label: A greedy/loosening capture in the opening that backfires self-inflicted, costing the player's own material or allowing mate; the specific piece lost varies (rook, queen, knight, or a mating attack), so it cannot be pinned to one piece.

765.label: In each middlegame the player moves a piece off (or fails to take up) a critical defensive post—removing a king/key-square defender, blocking the king's own escape, or leaving a piece unguarded—letting the opponent crash through with either forced mate (boards 1,2,4,7,9) or decisive material loss (boards 3,5,6,8,10); the piece moved (rook 3, queen 2, knight 2, pawn/king/bishop) and the concrete outcome vary too much to name a single piece or result, but the core defensive-neglect mistake is consistent.

769.label: In every position the player throws away a won game by giving an aimless queen check instead of the decisive queen capture/trade that simplifies into a clearly winning (usually pawn) endgame.

766.label: In a winning position the player makes a tempting capture (often a knight grab) that throws away the advantage instead of finding the one precise winning continuation.

773.chip: Trades rook into lost pawn endgame
773.label: Voluntarily exchanges (or allows the exchange of) the last rook, simplifying a holdable endgame into a lost king-and-pawn ending.

767.label: The player chooses a tempting forcing check instead of the objectively best move (usually a quiet, trading, or stronger capturing move), which typically backfires by hanging material or walking into mate and sometimes merely settles for a smaller advantage; the only reliable invariant is that the played move is always a check.

756.label: A self-defeating move—usually a pointless check—that hangs the player's own piece (most often a rook) and is captured immediately or within a couple of moves.

763.label: In all ten boards the player held a winning or clearly better position and squandered it with a passive or careless move—often missing a forcing win/mate, sometimes self-inflicting material or king-safety loss—but there is no single consistent hung piece (queen, knight, rook, bishop and pawn moves all appear).

772.label: An endgame blunder—usually a king move—that throws away a won or drawn position (king is misplaced, abandons a pawn, blocks its own pawn, or walks into checks/mate).

776.chip: Hangs material via pawn recapture (opens diagonal)
776.label: A pawn capture in the opening (usually bxc6) opens a diagonal/line that lets the opponent win material with a check or fork — a self-inflicted material loss, most often the exchange to Bxc6+.

781.label: Plays a quiet, materially-safe developing/retreating move that misses an available winning tactical strike (often a fork) in the opening, letting the opponent consolidate.

775.label: The played move loses the player's own material — directly hanging a piece (most often a bishop) or dropping it within a 2-3 move tactic — though a couple of boards are closer to tempo/positional losses, so the exact piece varies.

771.label: In a favorable/winning middlegame the player plays a quiet, materialistic, or otherwise passive move and overlooks a forcing winning tactic that in 8 of 10 boards centers on a bishop capture or sacrifice (e.g. Bxh3, Bxh6, Bxg5, Bxg6, Be3, Bxe4); on the remaining boards the same slow choice instead hangs material.

770.label: Plays a tempting, premature CHECK (knight 66% / bishop the rest) instead of the stronger quiet or mating move—the check lets the enemy king escape to safety or releases the attacking pressure, converting a winning/better position into drawn-or-lost, and in several boards (Nd7+, Bxf2+, Nxc7+) the checking piece itself ends up hung or trapped.

780.label: In a roughly equal opening, the player captures a defended pawn (most often on d7/e7) with a minor piece—usually the bishop—and after the recapture has surrendered a full piece for a pawn; a minority of boards instead show a bishop trade or a knight capture that either loses material or throws away a win.

787.label: The player chose a quiet, non-forcing move and squandered a winning attack, missing a decisive forcing continuation that was almost always a check (often a mating sacrifice).

785.chip: Hangs own piece after capture (queen often)
785.label: A greedy capture in the opening leaves the player's own material hanging to an immediate refutation—usually the queen on the open d-file (Qxd8/Qxd1), though in a few boards it's a rook or bishop lost to a queen check/fork.

774.chip: Queen check instead of winning capture
774.label: In every board White plays a tempting queen check instead of the correct simplifying queen capture (Qxd5/Qxf7+/Qxf6+); the core action is unanimous (queen, check-over-capture) but the consequence splits 5/5 — boards 2,6,7,8,9 hang the queen outright (often into mate), while boards 1,3,4,5,10 are materially safe and only throw away a won game, so direction is genuinely mixed.

782.chip: Mixed: hangs material or squanders edge
782.label: Genuinely mixed opening/early-middlegame feature: ~4 boards hang own material to a recapture/fork/zwischenzug (varied piece: bishop, knight, queen), ~3 miss a clean win or pawn break (fxe5, c5, c6), and ~3 squander an edge via a bad trade or positional drift — no single piece or mistake type dominates, and the SEE 'bishop/capture/losing 100%' signature is contradicted by the actual moves.

788.label: The played move (often a capture that strips a defender or opens a line) loses the player's own material, with the refutation winning a piece or pawn — the specific unit hung varies, so the invariant is material, not one piece.

791.chip: Hangs own piece with a check
791.label: A check that loses the player's own material (queen or rook, occasionally bishop) — every one of the top moves is a check that hangs the piece or trades it disastrously, throwing away a winning position.

786.label: Mixed self-inflicted-loss feature: most often a queen or king move that vacates a key defensive square or walks the king into trouble, allowing checkmate or loss of material (boards 1,3,4,7,8,10), but it also fires on non-forcing tempo/prophylactic moves that miss a clean win (g5, g6, Kf1) and one positional rook concession (Rf7), so the core is fuzzy though the queen is the central piece in nearly every refutation.

784.label: Plays a forcing, tempting check (most often a knight fork/discovery, sometimes a rook or queen) that throws away a winning position — usually the checking piece is simply captured, occasionally the check merely substitutes for a stronger winning capture or trade.

783.label: The played move loses the player's own material—donating a piece or pawn that the opponent captures, often with a tempo-gaining check against an exposed king—rather than choosing a safe alternative; the specific unit hung varies (knight/bishop/pawn), so no single piece is named.

778.label: Greedily captures a pawn with the knight (Ncxb5 / Nxb4) only to be immediately recaptured, hanging the knight for a single pawn in the opening (9/10 are knight grabs; one case hangs a bishop on Bxg4).

793.label: A developing/pinning move (usually a bishop, often Bb4 or Bb5) that leaves own material undefended and losing, while ~3 of 10 instead skip a clear win or mate; the hung piece varies so no single piece is decisive.

795.chip: Hangs own piece via capture (often queen)
795.label: In every position the player makes a move—usually a material-grabbing capture—that leaves their own piece undefended and loses it to the refutation, most often the queen but not always.

798.label: In a winning king-and-pawn endgame, plays a premature/wrong-order pawn advance (often dissolving connected passers, allowing a blockade, or under-promoting) that throws away the win rather than hanging material.

794.label: In every position the mistake centers on the queen: the player repeatedly fails to make an available winning/equalizing queen exchange, and in about half the boards literally hangs their own queen — usually by playing a move in the wrong order or ignoring the trade so the queen is captured (Qxa4, Qxf5, Qxh4, Qxe5, Qxb7), while the other half passively keep queens on and squander a win; direction is split between self-inflicted hangs and missed trades, so review is warranted.

779.label: Plays a natural-looking developing move that ignores an opponent's tactical threat in the opening — usually a knight fork on f7/c7 — hanging a piece or the exchange (one board is instead a missed rook capture).

802.label: In all ten positions the player overlooked an available capture of the opponent's queen (usually the only move to avoid mate or save the game) and instead played a losing move.

801.label: In every position the player loses their own rook — usually leaving it en prise for a free capture (Bxh8, Bxe1, Bxa1, Bxe2, Bxf8), and otherwise trading it badly for a bishop — squandering a winning position.

789.label: Advances a knight to a central outpost (often d4) that the opponent simply trades off, collapsing the position — sometimes positionally, sometimes losing material.

796.label: A move (usually the king itself) exposes the king to a decisive attack, either walking into checkmate or getting checked/forked into losing material (often a rook).

777.label: Predominantly (~7/10) plays a move that loses its own material to a tactical refutation—often a multi-move hang via pin, overload, or undefended/wrong-order piece, with the queen most often in the decisive line—though ~3 boards are instead missed winning-tactic omissions and the hung piece itself varies.

800.chip: Missed faster forcing win (often a check)
800.label: In mostly-winning endgames the player chooses a safe, slow continuation and overlooks a faster forcing win — usually a check (Rf2+, Rd4+, Rf4+, Nf6+ fork, d5+) or a pawn break (h5) — though about three of the flagged boards are actually 0cp non-blunders, so the feature is partly mixed.

730.label: Fires on moves that ignore the opponent's best immediate response—a capture, forcing trade, or tactic (frequently a knight fork/recapture)—which in most cases drops the player's own material but in others merely throws away a winning advantage via an unfavorable trade or passive retreat; mixed in piece and outcome.

799.label: In a winning middlegame the player skips the single critical winning resource (very often a knight move like Nxd4/Nf5+), letting a won position slip to lost or drawn.

807.chip: Trades rooks into lost pawn endgame
807.label: The feature captures rook trades that liquidate into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn endgame, where eliminating an enemy passed pawn by exchanging rooks removes the defender's only counterplay and lets an outside/connected pawn promote unstoppably.

804.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the king goes the wrong way, wasting a critical tempo and losing the passed-pawn promotion race rather than hanging any material.

813.label: A materially-safe developing or castling move is played in the opening, missing a forcing tactical shot (often a queen check like Qb4+, or a knight/queen fork) that wins material or a decisive advantage.

797.label: In the opening the player plays a slow developing or pawn-grabbing move instead of a forced winning tactical breakthrough — most often the e6 pawn break — letting a winning advantage drain to equality.

792.label: The feature mostly fires at critical endgame moments where the player botches a passed pawn or promotion—losing a pawn race (board 2), entering a lost pawn ending by grabbing material (board 3), promoting into a knight that captures the queen (board 4), or playing a king move instead of the winning immediate promotion (boards 5-6)—but it also catches two unrelated missed Bxg7 winning-exchange tactics (boards 7-8) and one false positive where the played capture was actually best (board 1), so it does not resolve to a single clean mistake.

790.label: In a (usually losing) rook endgame, the player makes a move that fails to blockade or stop the opponent's passed pawn — typically misplacing the rook instead of getting it behind the pawn — allowing it to promote; a minority of boards instead permit a mate or hang a rook.

805.label: The move ignores the forcing queen trade or queen capture the position demands, and is punished by hanging the player's own piece, allowing mate, or simply losing material.

806.chip: Missed winning capture in won endgame (often rook)
806.label: In a winning endgame the player advances a pawn or king toward promotion instead of making the simplest winning move (usually a free capture, frequently of a rook), throwing the win away.

809.label: In the d4-vs-e5 opening tension, Black plays an unrelated move instead of the forced ...exd4, allowing White to win the e5 pawn (sometimes escalating to a full piece) by Nxe5/dxe5 or a Bxf7+ shot.

814.label: A middlegame move that loses the player's own material to an immediate or short-term capture (the hung piece varies — queen, rook, or knight — so no single piece dominates), with a couple of boards instead just missing a material-winning capture.

812.chip: Quiet pawn move skips decisive play
812.label: From a winning position the engine plays a slow prophylactic/luft pawn push (h3/g3/h4/g6) instead of the decisive move — usually a forcing capture or forced mate it fails to grab (6/10), but in the rest failing to save its own attacked piece (4/10) — with the piece involved varying.

816.label: In the opening, the player captures a pawn with a knight (Nxe5 or Nxe4) that is then simply recaptured, hanging the knight for a pawn.

810.label: A middlegame material error—most often failing to grab a free or winning capture (frequently an enemy knight or bishop), but in a sizable minority hanging its own piece or walking into a knight fork—with a knight involved in the decisive tactic on most boards; direction is genuinely mixed between missed wins and self-hangs.

808.label: The player overlooks an undefended enemy bishop that could be captured for free, instead making a quiet move that lets the bishop escape to safety.

803.label: In a winning or drawing position the player plays a hasty forcing move—either a purposeless check (1,2,3) or a greedy / wrong-move-order capture (5,6,7,8,9,10)—that throws away the advantage, most often by hanging own material (frequently the queen) to a recapture or zwischenzug, with a couple of cases that simply miss a forced mate or stronger win.

815.chip: Trades active bishop for passive knight
815.label: Player captures a passive/undeveloped knight with their active bishop, an unfavorable trade that surrenders the superior minor piece (and occasionally drops material in the follow-up).

822.label: From an already-winning position the player makes a materially-safe but suboptimal move that throws away a forced mate or a decisive material gain, converting the win into a merely large advantage.

817.label: The player repeatedly squanders a winning advantage by choosing a slow or passive move instead of the decisive tactic/capture (mostly missed wins, though a couple of boards instead hang the player's own material), with no single piece consistent across positions.

827.label: Advances a (passed) pawn prematurely in an endgame instead of activating the king or choosing a sounder plan, squandering a winning or drawn position; two boards instead just hang a piece.

823.label: A materially-safe move that skips a winning material capture — almost always a queen capture (frequently of an undefended rook on d4) — turning a winning or holdable position into an inferior one.

820.chip: Abandons a defender (king or piece falls)
820.label: The move pulls a piece off its defensive role (or pushes a shielding pawn), after which the thing it was guarding collapses — about half the time a piece (usually a knight) hangs and half the time the king is exposed to a mating attack.

819.label: In king-and-pawn / passed-pawn endgames the player most often marches the king the wrong direction — blockading incorrectly, too slowly, or stepping away from where it's needed — squandering a win or worsening a loss, while the rest are a mixed bag (releasing pawn tension, trading a knight/bishop for a passer, hanging a knight).

828.chip: Trades queen via capturing check, missing win
828.label: Player plays a queen capture-with-check that gets recaptured by the king, needlessly trading the queen for inferior material (rook/minor/pawn) and squandering a forced mate or winning attack.

832.label: Fires on king-and-pawn / passed-pawn promotion-race endgames at the push-vs-king-activation decision; when a real error exists it's a tempo/move-order slip (wrong king move or pawn push) with no material lost, but 6 of 10 top boards are near-optimal 0–6cp moves rather than mistakes.

824.label: In already-lost positions the player — most often with a rook — makes a move that abandons a defensive duty and ignores the opponent's immediate decisive threat, usually allowing a forced checkmate (6/10) and otherwise dropping material (3/10), instead of the sole saving resource.

821.label: Across all 10 boards the player skipped an available winning capture of an undefended enemy piece (most often a bishop, usually grabbed by the queen), playing a quiet or positional move instead.

826.label: In all 10 boards the queen is the decisive piece, but the player's error is mixed: ~5 hang material to a queen capture, ~3 miss capturing an exposed/hanging enemy queen, and ~2 are bad queen trades or failed attacks on the queen — unified by misjudging a queen interaction rather than one consistent direction.

836.label: Plays a move that hangs the player's own material instead of taking the available simplifying queen trade that would neutralize the threat.

811.label: In the opening with the queen on d5 and Bg4 pinning Nf3, Black repeatedly skips the equalizing/material-winning 7...Bxf3 (or 6...Qxd4 / Qh5) in favor of a passive queen retreat, getting punished by 8.d5 advancing with tempo against the c6-knight (one board instead hangs the g4-bishop to hxg4).

829.chip: Hangs knight on the rim (pawn grab)
829.label: A piece—almost always a knight—wanders to a rim or corner square (often to snatch a pawn) where it gets trapped and lost over the next couple of moves, throwing away the player's advantage.

825.label: The player makes a tempting capture or aggressive (usually knight) move that pulls a piece off a critical defensive duty — guarding the king's zone or shielding a hanging piece — and the refutation either forces mate (about half the boards) or wins the now-undefended material in the rest.

837.chip: Missed winning capture in opening (knight captures)
837.label: In the opening the player repeatedly declines a free, material-winning knight capture (most often Nxe5 against an undefended piece/pawn) in favor of a quiet developing move, throwing away a winning advantage.

838.label: In passed-pawn and king-and-pawn endgames, the player makes an inferior king (occasionally knight) move that loses a tempo in the pawn race—failing to stop or escort the passer—rather than hanging any specific piece.

841.label: In every board a bishop is left on a square controlled by an enemy pawn (usually c5/f4/c4/b4/f5) and is captured for free in the opening — a self-inflicted hung bishop, even on boards 8 and 10 where the played move (O-O, Re8) ignores the already-attacked c5 bishop.

842.label: Moves a knight to an undefended square (g5/g4/h5/h4) in the opening where it is captured for free, almost always by the enemy queen.

839.label: In drawn/defensible endgames the player passively blockades or centralizes instead of playing the only saving active resource—usually a perpetual or defensive check (rook in ~9/10, queen once)—and loses; one board (Kd2) isn't actually a blunder, lowering consistency.

835.chip: Hangs own piece, skips winning capture (often a check)
835.label: In a winning position the player throws the game away by hanging their own piece — frequently with an unnecessary forcing check — instead of making the simple winning capture; the hung piece varies (rook/queen/bishop), so it's 'a piece', not one specific piece.

834.label: Voluntarily trades or gives up the active rook — the piece providing the winning counterplay — converting a winning/better position into a draw or loss (one board hangs the queen instead).

847.label: In nearly every position the player overlooks a free capture of a hanging enemy piece—almost always an undefended rook taken by the king—throwing away a winning material advantage.

846.label: Plays a premature, pointless queen check that—across all ten boards—drives the enemy king to safety while losing tempo, hanging the queen along a rank/diagonal, or skipping a forced win/mate.

845.label: An over-aggressive piece move (usually a rook, sometimes the queen) that chases or attacks an enemy piece while abandoning a critical defensive square or duty — sometimes hanging material over a few moves, sometimes just collapsing the position.

833.label: The feature mostly fires on premature pawn promotions (usually to a queen on an open file) that get immediately captured by a rook/king, throwing away a winning endgame when an intermediate check (zwischenzug) was needed first; a couple of boards instead show a hasty capture that trades away a forced mate, and one board isn't a blunder at all.

852.label: The player delivers a check with the queen onto a square defended by an enemy piece (almost always a bishop), and the queen is simply captured next move.

831.label: A move that fatally weakens or exposes the player's own king, allowing the opponent a forcing series of checks (usually forced mate) instead of keeping the king safe or holding the initiative.

850.label: Mixed feature: fires on single-move blunders that flip the evaluation — roughly six hang the player's own material (queen most often, also rook/bishop/pawn, frequently with an exposed central king) and four omit a forced win or mate, so neither direction nor piece is consistent.

853.label: Fires on rook moves played to attack/challenge the opponent's queen, which backfire by abandoning a defensive duty (usually hanging the player's own material, occasionally missing a stronger tactic instead).
