848.label: The player grabs material with a capture but overlooks the tactical refutation, hanging their own material — often allowing a recapture with check or even mate — and squandering the position.

840.label: Genuinely mixed: fires on game-losing blunders, of which ~4/10 are king moves that hang material (rook to a fork, bishop to checks) or abandon a defensive resource, while the rest are a greedy pawn-grab losing the exchange, two missed forced wins, a king-safety collapse into mate, and lost endgame technique—so no single piece or single direction (hang vs. miss) honestly fits all boards.

854.chip: Missed forcing win, grabbed material (exposed king)
854.label: Across all 10 boards the player skips a forcing checkmate or king-hunting attack against an exposed king, instead playing a slower/greedy material grab (frequently snatching a rook in the corner with the queen).

849.chip: Hangs piece via wrong capture order
849.label: The recurring mistake is a move-order error—grabbing a piece (usually with a pawn) before inserting the necessary intermezzo (typically trading bishops first), which leaves the player's own piece hanging; in ~8/10 boards this self-inflicts material loss, with the hung piece most often a bishop but occasionally a knight, while 2 boards are merely missed wins reaching equality.

861.label: Fires on king moves in endgames (mostly already-losing/drawn positions); the actual error is inconsistent — about half are real wrong-square/tempo or key-square losses, several are negligible or even optimal, and one walks the king into a skewer that drops a bishop.

859.label: The player repeatedly fires off an inferior queen check (always queen, always check) that lets the king escape into safety or perpetual, missing the stronger move — often a forced mate or winning sequence — that the position demanded.

855.label: The queen leaves a critical defensive duty—most often guarding the king, sometimes a hanging piece or key pawn—to chase offense, allowing a decisive attack or material loss.

844.label: In a winning opening the player plays a passive or careless non-best move that abandons the strongest continuation — usually a winning queen capture or mate (~6/10) — or else lets their own queen/piece fall in the refutation (~4/10), with a queen central to the decisive play on nearly every board.

856.label: In the opening, plays an unsound sacrifice or 'tempo-loss' move that drops the player's own material — bishop, queen, or pawn varies (often via an early queen sortie or f2/f7 theme) — though two of the ten boards instead miss a winning tactic.

860.label: Played a quiet, non-forcing move and skipped the available decisive forcing continuation — almost always a queen check that delivered mate or won material — squandering a winning position.

843.label: In the opening the player declines to recapture a sacrificed/hanging bishop with the king (almost always Kxf7), letting the opponent retreat the piece and squandering a free win.

830.label: The player makes a pawn move—almost always one attacking an enemy piece—instead of an available forcing line, missing a winning tactic or mate in most boards and hanging own material to the refutation in the rest.

858.label: Plays a slow, purposeless move (king shuffle or quiet pawn move) instead of the time-critical push of a passed pawn, wasting the one tempo needed and letting the pawn be blockaded — turning a winning or drawn position into a lost one.

864.label: A king move to an exposed square (or, in 2/10, a pawn push that strips the king's shield) walks the player's own king into a decisive check sequence — perpetual check that throws away a win, outright mate, or checks that win material.

869.chip: Wrong king square in K+P endgame
869.label: Fires on king moves in king-and-pawn endgames; about half are genuine blunders where the king goes to the wrong square (loses the opposition or fails to occupy the pawn's promotion/blockade square, letting the pawn queen), while the other half are 0cp non-blunders, so the feature is fuzzy and needs review.

870.chip: Missed capturing free hanging piece (opening pawn-grab)
870.label: In every one of the 10 opening positions the player declined a simple pawn capture of an undefended enemy piece (a knight in 8, a bishop in 2), giving it a tempo to escape and converting a winning material advantage into equality.

862.label: A material-grabbing capture or a careless king move neglects king safety and walks into a forced mate or decisive king attack, most often a back-rank or promotion-check mate.

863.label: In favorable positions the player chooses a simplifying capture or queen/piece trade that throws away the advantage—about six boards skip a stronger forcing tactic (fork/deflection/discovery) while four hang or walk into material loss, so the direction is genuinely mixed.

867.chip: Gives up queen unfavorably (sac or trade)
867.label: A queen move that unfavorably surrenders the queen — in 6/10 cases an unsound sacrifice/check that simply hangs it (e.g. Qh7+ Nxh7, Qh2+ Kxh2), and in 4/10 a premature queen trade that throws away a winning advantage; the piece given up is always the queen, but the direction splits between outright hang and bad trade.

873.label: In a won endgame the player throws a tempo-losing, usually pointless check (most often with the queen) that lets the opponent's king escape or counterplay arrive, reducing or squandering a decisive/forced-mate advantage instead of the precise consolidating move.

871.label: Plays a counterproductive check (almost always a rook check) that loses a tempo, lets the opponent's king improve to a safer/more active square, and squanders the player's winning or better position — occasionally hanging the checking piece outright.

865.label: In the opening the player botches a material/capture decision with a knight usually the focal piece — most often declining to grab a free hanging piece (6/10, e.g. skipping cxd5/dxe4/bxc3), but in ~4/10 instead hanging its own piece or ignoring a refuting tactic (Nc3 into dxc3, Nf6 into exf6, d6 into Qh5+); direction is genuinely mixed, flag for review.

851.label: In a winning or mating endgame the player throws the result away with an inferior king/queen move — often outright hanging the queen, but sometimes only missing the fastest win — with a queen central to every position.

875.label: A move that loses the player's own material—usually by stripping away a key defender or walking into a tactic/king attack—where the hung unit varies across boards (pawn, bishop, knight, rook, even the queen), so no single piece can be honestly named.

868.label: Across all 10 boards the queen is the decisive piece the player loses—7 by leaving it en prise (directly or by a pawn move that opens a line, e.g. Qd7→Rxd7, exf5→Rxe7, Qd4+→Nxd4) and 3 by a queen trade that drops material or throws away a winning position—so the unifying feature is queen loss, though the hang-vs-trade mechanism varies enough to warrant review.

866.label: Plays a move that loses material—usually self-inflicted, dropping its own piece within the refutation (knight frequently in the mix), with the specific hung piece varying and a couple of cases being missed winning tactics instead.

884.label: The queen greedily captures a piece that is defended (often capturing a rook), and is immediately recaptured—frequently with check or mate—losing the queen for inadequate material.

877.label: The move directly drops the player's own material — leaving a piece (most often a rook, but also bishop or knight) en prise for a free capture, frequently via a pointless 'spite' check or greedy grab that ignores the hanging unit.

882.label: A tempo move meant to attack/chase the opponent's queen instead leaves the player's own piece (queen, rook, or knight — it varies) hanging and lost by force.

881.label: A move that abandons a defensive duty or steps onto an attacked square, losing the player's own material (the specific piece varies — pawns, rook, bishop, or knight) over the next one-to-three moves.

878.label: In every position the player passed up a clearly winning capture (most often of a bishop) in favor of a quiet, retreating, or wrong-move-order move that squandered the material/advantage.

879.chip: Trades off knight into lost endgame
879.label: Liquidates the knight—the only active/defensive piece, often for just a pawn—turning a drawn or defensible position into a lost pawn or rook endgame.

883.label: A move (frequently a king move) that exposes the player's own king to a decisive attack — checks leading to a skewer, fork, or mating net that wins material or forces mate; the exact piece lost varies (queen in some, mate in others), so the invariant is king exposure rather than one specific hung piece.

876.label: In winning endgames the player fails to convert—hanging its own queen or missing a winning queen capture/mate—with a queen central to nearly every board's decisive tactics, though 3 of 10 are actually best moves (not mistakes) and the direction (hang vs. miss) is split.

880.chip: Slow rook maneuver over forcing move
880.label: The player prefers a slow, thematic rook maneuver (doubling on an open file, a rook lift, or a rook swing) over the concrete forcing continuation—most often missing a forced mate or decisive win (6/10), but in about a third of cases the slow rook move itself hangs a piece (knight, pawn+tempo, or even the queen), so the outcome direction is mixed even though the misbehavior is consistent.

888.label: A self-inflicted check — almost always a knight check (Ng4+/Ng5+/Nxe5+) — that loses the player's own material, since the opponent calmly captures the checking piece (or wins material in the short refutation) rather than fearing the check.

889.label: A self-inflicted opening/early-middlegame move that loses the player's own material—most boards drop a piece outright (knight on e5/h6, queen on f2, bishop left undefended) or greedily grab a pawn and drop more (boards 1,2,3,5,7,10), with a couple also entombing a piece (8) or giving back material in a clumsy exchange (9), while two are really positional/missed-win errors (boards 4,6), so the hung piece type and exact mechanism vary.

874.label: In all 10 positions the player ignored a hanging or dangerous enemy rook (the clear best move was always to capture it — Rxf2, Qxg7, Nxe7, Qxe2, Qxc3, Nxe6, Nxg2, etc.) and instead made a lesser capture or pawn grab, squandering the win or inviting a losing counterattack.

857.label: Genuinely mixed middlegame feature: exactly half the boards hang material or allow mate by moving a piece (the queen in most) off its defensive post (Ne6 drops Bh4, Qa6 allows mate-in-2, Qg5/Qc8 abandon c7/e3 pawns, b6 leaves Bg7 en prise), while the other half are clean missed wins (the Qxd1+/Nf2+ back-rank fork twice, Qh6 mate threat, Rxd8+, free Rxd4); the only reliable thread is a queen/piece move that fails the position's decisive tactic, with no consistent direction or single piece, so the first labeler was essentially right.

872.label: In a winning/forcing position the player chooses an inferior move — frequently a premature check or a move-order/tempo error — that hands the opponent a defensive resource, throwing away a much larger win, a forced mate, or letting own material fall (the squandered/hung piece varies: pawn, bishop, rook/exchange), so no single piece can be named and the direction is mixed between missed-win and self-inflicted loss.

886.label: The player squanders a winning or defensible position by playing a quiet, natural-looking move instead of the available forcing move (in ~8/10 boards a check that wins material, forces a won trade, or mates), often then allowing a decisive counterattack against its own king.

887.label: From a winning opening the player skips a decisive knight blow (most often Nxg6, sometimes Nxb3/Ng3+/Nxg3) and the advantage collapses; 9/10 boards have a knight in the winning line and 8/10 are missed wins, though two boards instead hang the player's own queen.

885.label: In a mostly winning position, a quiet/greedy move (often king centralization or a pawn-grab) overlooks the position's tactic, usually hanging the player's own material or walking into mate (king ×3, knight ×3, queen ×1), though ~3/10 instead simply miss a winning capture — so direction is mixed.

895.label: Across all ten boards the player throws away a winning position by playing a slow/passive move (or a careless trade) instead of the forcing line that removes the blockader and pushes the passed pawn to promotion.

893.label: From a favorable position the player chooses a safe but inferior continuation—frequently a needless/wrong queen trade or a missed stronger check or fork—squandering the win rather than hanging material outright (one board is an outright greedy capture).

891.label: In most positions the player shuns or fumbles a queen exchange that was the engine's best move, instead playing an active (often queen) move that hangs material or squanders the advantage; the specific material lost varies (pawn, knight, or none), so the true invariant is the missed queen trade rather than any one hung piece.

892.label: Plays a forcing check that captures a rook with the queen, but the queen is immediately recaptured, trading queen for rook and throwing away the game.

894.label: In a mostly winning/holdable endgame the player makes a king step or queen move that loses material on the 2nd-3rd move of the refutation—usually the queen, via a knight fork or by leaving it undefended—but the feature is mixed: ~6/10 hang material, 2 are missed forced mates, one is a tempo slip, and one is a false positive.

903.label: Recaptures/trades a rook to 'simplify,' removing the last back-rank defender and walking straight into a forced back-rank checkmate (one board instead loses to passed pawns after the same first-rank capture).

899.label: The rook captures a single pawn on a defended square and is immediately recaptured, throwing away the rook (usually a full exchange) for just a pawn.

901.label: In the opening, the player hangs an unprotected piece — most often the queen, but a bishop in several cases — by making a developing/supporting move that ignores an existing attack or steps onto an attacked square.

897.label: In nearly every board the player advances a KNIGHT to attempt a fork/attack, but it abandons a key defensive or blocking role and is refuted — most lines lose the player's own material (bishop or knight) while several instead allow a forced mating attack, so the punished outcome is mixed (hung piece vs. mate) and no single hung piece dominates.

900.chip: Losing king move in passed-pawn endgame
900.label: In endgames dominated by a passed pawn, the player (usually with a king move) mishandles the situation and worsens an already-losing position — variously hanging a rook/knight, letting a pawn promote, or missing the only saving/winning path — so the unifying error is a losing endgame king move rather than one specific hung piece.

905.label: Mixed feature that mostly fires on throwing away a better/winning position by hanging own material — knight (boards 2,3,4), bishop (7,9), or pawn (8) — but ~4/10 are instead tempo-loss or greedy captures (1,5,6,10) that miss the decisive move rather than directly hanging a piece, so no single piece or position-state dominates.

906.label: A move that abandons a defensive duty or exposes the king and lets the opponent win the player's own material — but the hung unit varies (rook, knight, or pawn), so no single piece can be named.

902.label: In an endgame the player makes a self-inflicted, losing major-piece move that either hangs the piece outright (≈6/10, rook or queen) or trades into a lost king-and-pawn endgame (≈4/10), turning a drawn/holdable position into a loss.

896.label: An opening move — often a flank pawn poking an enemy bishop while ignoring central tension — that hangs the player's own material via a short tactic (the specific piece lost varies, so it's 'a piece', not one consistent piece).

907.label: From a winning/advantageous position the player plays a passive 'safe' move and misses the single forcing winning continuation—most often a passed-pawn breakthrough or promotion race in the endgame (e5+, g4, e2)—occasionally instead hanging own material or blundering into mate, converting a clear win into a loss.

910.label: Fires on a queen check (occasionally a non-checking queen move) in an endgame that backfires—most often it allows/offers a queen trade into a lost pawn endgame (1,5,6,7,9), but it also covers checks that waste a tempo and help the enemy king instead of grabbing a free pawn or winning resource (2,3,10) and ones that outright hang the queen (4,8); the only constant is the player's queen in decisive endgame play, so the specific error is genuinely mixed.

904.label: Plays a material-grabbing capture that removes a critical defender (or ignores a stronger in-between threat), collapsing the player's own position within a few moves.

909.label: Player makes a capture (or pawn move) that opens a file/diagonal toward their own king or strips a key defender, exposing material or the king to a decisive tactic — though several boards are already-lost positions where the move is near-best, plus one pure positional error, making the core only partially uniform.

890.label: In a (usually winning) position the player fires off a tempting forcing move—most often a queen check—instead of the precise continuation, throwing the advantage away by either missing a forced mate/win (boards 1,2,4,5,10) or hanging the queen/rook (boards 3,6,7,9), so the unifying element is the impulsive check/forcing move rather than any single piece or outcome.

908.chip: Hangs a piece in winning position
908.label: A move that leaves the player's own piece (rook, bishop, knight or even queen) en prise, throwing away a winning position; the specific piece varies across boards, so no single piece is named.

913.label: A slow, passive, or 'tempo-wasting' move that ignores a live tactical threat and lets the player's own material fall — usually self-inflicted, though the hung unit varies (queen, knight, or pawn) and a couple of boards are instead a missed capture or an allowed mate.

918.label: The player repeatedly skips a forcing tactical win — usually a queen check delivering mate or winning material against an exposed king — in favor of a quieter, non-forcing move.

920.label: In all ten positions the player skipped a free capture of the opponent's hanging queen (most often with Nxd4/Nxd5-type knight grabs), playing a quiet developing move and throwing away a winning advantage.

915.label: Prematurely advances a passed pawn instead of activating the king/pieces first, letting the pawn be blockaded or captured and throwing away a winning or drawing advantage.

924.label: Develops a bishop to g4/g5 in the opening where it is completely undefended and simply captured for free by the opposing queen, losing a full piece.

919.label: In a winning endgame the player repeatedly overlooks the decisive forcing continuation (a forced mate or material-winning tactic) and plays a passive/greedy move that lets the win slip to a draw or even a loss.

914.chip: Poor rook move loses holdable position (rook)
914.label: The player mishandles their rook—usually by placing it passively (1,2,9,10), occasionally by hanging it (6,8) or trading it into a lost pawn endgame (3,5,7)—surrendering the rook's activity and converting a drawn or defensible position (often an endgame) into a loss; the rook is the decisive piece in nearly every board even though the precise mechanism is mixed.

912.label: From a winning/won position the player fails to play the decisive move (frequently a free capture of the enemy queen, or a forced mate), either missing the win outright (boards 1,2,6,7,9) or playing a move that hangs their own piece — usually a rook (boards 3,5,8,10) or queen (board 4) — so the recurring core is 'throws away the win', but the direction (omission vs self-inflicted hang) and the piece involved both vary, hence low confidence.

898.chip: Abandons key pawn, blows won endgame
898.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a king or capture move that abandons a strategically critical pawn or square, squandering a winning (or drawn) position.

916.label: In passed-pawn endgames, plays an imprecise move that loses the promotion race—failing to advance or support its own passer (or to stop/clear the blockader of the opponent's) when one exact move was required.

917.label: A self-inflicted move—often a structure-weakening f-pawn push or an undefended developed piece—that loses the player's own material, but the unit lost (rook, bishop, knight, or pawn) varies too much to name one.

921.label: A materially-safe move that squanders a winning or drawn position by missing the forcing material-winning continuation, almost always in the opening, with the winning target varying (bishop, knight, pawn) and one outlier that actually hangs its own piece.

928.label: A materially-safe but passive move that overlooks an available winning tactical shot (often a knight capture/fork), forfeiting a clear material advantage — an omission, not a hang.

931.label: In endgame pawn races the player mishandles the opponent's passed pawn — walking the king into promotion-with-check, failing to capture/blockade the runner, or trading off the only defender — letting it promote.

925.label: An opening bishop sortie to g4 or g5 that loses material — most often the bishop itself is won after a defender is deflected (Nxf6+) or a pawn (f3/f6) kicks it, though a couple of cases are pure tempo loss or a missed Ng5 win.

932.chip: Missed fastest win in won endgame (king move)
932.label: In a winning endgame the player makes a slow king (or other) move that keeps the win but squanders the fastest forced route — typically a pawn promotion or forced mate — though several flagged boards are negligible/non-blunders and one is a flat hung rook.

923.label: From a winning position the player misses a forcing knight capture on the c-file (Nxc6/Nxc3) that wins material, instead playing a slow or wrong-move-order move that squanders the advantage.

929.label: In opening positions built around a Bg4-pin on Nf3 (where Bxf3 — or keeping f3 pressure — was the right resolving move, ~7/10 boards), the player makes a move ignoring the tension that either drops a minor piece in the multi-move refutation (~6/10, e.g. Nxd4 then Bxg4) or fatally exposes the uncastled king/structure (~4/10); the f3-knight/Bg4 pin is the recurring element, but the resulting mistake type is mixed and 3 boards (trapped Ba5, hanging Be4, Nd5) don't fit the pin theme at all.

933.label: A greedy/distracting capture (usually a pawn grab) abandons a defensive duty and lets the player's own piece fall, turning a winning or holdable middlegame into a loss; the hung piece varies (queen, rook, bishop, knight).

922.label: Fires on aggressive, active-looking moves (often pawn thrusts like ...e5/...f5/...g4, but also rook sorties and a greedy ...Qxd4+) that collapse an equal or winning position; most are punished by the player's own material being captured in the refutation (queen on d4, rook on d6/g7, bishop on g2), while a few are pure positional weakenings (e5/f5 ceding key squares) or missed wins (Kc7/g4+ skipping a material-winning capture), so the mechanism is mixed and no single piece or state is consistent.

926.chip: Hangs queen, throwing away forced mate
926.label: In every position the player gives up their strongest piece to a simple king recapture (Kx... on all 10 boards)—queen in 8, rook in 2—abandoning an available forced mate/win and converting it into a 'merely winning' position; queen is the typical piece (~80%) so the rook cases warrant a human glance.

934.label: A self-inflicted opening blunder that loses the player's own material to a forcing capture/recapture sequence (the specific piece varies — knight, bishop or queen — with a pinned f3-knight recurring in several lines).

935.label: In a winning opening, the player makes a safe-looking retreat or developing move instead of capturing the undefended enemy knight on h5/h4 with the queen (8/10), squandering a free piece — with two boards instead missing a Bxf7+ tactic.

936.label: Across all ten boards the player passes up the elementary h-pawn capture (almost always hxg4) that wins a hanging enemy bishop on g4, instead playing a quiet developing or pawn move and squandering a winning material advantage.

939.label: On most boards the player overlooks a tactical refutation (recapture, fork, or opened diagonal) and loses their own material — but the hung piece varies (bishop, knight, queen) and 3-4 boards are instead missed wins or bad trades/endgames rather than clean hangs, so a human should review.

927.label: In the opening, the player ignores an enemy pawn attacking one of their minor pieces and plays another move (often a pawn push), leaving the piece to be captured for free.

911.label: A forcing/aggressive move (most often a bishop capture, occasionally a check or pawn break) made from a winning or favorable position that squanders the advantage — roughly 6/10 boards by leaving the player's own piece hanging (frequently the queen) and ~4/10 by missing a stronger capture or a forced mate, so direction is genuinely mixed.

945.label: In a 100%-winning position the player plays a safe/natural pawn push or king move that throws away an available forced checkmate (mate-in-1 or mate-in-2), though the feature is mixed: ~7/10 are missed forced mates, 1 loses a win via wrong move order, and 2 are instead self-inflicted material hangs (e7 dropping the queen, Rc1 allowing Bxb4+).

947.label: In every position the player overlooked a forced checkmate-in-one delivered by a queen capture (most often Qxg2#) and played an irrelevant move instead, throwing away the immediate win.

942.label: A bishop is developed to harass the enemy queen with apparent tempo in the opening, but the move is unsound: in about 60% of cases it hangs material (an undefended b7/b2/g7 pawn, or the bishop itself via an Nxf6+ deflection), and in the rest it merely wastes tempo letting the queen improve or skips a stronger move.

938.chip: Hangs a piece grabbing a pawn
938.label: The played move is a capture—frequently grabbing a passed pawn or trading off a defender—that backfires in the middlegame and self-inflicts loss of material (most often a rook or the exchange via a recapture/opened file, occasionally walking into mate).

937.label: A move that neglects the king's defense — often abandoning a critical square near the king (f7 recurs) — allowing the opponent a decisive attack, frequently forced checkmate.

941.label: Each move directly hangs the player's own material with no compensation (mostly a full piece, occasionally a pawn), but the lost unit varies across boards — knight, bishop, rook, and pawn — so the invariant is self-inflicted material loss rather than any one specific piece.

940.label: In nearly every position the player fails to play the tempo-gaining knight jump to the d5/d4 central outpost (often setting up the Nxc7 fork), instead choosing a passive/wrong move that squanders the advantage or invites the opponent's own Nd5.

943.chip: Squanders advantage with passive move (forcing queen trade skipped)
943.label: The player throws away a winning or equal position by choosing a slow, non-forcing move instead of an available forcing capture/trade (frequently a queen trade), with outcomes split between hanging own material and simply missing a win.

953.label: In a winning position the player skips a forced mate or material-winning tactic, instead playing a slow/tempo move (frequently just chasing the enemy queen).

952.label: The played move self-inflicts material loss by leaving the player's own piece en prise (most often the queen, sometimes a rook traded/given into a lost position) for immediate capture.

948.label: A self-inflicted move that drops the player's own material—most often the queen, but sometimes a rook/exchange—to a tactical refutation that frequently arrives via an intermezzo or discovered check.

944.label: A greedy material grab or careless move that hangs the player's own piece — varying between rook (≈6/10) and queen (≈4/10) — to an immediate recapture or short tactic, turning a worse position into a lost one.

954.label: Captures material (most often snapping off the opponent's queen) instead of playing the available forced checkmate or stronger winning tactic.

950.chip: Misses the winning move (often a fork)
950.label: Repeatedly fails to play the precise winning continuation — frequently a knight/bishop fork — squandering a winning or clearly better position by choosing a passive or greedy alternative instead.

930.label: Player repeatedly declines the engine's Bxb2/Bxb7 capture of the undefended b-pawn on the fianchetto long diagonal, missing a free pawn — though in several boards the chosen move also hangs the player's own material.

949.label: In a winning opening position the player plays a quiet developing or retreating move and overlooks a decisive queen move — almost always a check or capture (Qxe5+, Qh5+, Qxd4+, Qa4+, Qxf7#) — throwing away the win and drifting to equality.

962.label: A queen move that offers or allows a queen exchange, liquidating the player's most powerful attacking asset and converting a winning or holding position into equality or loss.

951.label: Plays a tempo-wasting move—frequently a pointless check—instead of the forcing capture that wins or holds material, throwing away the advantage.

946.label: A knight move—usually retreating or recentralizing the attacked knight instead of the correct central break (often ...d5)—that loses material or throws away the advantage in the opening; the knight is the acting piece but only ~2/10 actually hang it outright.

957.label: Plays a materially-safe move that overlooks a tactic (Rb1/Ra1/Bc3/Rb8/c6-type) which traps or wins the opponent's exposed queen, letting it escape and squandering a winning advantage.

963.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a slow king move instead of the decisive ...f5/e5 pawn break, missing the win or only draw — but ~half the boards are non-blunders where the king move is actually optimal (plus one unrelated rook-trade error).

965.label: In the opening, the player repeatedly passes up a winning free capture of the opponent's undefended (usually fianchetto-flank) bishop on h6/h3, playing a routine developing/castling move instead of grabbing the hanging piece.

960.label: In a winning passed-pawn endgame, the player advances a pawn (or makes a slow move) instead of capturing the lone enemy piece blockading/stopping promotion, throwing away the win.

961.label: A move that pulls a piece off its critical defensive duty (or the king's safe square), self-inflicting either a lost piece/pawn or a forced mate, usually in an already-losing position.

967.label: The player makes a materially-safe queen move (often a check) that squanders an available forced mate or material win, missing a more forcing line — typically with another piece (rook/bishop/knight) — that was clearly winning.

964.label: A move that walks into the opponent's immediate refutation (usually a queen check, pin, or trap), self-inflicting loss of material or even checkmate; because the hung material ranges from queen to bishop to exchange to outright mate (and one board is a missed win), no single piece can be honestly named.

955.label: The player skips a material-saving exchange — almost always a defensive queen trade (Qxc6/Qxe6/Qxd6/Qxf6/Qxe7/Qxe3, etc., with two rook-trades) — and the move played instead hangs a piece or invites a decisive attack.

959.chip: Idle move ignores tactic, hangs material
959.label: The player makes an irrelevant/idle move (king shuffle, aimless pawn push, or wrong-piece move) that overlooks the live tactic and loses material in the refutation; the hung piece varies (rook most common, also bishop, knight, queen, or even allowing mate), and in 8/10 the move also skips an available winning or saving capture.

956.label: A move that collapses a winning/holdable position — in the opening by grabbing a piece (dxe7) but hanging the queen to Bxf2+, and in the endgame by mishandling the king/pawns so the opponent's passed pawn promotes — but the mechanism and piece vary too much to name one specific thing hung.

969.label: In a winning or drawn endgame, plays a careless move (often a reflexive check) that leaves the rook en prise, hanging it and converting the result to a lost king-and-pawn ending.

973.label: The feature fires on rook moves—usually an early 'rook lift' to the 3rd or 6th rank—that leave the rook undefended on an exposed square, where it is simply captured (typically by a bishop) for the loss of the exchange.

978.label: In all ten middlegame positions the player makes a safe but passive move and overlooks a winning knight fork (usually Ne2+/Nd6+/Nb6+) that would win the enemy queen — a clear omission, not a self-hang.

972.label: In nearly every position the player skips a simple, available capture of a hanging enemy piece (or a winning pawn break) that wins material, instead playing a materially-safe but non-winning move.

970.label: Player plays a slow, greedy, or natural move that overlooks a decisive forcing resource — most often a checkmate (5 mate-in-1, 2 allowed mates) — with the remaining boards missing a winning or drawing resource in passed-pawn endgames.

975.label: A move that fatally compromises the player's own king safety—most often castling directly into a prepared attack, but also pawn pushes/captures that strip the king's shield—exposing the king to a decisive assault or forced mate.

968.chip: Weakening pawn push in lost endgame
968.label: In an already-losing endgame the player makes a pawn advance or capture that either concedes the pawn or wrecks their own structure, hastening the loss rather than holding the line.

974.label: The player makes a capturing exchange (usually a rook, frequently with check) that simplifies the position and throws away a forced mate or winning tactic that a more precise non-trading move would have delivered.

966.label: In a winning/better middlegame the player throws the advantage away — most often by greedily capturing or 'eliminating a dangerous' pawn (7/10) — but the punishment is mixed: about half the boards simply miss a decisive material-winning capture (Nxe7, Kxc5, Bxd5, Nxe3) while the rest hang own material straight into a mating net (Rxf2, Qxb6, g4, Qxf3), so direction (missed-win vs self-hang) is not consistent.

1110.label: In a winning position the player plays a quiet safe move and skips a winning capture (frequently a king grabbing a hanging bishop), but the feature is mixed — about 6/10 are missed winning captures while 4/10 are unrelated tempo/positional/endgame drops.

1099.label: A quiet or wrong-move-order move that fails to resolve a knight exchange/tension at the critical moment — a knight is the decisive tactical piece in all 10 refutations — most often losing the player's own material (≈6 boards: hangs a piece/exchange/queen or gets the king mated) but sometimes merely skipping a winning knight capture (≈4 boards), so the direction is genuinely mixed around a single knight-timing core.

1101.label: In every position the player had a decisive forcing continuation—almost always a check, sometimes a forced mate—but instead played a passive, greedy, or king move that threw away the win.

1119.label: In every opening position the player skipped a material-winning capture made by their own knight (Nxd4/Nxe4/Nxc4/Nxe5/Nxd5), instead playing a safe developing or prophylactic move that threw away the win.

1102.chip: Misses forcing rook trade (back rank/open file)

1117.label: In a winning/holding endgame the player makes a materially-safe but suboptimal king or pawn move that throws away the win or draw — an omission (e.g. failing to grab a hanging rook with Bxc6, missing Kxe6, or putting the king on the wrong square) rather than hanging its own material; the missed element varies, so it is best described as a missed win rather than tied to one piece.

1109.chip: Misses winning forcing move (often knight check)

1123.label: A quiet/developing move that passes up a forcing winning tactic against the enemy king (frequently the Greek Gift Bxh7+ sacrifice), though two of the ten instead hang the player's own piece.

1124.label: In all 10 positions the player plays a quiet/slow move and skips a winning forcing CHECK — either mate-in-one or a check that wins material — and the winning shot is delivered by the queen in 9 of 10 cases.

1125.label: Greedily captures the enemy queen (often ...Bxd1) in the wrong move order, so the opponent recaptures the queen and the player nets a lost piece — or even gets mated — instead of winning the available material.

1122.chip: Self-inflicted loss: hangs piece or mate

1120.chip: Missed decisive move when winning (often free capture)
1120.label: In winning positions (mostly endgames) the player skips the decisive move—most often failing to capture an undefended enemy piece (queen/rook/bishop/knight, varies), but a sizable minority are tempo-wasting rook checks plus one outright self-hang and one non-blunder, so the feature is mixed and only loosely centered on missed wins.

1115.chip: Skips rook exchange, hangs material (rook tension)

1132.label: In pawn endgames the player makes a committal pawn advance that ruins their own structure — letting the opponent fix, bypass (often h5!), or liquidate the pawns into a loss, rather than holding with king moves or keeping tension.

1116.label: The player makes a developing or move-order move that ignores an existing threat, leaving their own major piece en prise—most often the queen, sometimes a rook—for a self-inflicted loss of material.

1133.label: A materially-safe (usually greedy capturing) move that overlooks a forced back-rank checkmate, so the player wins material instead of delivering mate.

1136.label: The played move places the player's own piece (knight, bishop, queen, or even a pawn — it varies) directly on a square where it is immediately captured for free, a self-inflicted one-move material blunder, often delivered as an aggressive but unsupported check.

1137.label: A premature king move in the opening that forfeits castling rights and leaves the king exposed in the center, conceding tempo and often material to a quick refutation.

1142.label: A move that leaves the player's rook undefended and immediately captured by the enemy queen (e.g. Qxa1/Qxa8/Qxh1/Qxh8), with one board instead hanging the queen to a diagonal fork.

1141.label: In the opening, the player makes a self-inflicted material loss—hanging their own piece or pawn (most often a bishop to a d-pawn capture, but also pawns)—dropping from equality into a losing position.

1150.label: In losing/sharp pawn endgames the player makes a king (or pawn) move that wastes a critical tempo — heading the wrong direction or capturing an irrelevant pawn — letting the opponent win the promotion race rather than racing the king toward the decisive pawns.

1139.label: The player sends a rook off to chase or grab a wing pawn (or otherwise abandons its key central/supporting duty), throwing away a winning or clearly better position.

1148.label: A natural-looking developing or pawn move (often castling/a pawn push) that self-inflicts the loss of the player's own material to a tactical refutation a move or two later, with the hung material varying (pawn, knight, exchange, or queen) so no single piece dominates, mostly in the opening.

1145.label: Plays a move—frequently a premature promotion, but also unfavorable trades or greedy captures—that loses the player's own material and liquidates into a lost position.

1146.label: Fires on queen-driven tactics centered on one undefended piece (usually a bishop, the queen decisive on nearly every board), but direction is mixed: ~6/10 miss a free queen capture of an enemy piece while ~4/10 hang the player's own piece.

1155.label: Player moves a knight to a square where it is immediately captured — hanging the knight for inadequate compensation — most often jumping to f5/f6 to attack the queen, though two of ten outliers hang a bishop (Bd6) or merely lose tempo (h4).

1149.label: The player repeatedly overlooks a stronger material-winning capture—frequently an undefended piece or a capture delivered with check—and instead grabs the wrong piece or makes a safe-looking move, squandering a winning position.

1159.label: A pawn push or capture that dissolves a locked/drawn pawn structure, handing the opponent a decisive passed pawn or king penetration and converting a held/drawn position into a loss.

1160.chip: Trades rook into lost pawn endgame
1160.label: Offers a rook exchange that transitions into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn endgame.

1151.label: In a losing middlegame the player skips the only defensive move (usually a rook move) and instead plays one that hangs material or exposes their king to a forced mating attack — the hung unit varies (rook, bishop, or the king itself), so no single piece can be named.

1166.label: The player delivers a queen check that is immediately captured by the opponent's queen, hanging the queen outright (all 10 boards are a queen check refuted by QxQ).

1154.label: In already-difficult endgames the player makes a self-inflicting pawn advance or piece relocation that abandons a strong/defensive square, worsening the position or losing material over the next moves, though the specific piece and error subtype (material hang, tempo loss, or back-rank mate) vary too much to name one confidently.

1162.label: The played move ignores or enables a knight tactic (fork, capture, or mate) that costs material or mates — a knight is the punishing weapon in all 10 boards, but the piece actually lost varies (queen, rook/exchange, bishop, knight) so no single piece can be named.

1163.label: A tempting forcing move (check, capture, or pawn push) that squanders a winning or near-equal position by failing to find the precise best continuation; the direction (greedy grab vs. omission vs. occasional hang) and the piece involved both vary across boards, and 2/10 are not actually blunders.

1144.label: On about half the boards the player greedily grabs material—usually the enemy queen—and overlooks a forced refutation (mate-in-one/few or a missed perpetual/win), but the rest are a mixed bag of hanging a piece via a non-capturing king/bishop move, a failed sacrifice, and pointless 'hope' checks, so the feature is not cleanly one mistake.

1158.label: In the opening the player drops a piece — usually a knight via a greedy/loose move (Nxe5, Nxe4, Nd4, Ne5) that a simple recapture wins for at most a pawn — with two outlier Bc5 moves that likewise leak material a couple moves later.

1164.label: The player repeatedly overlooks a free winning capture—most often snatching the undefended enemy queen (via a knight fork or a mutual-attack diagonal/rank), or at least winning a piece—and instead plays a materially-safe lesser move that throws away the decisive material.

1172.label: Plays a slow non-forcing move and misses a decisive winning attack on the enemy king, usually a queen check / king hunt that wins material or mates.

1167.label: Plays an irrelevant or distracting move (often a slow positional/pawn push) that ignores an immediate decisive threat—usually a forced mate against its own king—and gets punished by checkmate or a crushing attack.

1170.chip: Squanders winning position via material decision

1174.label: A materially-safe move—almost always the queen offering a trade—that throws away a forced checkmate or decisive win, downgrading it into a merely winning position.

1161.label: The player makes a materialistic capture or queen trade (often recapturing or swapping the queen) that is roughly material-safe but throws away a much stronger forced win or checkmate; a couple of boards even let the grabbed material hang to a fork, so direction is mostly omission with some self-inflicted cases.

1177.label: Plays a natural opening/developing move but overlooks a forcing queen check (Qa4+/Qa5+/Qh4+/Qh5+) that wins material by exploiting the exposed enemy king or a weakened diagonal.

1178.label: In all 10 positions the player skips a one-move queen capture of an undefended rook with check (9/10 are Qxa1+, one Qxc8+) and instead plays a materially-safe quiet move, letting the rook escape — a clear omission, not a self-inflicted hang.

1176.label: In the opening, the player makes a move that loses their own material—the specific piece varies (queen, knight, bishop, or pawn)—typically by ignoring the central pawn tension instead of simply recapturing.

1169.label: The player makes a move that fails to address the opponent's existing decisive threat—most often an immediate king-side mating attack (Qg2#, back-rank Rd1#, etc.), sometimes a material-winning tactic—either by playing an unrelated move, removing a critical defender, or stepping the king/queen into the attack, and is crushed; the punished outcome varies between mate (~6/10) and material loss (~4/10), so no single piece is decisive on every board.

1184.label: In every position the player passes up a winning/equalizing knight capture in the opening (Nxd5/Nxe4/Nxd4/Nxe5 — usually grabbing a centralized enemy piece) in favor of a slow developing or castling move, so it is an omission rather than hanging their own material.

1173.label: The player makes a move—most often retreating or deflecting the queen (6/10 are queen moves), or pushing a pawn that vacates/opens a line (b3, c3, a5)—that strips their own king of its last defender or shelter, allowing decisive checks or mate; 2-3 boards instead miss a forcing win (Qe5+, Ne6+, Qxe5).

1165.label: The player makes an unfavorable, voluntary capturing exchange — almost always a bishop trade — that relieves tension to the opponent's benefit, squandering an existing advantage (and occasionally backfiring into a lost/trapped piece) instead of playing a stronger non-capturing move.

1189.label: In the opening the player makes a move that ignores a bishop bearing down the open diagonal on the undefended queen (Bxd8/Bxd1), losing the queen for a bishop.

1181.label: In most positions the player plays a passive move and overlooks a free capture of the opponent's undefended queen, while a couple instead hang their own rook.

1183.label: In an endgame the defending side plays an inferior move that fails the best defensive resource (a saving capture, drawing trade, or king centralization), converting a draw to a loss or accelerating a forced mate — though several boards are already lost and a couple are not real errors.

1180.label: Across the boards the recurring fault is a self-inflicted losing move — dropping the player's own material (knight, pawn, queen, rook, or the exchange) or fatally exposing the king to mate — but the specific piece hung varies too much to name one, and a couple of boards are actually a missed win or a non-blunder, so it needs review.

1186.label: In the opening the player loses their own material self-inflicted—either leaving a piece en prise or removing its defender (most often a knight, sometimes a bishop or pawn)—turning an equal position into a losing one.

1179.chip: Ignores threat; hangs piece or allows mate

1168.label: The player makes a capture meant to rip open the enemy king's pawn shield (most often a bishop or pawn taking on g6), but the move is unsound and loses their own material—usually squandering a winning position—though a couple of boards instead miss a winning tactic.

1192.label: The player voluntarily captures into a queen trade that liquidates their winning advantage—usually killing an attack on the enemy king or, in one case, declining a mate/free piece—turning a winning position into equality or worse.

1182.label: Mixed feature: a knight is the decisive piece in nearly every board, but the precise error varies — roughly half the positions hang/lose the player's own knight (immediately as in Nd3/Nc3, or over 2-3 moves of the refutation via move-order slips like Rd3/Rg1 dropping the d6 outpost), while the other half fail to capture or trade a key enemy knight (missed Bxg5, Bxc3, Nxe4), in each case throwing away a winning or equal position.

1188.label: In winning endgames the player repeatedly plays a materially-safe but inferior move and misses the precise winning continuation (often a forcing check such as d3+), though a couple of boards instead hang material over 2-3 moves.

1200.label: In rook-and-pawn endgames, plays a passive or poorly-placed rook (occasionally king/pawn) move that surrenders a tempo and lets the opponent's passed pawn run to promotion, rather than the active rook placement that would stop it.

1187.label: The player makes a move that abandons defense of their own king (removing a key defender or skipping the only prophylactic move), allowing a decisive attack that is usually forced mate, though two boards instead simply squander a winning advantage.

1191.chip: Ignores threat, allowing mate or material loss

1193.label: In the opening the player makes a move (usually a greedy capture) that hangs one of their own pieces for at most a pawn—the piece varies (knight ~7/10, bishop ~3/10), so it's 'a piece'—losing material to a simple recapture.

1204.label: A king move that exposes the king and walks it into a forced checkmate (or, in a couple of cases, decisive material loss via an unstoppable check).

1199.chip: Missed capturing a hanging piece (usually rook)

1190.label: In a worse middlegame the player makes a non-forcing move (usually a rook) that abandons a critical rank or file instead of trading off the dangerous rook, allowing the opponent to crash through with a decisive tactic — back-rank mate, a fork, or a forced win of material.

1201.chip: Misses free capture of hanging piece

1203.label: Plays a quiet opening developing move and overlooks a forced material win — almost always a bishop grabbing an undefended pawn on the long diagonal (Bxg7/Bxg2) to win the exchange.

1194.label: The player repeatedly makes a losing queen move — either hanging the queen (often to a knight fork) or making/offering a disadvantageous queen exchange (e.g. queen-for-rook) — that squanders material or a winning position.

1210.label: In every position the player skips a simple capture of an undefended enemy knight (f4/e4/d5/d4/e5), passing up a free piece — a clear missed-win omission, not a hang of their own material.

1197.label: Player grabs material (usually a capture) or follows an own plan instead of the strongest continuation—most often a forced mate or decisive, frequently queen-led attack—squandering a winning position, with a couple of boards instead being tempo/fork blunders that simply hang material.

1208.label: A move that loses the player's own material to a refutation within 1–3 moves, but the hung unit varies widely (knight, rook, bishop, queen) and two boards are more positional (king-weakening/tempo loss), so the safe label is 'hangs a piece/material' rather than any specific piece.

1220.label: In a winning endgame the player plays a materially-safe king move that squanders the win (often a forced mate or pawn promotion) instead of the one precise winning continuation.

1209.label: The player makes a slow/passive move (usually a queen retreat or shuffle) that fails to find the demanded active continuation — surrendering the initiative and either missing a winning/saving shot or letting the opponent's attack crash through.

1214.chip: Avoids forcing queen trade, hangs material
