1215.label: In positions revolving around a queen that is en prise (75% winning), the player mishandles it — either failing to capture the opponent's free queen (boards 2,4,5,6,9) or removing a defender that leaves its own queen hanging (boards 1,3,8), with two queen-check/no-trade king-safety variants (7,10); the queen is the decisive piece on nearly every board but the direction (missed-capture vs self-hang) is genuinely mixed.

1207.label: Mixed 'blunders the win' feature in sharp middlegames: 5 boards hang material outright (Rf4, g3, Qe6+, Qxe2, Bb4) and 5 skip a winning capture (Rxa3+, Qxd8+ x2, Bxf8, dxe5); the only consistent element is that the queen sits in the decisive line on ~9/10 boards, but its role varies too much to fix a single direction.

1229.label: Across all ten endgame positions the player skipped a winning knight-check tactic (fork/discovered attack/clearance, usually winning a rook) and instead played a passive or pawn-grabbing move that let the advantage slip to a draw or near-equality.

1219.chip: Missed bishop capture of hung rook
1219.label: Repeatedly missed a bishop capture of an undefended enemy rook (winning the exchange or a full rook), instead playing a slow developing or structural move.

1234.chip: Wrong-way king move, lost pawn endgame
1234.label: In already-losing king-and-pawn endgames (mover is losing on all 10 boards), the player makes a king move in the wrong direction — passive/retreating or toward the wrong wing — losing the king-activity/counter-race instead of running the best defensive march; it's fuzzy because 3 of the 10 boards (2, 5, 6) lose ~0–15cp and the named move is essentially best, so the feature mostly fires on 'misdirected king in lost pawn endgames' rather than a clean blunder.

1227.label: The player squanders a winning or drawn position by playing a natural capture/developing move instead of a forcing intermediate check that wins material or mates (a minority of boards instead self-inflict a hang).

1226.label: A developing or pawn move in the opening that fatally exposes the player's king/queen line — in 7/10 boards it opens the light-square diagonal allowing a devastating Qh5+/Qh4#, while in 3/10 it leaves the queen on c3 with the king on e1 to be won by a ...Bb4 pin; the mechanism is mixed, but the queen (as attacker or as the pinned victim) is the decisive piece on nearly every board.

1221.chip: Throws away advantage; often hangs bishop
1221.label: Genuinely mixed 'blunder' feature: about half the moves directly hang the player's own material (bishop ×3, queen ×2) to a 1-3 move tactic, while the other half are positional or king-safety errors (allowing Ndb5/Ba3, premature breaks, Bf7+ on an uncastled king) that squander a winning or equal position; a bishop appears in the decisive line of most boards but in varying roles, so no single hung piece can anchor the label.

1230.chip: Squanders win with quiet move (kingside attack)
1230.label: In nearly every position the player held a large or winning advantage and threw it away by playing a slow, natural move (passive rook/queen developing move) instead of the strong continuation — most often a crushing kingside attack (Qh5 / b1-h7 battery) — making this an omission/missed-win feature rather than a material-hanging one (hung-own only ~33%).

1223.label: Fires on early opening queen sorties (Qb3/Qb6/Qf3); in ~75% the exposed queen is punished by a knight fork or Bxf7+ break that loses material, while ~25% are winning positions where the slow queen move skips an immediate Bxf7+/Nxe5 tactic — so the piece (queen) is constant but the direction is mixed.

1228.chip: Skips forcing line at critical moment
1228.label: At sharp tactical positions the player rejects the forcing best move (usually a check or capture) for a slow, natural, or greedy alternative, either squandering a winning tactic (boards 1,3,4,6,8) or walking into a forced material loss/mate (boards 2,5,7,9,10).

1239.label: A materially-safe move that ignores an immediate capture of the opponent's undefended queen, squandering a winning advantage (9/10 boards miss a direct queen grab).

1224.label: Moving a piece (usually the knight off e4) clears the e-file, allowing a discovered check from the e2-queen to the e8-king that wins the player's own queen in the opening.

1238.label: A self-inflicted endgame blunder—usually a capture that grabs material or removes a key defender—which loses the player's own piece (varied: rook most often, but also bishop/knight) to a tactical refutation, frequently a check or back-rank threat.

1241.label: The player relocates a piece—most often a knight (~7/10)—to a square where it is captured outright or refuted by a short follow-up tactic, losing material; a few boards are positional/tempo self-inflicted losses rather than clean hangs.

1231.label: In the opening Black greedily grabs a central pawn with a knight, a self-inflicted material loss that is punished by a tactic (usually Qa4+ or a recapture) winning back the knight or the exchange.

1232.label: A self-inflicted blunder, usually an over-ambitious forcing move (frequently a check or knight sortie) that hangs the player's own material—the specific piece varies (knight, queen, exchange)—while a couple of boards instead miss a defense or a forced win.

1233.label: Across these middlegame boards the player makes a tempting active move—usually a check, capture, or trade-offer (rook/bishop/knight/queen all appear)—that throws away a winning or equal position, sometimes hanging material outright (boards 4, 9, 10) but more often trading off the key attacking piece or missing a stronger tactic / the only saving move; piece and exact mechanism vary, so it's genuinely mixed rather than a single-piece hang.

1237.label: A premature knight sortie to the rim (almost always ...Na5 hitting the c4 bishop) that neglects king safety and loses material, typically refuted by the Bxf7+ sacrifice exploiting the now-undefended f7.

1243.chip: Hangs rook chasing queen with g-pawn
1243.label: A g-pawn push (g6/g3) to chase the enemy queen off h5/h4 opens the e-file and long diagonal, letting the queen check (Qxe5+/Qxe4+) and capture the now-exposed corner rook.

1235.label: Every position ignores a one-move queen checkmate against the castled king (Qh7# or Qh2#/Qg2# along an open diagonal), playing an unrelated/greedy move instead of the forced defensive block and getting mated next move.

1240.label: In already-winning positions the player plays a premature forcing check or non-capturing move instead of first making the clean capture/trade, throwing away tempo or hanging a piece — most often the bishop — though boards 2, 3 and 9 are not actually blunders, so the pattern is partly noise.

1242.label: In a critical (mostly winning) position the player overlooks the single decisive move — a free capture (Nxh4/Qxg5), a saving castle (O-O), a king escape, a forcing check, or the right capture/move-order — and plays a passive or wrong move that squanders the win or walks into mate; ~8/10 are pure omissions, but 2 boards (Qe8, f3) are self-inflicted hangs, so direction is mixed.

1247.label: A middlegame move—often a greedy capture or careless reposition—that loses the player's own material, with the hung piece varying widely (rook, knight, bishop, or queen) rather than one specific piece.

1250.label: A move leaves an own pawn or piece undefended, allowing the opponent's knight to win the material—frequently via a fork or capture-with-tempo.

1245.label: A move that throws away a clearly winning or large advantage — about half the time by skipping the only strong continuation (positional/tempo omission), the other half by hanging material outright, with no consistent piece.

1249.label: Across the boards the player makes a passive or tempo-losing move (retreat, flank pawn push, or grabbing a side pawn) that abandons a key defensive or attacking role and skips a forcing winning continuation, surrendering the advantage — sometimes letting their own material (a piece, varying between knight/rook/pawn) or king fall a few moves later.

1236.chip: Hangs material via weakening opening move
1236.label: A premature/weakening move in the opening—most often a pawn push (h6, h5, e6)—that throws away equality by letting the opponent win material or shatter the player's structure (commonly a capture/sacrifice on g6 against the kingside bishop), but the specific piece lost varies (g6 bishop, d3 bishop, rook, knight, pawn) and two boards aren't pawn moves, so the only firm invariant is 'self-inflicted material/positional collapse in the opening.'

1248.label: The player plays a quiet, non-forcing move and overlooks an available forcing check (usually a queen or bishop check) that wins material or saves the position.

1253.label: The player plays a natural-looking developing, trading, or 'tempo' move that throws away an immediately available forced mate or winning combination — a materially-safe omission rather than a self-inflicted hang.

1244.label: In a winning/advantageous middlegame the player skips a concrete forcing tactic (often a check or capture) and plays a slow or weaker move, throwing away the win — the missed material varies, so no single piece is named.

1259.label: Pushes a bishop into a square where it is captured for free (or sacrificed on f7 for a single pawn) in the opening, losing a full minor piece across all ten positions.

1258.label: In the opening, the played move hangs an undefended piece (most often a bishop, sometimes a knight or queen) to a simple pawn capture.

1255.label: In every position the player squandered a winning advantage by playing a passive or aimless move instead of an available material-winning capture, which in 9/10 cases was a bishop capture (often netting a full piece).

1260.label: A materially-safe, non-forcing opening move (castling, retreat, or quiet pawn move) that squanders a concrete winning knight tactic — most often Nxf7, sometimes Nxc3/Nxf2 — turning a near-winning position into equality.

1246.label: The played move is a self-inflicted blunder that loses the player's own material — a piece falls (queen, rook, knight or bishop, varying board to board) either immediately to a free capture or within 2–3 moves of the refutation, so no single piece can honestly be named.

1256.chip: Pawn capture opens lines toward own king
1256.label: Resolving pawn tension with a pawn recapture/capture that rips open a file (usually toward the player's own king), handing the opponent a decisive attack rather than losing material outright.

1252.label: A move that fatally exposes or neglects the player's own king, inviting a decisive attack that ends in checkmate or heavy material loss.

1265.label: A safe move that overlooks an immediate capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away a winning position.

1251.label: In a clearly winning position (usually an endgame) the player makes a tempting forcing move—often an impulsive check or a material grab—that throws away the cleanest win (a forced mate, a free piece, or a superior endgame) yet stays winning, so the recurring error is a missed/squandered win rather than a single consistently-hung piece.

1254.label: From a winning position—almost always an endgame involving a passed pawn or promotion race—the player throws away the advantage (a pointless tempo-losing check, allowing the enemy pawn to queen, or skipping the only winning move), flipping winning into losing/drawn; the moving piece and exact mechanism vary, so no single piece is hung.

1261.label: Most boards play a move that leaves one of the player's own pieces undefended and lost — immediately or within the refutation (the d5-knight, the g4/g6 bishop, or the a5-knight) — but the hung piece varies and three boards are instead a missed-win capture, a tempo slip, or a bad positional trade, so it's best named generically as 'hangs a piece.'

1270.label: Player leaves a rook undefended on an open line where the enemy queen captures it for free, hanging a full rook (or the exchange) in nearly every case.

1268.label: Captures a dangerous passed pawn with the rook, allowing an immediate recapture that loses the rook for a single pawn in a losing endgame.

1266.label: Plays a greedy or passive move—usually grabbing a pawn instead of a forcing rook check—throwing away a forced mate or winning attack.

1257.label: Plays a slow, non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo — instead of the precise forcing shot — and is then punished either by missing a win or by allowing the opponent a decisive tactic or king attack.

1263.label: From a winning (75%) or drawn (25%) position the player throws away the advantage — via a slow/king or rook move that misses the decisive shot, a greedy capture, or a bad trade — with the queen central to the decisive line/refutation in most boards, though the exact mechanism (missed win vs. hung piece vs. losing trade) is mixed.

1267.label: From an equal middlegame, the player makes a move (often skipping the neutralizing ...Bxe5/...Bxe4) that lets a knight fork or infiltrate — or leaves their own knight hanging — dropping material within two or three moves.

1272.label: In a winning or clearly better position, the player plays an inferior/slow move that throws away the advantage instead of the available decisive continuation (frequently a forcing capture or check), rather than hanging a specific piece.

1274.chip: Missed winning capture in endgame (often a hanging rook)
1274.label: In a winning endgame the player chose a materially-safe but passive move, skipping a clear winning capture (most often grabbing a free rook, sometimes a knight fork) and throwing away the won position.

1271.label: Throws away a won position by prematurely exchanging or playing a slow move instead of establishing/exploiting the pin (usually on the f3- or f6-knight).

1276.label: In endgames the player mishandles a passed pawn—skipping the key capture of its supporter, the needed blockade, or the correct king route in the race—allowing the pawn to promote and turning a defensible loss into a decisive one.

1273.label: In every position the player makes a materially-safe but imprecise endgame move (a slow king move or wrong capture) instead of the one precise winning continuation—most often a timely pawn break like b4—squandering a winning or equal position without hanging any material.

1281.label: The recurring mistake is advancing a pawn that weakens the player's own pawn structure or king safety (or liquidates a winning pawn majority), squandering a draw or win — a purely positional error, with no piece actually hung.

1275.chip: Squanders won position, missed forcing line
1275.label: From a winning position (mostly passed-pawn endgames) the player skips the one decisive forcing continuation—typically a promotion or rook trade/sac—and instead plays a passive or greedy move that lets the opponent escape (often by perpetual check), though the boards are mixed in how the win is thrown away.

1269.label: In the opening, the player makes a move—usually a knight move—that leaves one of their own pieces (most often a knight) hanging to a simple pawn capture or short tactic, losing material for little or nothing.

1280.label: In winning endgames with pawn tension, the player captures (or plays a slow waiting move) to release the tension instead of the winning pawn advance/lock or break (f5/g6/g5/a5/hxg6), throwing away a forced mate or win — but the feature also fires on several boards where the capture is a 0cp non-blunder, so it really detects 'released pawn tension in a won position' regardless of whether it actually costs the win.

1282.label: A self-inflicted move that loses the player's own material—either marching a piece into capture or abandoning a defender so a piece falls over the next move or two—most often a knight but sometimes a bishop or the exchange, so the safe specificity is 'a piece'.

1277.chip: Releases pawn tension, ruins structure (enemy passer)
1277.label: Captures with a pawn that releases the tension or blockade and wrecks the player's own pawn structure—typically handing the opponent dangerous (often passed) pawns—rather than a true hung-piece tactic, since every board resolves as a structurally losing trade/recapture.

1286.label: In Italian-style openings the player makes a developing or tension-ignoring move (d4, castling, Qf3, Re8, Ng4) that leaves their c4/c5 bishop undefended, losing it to a simple capture.

1279.label: Plays a counterproductive check — almost always letting the enemy king capture the checking unit (pawn 73%, bishop 27%) — that hands over material or releases the king, squandering the advantage.

1264.label: The player moves a piece (usually a knight, ~7/10) off a critical defensive/guarding square — often to grab a pawn or piece — abandoning its duty, and the refutation shows the player's own king getting mated or their own material falling over the next moves.

1262.label: The player makes a self-inflicted move that loses their own material—hanging a piece (queen, knight, or rook) by ignoring a threat or moving it to a captured square; the exact piece varies, so it's 'a piece' not one specific type.

1283.label: Fires on moves that throw away a favorable/winning position by not finding the best continuation, but the mechanism is mixed: most often missing a stronger tactical or tempo-gaining move (6/10), sometimes outright hanging a piece (2/10), and sometimes trading off a key restraining bishop into an enemy passed pawn (2/10).

1284.label: Advances a pawn prematurely—usually with a check—letting the enemy king blockade it (or hide behind it as a shield), squandering a winning position.

1278.chip: Quiet move skips saving queen trade
1278.label: A passive, non-forcing repositioning move (usually the queen, sometimes the king) that ignores a forcing resource—most often a game-saving queen trade/simplification (Qxg3, Qxf4, Qxe6), but in several boards a hanging knight or a winning exchange-sac—and is punished by losing material or squandering the advantage.

1292.label: The player delivers a queen check that loses the queen for inadequate compensation — either captured outright for a pawn/nothing or traded into a hopeless deficit — with the move always being a check in all 10 boards.

1287.label: Plays a non-forcing or materialistic move that overlooks a winning checking move — frequently a forced checkmate — squandering a decisive advantage.

1291.label: In rook endgames the player mishandles material—sometimes hanging their own piece (rook on b5c5, bishop on f2e3), sometimes failing to win/save material (missed exd5, missed forced Rxe7+ exchange)—but the direction (self-inflicted hang vs. missed win) and the piece both vary, so only the broad 'endgame material error with a rook on the board' is reliable.

1294.label: A materially-safe but passive move that overlooks a winning tactical shot—almost always a bishop move (Bb5/Bb4/Be6/Bg4) that pins or deflects to win the enemy queen—in the opening.

1295.label: The played move leaves the player's own queen en prise, where it is captured by an enemy knight for inadequate compensation.

1285.label: In every position the player makes a premature simplifying capture (usually a queen trade with check) that cleanly converts a winning position into a smaller edge, passing up a more decisive tactic — frequently a knight fork.

1293.label: The played move self-inflicts material loss by leaving a piece capturable—either placed directly en prise or by abandoning its defense—though the specific piece varies (rook, bishop, knight, queen) and two boards deviate (one is a wrong-capture trade into a lost endgame, one squanders a forced mate).

1302.label: In most of the top positions the player overlooked a decisive winning move — either a forced checkmate (boards 1,5,6,7) or a capture/fork winning the opponent's queen (boards 2,3,4,8) — choosing a lesser materially-safe move instead, though two boards (9,10) instead self-inflicted a hang of the player's own material, so the core 'Missed win' invariant covers only ~8/10.

1299.label: An imprecise move—most often a kingside g/h pawn push or capture—that loses tempo or wrecks the player's own pawn structure and squanders a winning or near-equal position rather than cleanly hanging material, though about 2/10 boards instead drop a pawn/piece to a tactic (knight fork, undefended pawn).

1289.label: A defensive/trade-offer move (usually the queen) backfires, exposing the king to a forcing check that wins the player's own material — they should have stepped the king to safety instead.

1288.label: In drawn/winning endgames the player makes a non-self-hanging but inferior move that squanders the result—in the cleanest cases failing to capture a hanging piece (twice a free queen, once a bishop)—but several boards are positional or king-safety collapses (lost blockader, abandoned back rank, even a greedy capture into mate) rather than missed captures, so the feature is mixed.

1304.label: In materially-safe, already-winning positions the player repeatedly skipped a forcing rook check (skewer or back-rank, ~9/10) that won material — but the prize varies (rook, queen, bishop), so no single captured piece is named; it's a missed win, not a hang.

1300.label: A pawn advance (8/10) that wrecks the player's own position in an endgame — sometimes squandering a winning advantage, sometimes hanging material a few moves later — but the damage varies (positional weakening vs. material loss) and two moves aren't even pawn pushes, so the exact mistake isn't a single clean type.

1303.label: In the opening Black plays a developing or pawn move (Nf6/Ng4/Ne4/f5/c6/Bd7/Qf6) that abandons or fails to advance the central e5 pawn instead of the freeing ...e4, and e5 falls (boards 1-7,9); boards 8 and 10 are instead White Bd3 tempo-loss moves that skip a central pawn break (d5/cxd5), so the e5-hang core is ~8/10.

1301.label: Plays a quiet, safe repositioning move (retreat/develop/castle) instead of an available winning tactical strike, most often a bishop capture such as Bxd4+ or Bxe6.

1309.label: Promotes a pawn to a queen on a square where it is immediately captured (or, in one case, ignores a mating threat), hanging the freshly-promoted queen and squandering a winning position instead of playing the prep/intermezzo first.

1290.label: An unsound speculative capture/sacrifice in the opening — overwhelmingly a knight (Nxf7/Nxf2/Nxe4/Nxe5), once a bishop (Bxf7+) — that hangs the player's own piece for at most a pawn, cleanly refuted by a simple recapture with no attacking follow-up.

1296.label: The player voluntarily trades/captures with the queen to simplify when a stronger continuation (keeping queens on, a winning capture, a fork, or mate) was available, throwing away a winning position into roughly equal/drawn material.

1298.label: Genuinely mixed feature firing on over-optimistic, aggressive moves that backfire—most cleanly knights chasing a queen or going to the rim and losing tempo (1,2,3,6,7), but it also includes defender-removal/hangs (4,10), a back-rank lapse (5), and unsound sacrifices (8,9); knight is the moved or key piece in ~6/10, and material loss usually comes 2-3 moves deep in the refutation rather than immediately.

1314.label: In every position the player chose a slow/passive move and overlooked a forcing pawn advance — almost always a check, frequently the f5+ king-and-rook fork — that wins material outright.

1310.label: Plays a quiet, materially-safe move that squanders a winning advantage by overlooking an available material-winning tactic (capture, fork, or double attack).

1307.chip: Hangs fianchetto bishop on long diagonal
1307.label: Player self-inflicts material loss by leaving a fianchettoed bishop undefended on the a1–h8 long diagonal, allowing Bxg7/Bxb2 (occasionally via moving a piece that was shielding the diagonal), though one board is a pure positional tempo loss and one hangs a rook instead.

1308.chip: Trades active piece into worse endgame (knight)
1308.label: Voluntarily captures/trades off a well-placed piece (usually a centralized knight) into an even recapture that simplifies into a lost endgame — typically handing the opponent dangerous passed pawns or a winning pawn majority.

1306.label: The feature most often fires when the player makes a slow/passive move that fails to capture a trapped enemy knight (5/10: g7, g2, b3, b3, b7), squandering a winning advantage; a knight is in the decisive play of nearly every board, but the direction is mixed—3 boards instead hang the player's own piece via a counting/move-order error (Nd4, Rxa6 bishop, b4-Qf6 rook) and 2 are pure positional give-backs (e4, d6).

1305.label: In these Petrov-type openings the player fails to play the required ...Qe7 and instead makes a move (most often retreating the e4 shield-knight, sometimes a pawn grab or developing move) that hangs material — usually the queen — to a discovered check/attack down the open e-file.

1317.label: In the opening, the player repeatedly fails to grab a free, undefended enemy bishop (typically on b5/g4/b4/g5), playing a safe but passive move instead and throwing away a winning material advantage.

1319.label: Plays a move that ignores an existing/created attack and leaves one of its own pieces (varying — bishop, queen, knight, or rook) hanging for a free capture.

1320.label: Plays a reflexive forcing check instead of the stronger (often quiet) winning move, throwing away a forced mate or decisive advantage — sometimes even hanging the checking piece in the process — with the hung piece varying (queen/rook/knight/bishop), so the true invariant is the spurious check, not any one piece.

1313.label: From a winning or strong middlegame position the player throws away the advantage, splitting roughly 60/40 between hanging a piece (frequently by moving a key defender) and missing a forced mate or win — the mechanism and piece are too mixed to name specifically.

1321.label: Plays a safe but passive move while overlooking a decisive knight tactic—almost always a central capture like Nxd4/Nxd5 (or Nxe5/Nxe6/Ne4) that wins material via a fork or discovered attack.

1311.label: Repeatedly fails to capture or trade off the opponent's centralized knight (typically on e4/e5), instead playing a passive or wrong-order move that either skips winning material or lets the knight deliver a fork/check tactic.

1323.label: In endgames the player grabs material or wastes tempo with the wrong move/recapture instead of stopping the opponent's passed pawn, allowing it to queen and turning a win or draw into a loss.

1318.chip: Hangs a piece in winning position
1318.label: In a won/winning position the player makes a slow, non-forcing or wrong-order move that leaves their own piece (most often a rook) en prise to a free capture, throwing the game away.

1322.label: In a won endgame the player repeatedly passes up the fastest forced win — most often an immediate pawn promotion with check — and instead plays a slower king/piece move that squanders the guaranteed victory.

1327.label: In a winning middlegame position, plays a passive or non-forcing move and overlooks a forcing tactical sequence that wins material (the key shot is usually a rook capture).

1312.label: An inferior king move (8/10 are king moves) in a drawn-or-losing endgame that throws the game away — variously hanging a piece (queen, knight, or rook), walking into a mating net, or losing critical tempo to a passed pawn, so neither the hung piece nor the exact mechanism is consistent enough to name specifically.

1331.label: In every position the player skipped a forcing early queen check (Qh5+/Qh4+) that exploits the opponent's missing f-pawn / exposed king to win material, opting for a quiet developing move instead.

1315.label: In an already-winning opening, the player throws away the advantage with a knight featuring in the decisive line of nearly every board, but direction is genuinely split—~6/10 are self-inflicted greedy/careless moves that lose the player's own material (sometimes over 2-3 moves) and ~4/10 are missed winning captures, with the relevant piece varying.

1329.label: Every move walks into an immediate forced checkmate by ignoring an existing mating threat against the player's own king — frequently while greedily grabbing material — making this a self-inflicted king-safety catastrophe rather than a simple piece blunder.

1330.chip: Squanders win with quiet move (king attack)
1330.label: In a winning or crushing position the player makes a slow, non-forcing move instead of the decisive continuation (often a queen tactic or mate against an exposed king), throwing away the advantage.

1335.label: A materially-safe but passive, tempo-losing move (rook/king/pawn shuffles) that abandons the forcing/active continuation and throws away a winning position into equality.

1325.label: In the middlegame the player chooses a natural but non-forcing/passive move that skips a clearly stronger tactical shot, squandering a winning or better position; the missed resource varies (queen, capture, pawn break), with two outlier boards instead losing material/king safety.

1336.label: The feature flags moves that throw away a forced checkmate/winning attack — typically retreating or grabbing material with a safe move instead of delivering the mating sequence (mostly king-safety tactics).

1333.label: The player repeatedly overlooked a winning tactical fork—almost always a knight fork that wins a rook—choosing a passive or greedy move instead.

1326.label: In the opening the player makes a safe recapture or quiet move while overlooking a stronger pawn capture (frequently exf6) that wins material—most often a knight, though the won piece varies.

1328.label: The player makes the obvious immediate capture or natural move but skips a required move-order finesse (usually an intermediate check/zwischenzug); in the majority of lines this lets its own material fall over the next 1-3 moves (rook, bishop, knight, even mate), though a few boards are pure missed wins, so the hung piece and even the direction are mixed.

1338.label: In a (mostly winning) endgame the player makes a quiet, non-forcing king/rook move (0% captures, 0% checks played) instead of the decisive continuation—a winning capture, a check, or the faster mate—squandering efficiency or material, though the set is mixed (two are 0cp false-positives, and a couple actually hang material rather than just being slow).

1337.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight involved)
1337.label: In the opening the player makes a move that abandons support of a hanging minor piece (a bishop on c4/c5 or a knight on e4/e5, varying board to board), letting it be captured for free.

1341.label: Moves the queen out prematurely to an exposed central/attacking square in the opening, where it gets harassed with tempo (and sometimes leaves a piece hanging behind it), squandering the position.

1332.label: In critical, mostly-losing endgames the feature fires when the player fails to play the single best move—either skipping a free material grab (queen captures Bxc3/Rxb8/Rxh4, the only-saving Kc4) or instead playing a move that hangs own material (rook on 4 & 8) or drifts into a lost positional/trade situation (5, 7, 10)—so the shared core is 'doesn't find the only good move and collapses,' but direction (missed-win vs self-hang vs slow loss) and piece both vary, warranting review.

1340.label: In drawn endgames the player makes a materially-safe move that overlooks the single best move — most often a free capture of a hanging enemy piece (usually the queen), occasionally the only drawing resource — turning equality into a loss.

1346.chip: Slow king/pawn move in won endgame

1457.label: In a (mostly) winning endgame the player squanders the win by grabbing a pawn—usually with the king (6/10), which exposes a second pawn or abandons a defensive duty and is refuted by an immediate recapture—or by pushing a passer prematurely (3/10); mechanism is mixed, with one opening bishop-hang outlier.

1466.label: A materially-safe but passive/quiet move that squanders a stronger dynamic counterstrike (often a central pawn break or tactic), missing a win or the only save — not a hang, since the player's own piece is never given up.

1453.label: Captures a pawn with a tempting check but sacrifices a rook, losing material or throwing away the winning position when the piece is simply recaptured.

1468.label: In every position the player already had a winning game—often a forced mate—and threw it away by choosing an inferior move (a distracting check or a greedy pawn grab) instead of the decisive winning continuation; material stays safe, so the fault is the omitted win, not a hung piece.

1473.label: In every position the player overlooked an available forced checkmate — almost always a mate-in-one delivered by the queen.

1455.chip: Misses forcing queen move, cedes tempo
1455.label: Plays a quiet or slow move instead of the required forcing continuation (usually a queen check/tactic), handing the opponent a free tempo and squandering a winning or drawing position—sometimes even leaving its own queen hanging.

1461.label: The played move leaves the player's own piece—most often a rook—undefended, trapped, or walking into a pin/fork, and it is captured within one to two moves (9/10 self-inflicted hangs; board 3 is instead a missed recapture).

1460.label: A move—frequently a queen move—that abandons a defensive duty or ignores a standing threat, hanging a piece or allowing mate in the refutation; the queen recurs in the decisive play of nearly every board even though the dropped unit varies, with two boards instead missing free material.

1474.label: In a losing endgame, the player gives up their rook by capturing a (usually passed) pawn, allowing an immediate recapture that surrenders the rook for a single pawn.

1481.label: Plays an unsound bishop sacrifice with check in the opening (usually Bxf7+, once Bxf2+) that simply hangs the bishop for a single pawn with no attacking follow-up.

1477.label: An opening move that leaves the player's own knight en prise, refuted by a simple pawn or king capture winning the piece for free.

1472.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (often knight)
1472.label: In the opening the player plays a developing/capturing move that leaves one of their own pieces hanging to a simple capture, dropping roughly a full piece — usually a knight (8/10), occasionally a bishop, with the fix almost always the resolving trade Nxc6.

1467.label: The player makes a move (often a capture grabbing material or removing an attacker) that strips away a key defender of their own king, exposing it to a decisive attack or forced mate; the sacrificed defender varies (pawn, knight, bishop, rook), so no single piece is named.

1469.label: A move that opens a file or removes a key defender, letting an enemy rook crash onto the open line or back rank to win material or deliver mate (rook is always the punishing piece).

1475.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (chasing queen)
1475.label: An over-aggressive opening move—usually attacking the enemy queen for tempo—hangs the player's own material (knight, bishop, or queen) to a refutation, though two cases are merely tempo loss.

1470.chip: Trades only active piece, lost endgame (takes knight)

1476.label: Plays a slow/quiet positional move that squanders a decisive advantage, missing the forcing winning continuation (often a capture of a hanging piece or a mating/material-winning tactic) — an omission, not a self-hang, and the missed material varies (rook, knight, queen), so no single piece is named.

1482.chip: Fails to stop passed pawn (rook endgame)

1486.label: Fires on opening moves that self-inflict material loss by hanging the player's own piece (most often a bishop, sometimes a knight) for little or no compensation.

1488.label: In all 10 positions the player passes up a free capture of the opponent's undefended rook (Nxa1, Bxh8, Nxd8, Bxa1, Nxg1, Bxe2, etc.), instead playing an aimless king or pawn move and throwing away the won material.

1490.label: In losing king-and-pawn endgames, plays a king misstep or pawn push that loses the pawn race, letting the opponent's passed pawn promote (one board hangs a knight, one is essentially the engine's move, so the mechanism varies).

1483.label: A middlegame move that loses the player's own material to a short tactic — a fork, an undefended piece, or a tempo/move-order slip — but the dropped piece varies (bishop, knight, pawn, exchange, queen), so no single piece can be named.

1479.label: The player repeatedly declines an available capture — often a free recapture — leaving a hanging piece on the board and dropping ~500cp of material.

1485.label: The player repeatedly chooses a safe, quiet or retreating move and overlooks a stronger tactical shot (capture, fork, or discovered attack) that would have won material or a decisive advantage.

1487.chip: Missed winning capture, blew won game

1495.label: A materially-safe routine developing or retreating move that passes up a winning tactical shot — almost always a knight fork (Nb5/Ndb5/Ndb4 hitting d6/c7) in the opening, with no own material hung.

1498.label: An endgame move — most often a passive or mistimed king move — that wastes a tempo or abandons a defensive resource, converting a drawn or winning position into a loss (with one outlier that wasn't actually a blunder and only 2 boards that directly hang material).

1500.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player makes a slow move (usually a king move, sometimes a side pawn push, rook shuffle, or a needless capture) instead of immediately advancing the decisive passed pawn, squandering a winning or holdable race.

1494.label: A material error where a queen is decisive in nearly every position — most often hanging own material (frequently the queen) via a natural-looking move, but sometimes overlooking a free capture of the enemy queen.

1501.label: In endgames (100% endgame, king moves 67%) the player makes a passive or retreating king move—occasionally a passive/over-eager rook move—that concedes tempo and activity instead of the active centralizing/restricting continuation; no material is hung (100% safe), with severity ranging from trivial 0–11cp slips to walking into a forced mate.

1478.label: Throws away a winning/mating position by playing a tempting forcing check (often hanging the checking piece) instead of the decisive capture or mate.

1492.chip: Allows decisive attack on own king
1492.label: The player makes a passive or king-weakening move that ignores the position's forcing demands, allowing a crushing—usually mating—attack against their own king in the middlegame (with two outliers that instead simply drop material: a hung rook and a lost pawn).

1502.label: The queen moves out—usually to grab material—onto a square where it is immediately recaptured (or, in one case, abandons a back-rank defense), losing the queen and the game.

1505.label: A purposeless check (always a check, usually a rook check in the endgame) that drives the opponent's king to a better square, squandering a winning or drawable position by handing over a tempo.

1506.label: In the opening the player loses a knight—repeatedly leaving it attacked (usually by a pawn, e.g. ignoring exf6/dxc6 or lunging to an undefended square) and dropping it for at most a pawn.

1504.chip: Missed winning rook move (usually a check)
1504.label: Plays a materially-safe move while overlooking a winning rook move—almost always a forcing check (or mate) that exploits the exposed enemy king.

1499.label: A greedy grab—usually capturing the e5 pawn/piece—overextends and ends up hanging the player's own material to a pin (Re1), discovered attack, or tempo-gaining hit, with the hung piece varying (often a knight) so it's best called 'a piece'.

1510.label: The player leaves their own queen en prise—usually captured by an enemy bishop—squandering a forced mate or winning position in 9 of 10 boards (board 8 instead drops the exchange/rook).

1511.chip: Unsound forcing check/sac in king attack
1511.label: In a mostly winning king-attack position, the player abandons the calm winning or saving move for a flashy/forcing try — usually an unsound check or sacrifice (no single piece consistently lost) — that hangs material or lets the attack fizzle, with a few cases being quiet moves that abandon defense or skip a forcing win.

1507.label: Player chooses a slow, non-forcing/preparatory move instead of the demanded concrete forcing continuation; in ~6/10 this squanders a winning tactic with own material staying safe, but in ~4/10 the quiet move actually allows the opponent to win material (hanging a piece or walking into a fork), and the piece/tactic involved varies board to board with no single recurring piece.

1512.chip: Passive king move misses forcing win
1512.label: In a won endgame the player makes a quiet/passive move (usually a king move) that skips a decisive forcing win — most often an immediate promotion-with-check or a forcing check/mate sequence — though several boards (notably 6 and 8, and the minor 2/7) are not actually blunders.

1508.label: In every one of the ten (mostly middlegame) positions the played move loses the player's own material — a piece (rook, queen, bishop, knight, or pawn) falls either immediately or within two-to-three moves of the refutation.

1517.label: The player leaves a knight undefended (or moves a defender away), and in every refutation an enemy bishop captures the hanging knight for a near-free piece.

1509.label: In every position the knight gives a pointless/spite check (Nx+) that abandons its strong square or defensive duty, squandering the position—sometimes hanging material, often just losing tempo and a winning/holding setup.

1515.chip: Missed winning check on exposed king
1515.label: Plays a quiet, materially-safe developing/positional move while overlooking a decisive forcing check (Qh4+/Qh5+/Bg3+, sometimes mate) that punishes a wrecked, exposed enemy king — an omission, not a hang, and the winning move varies between queen and bishop so no single piece is named.

1520.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a passive or misplaced king move that loses a critical tempo or the optimal square, instead of activating the king toward the decisive zone.

1516.label: From a (usually winning) middlegame the player most often plays a safe but slower move that skips the cleanest forced win/mate, while a sizable minority instead hang their own queen — so direction is mixed, but the queen is the decisive piece in nearly every board.

1415.label: From winning positions the player usually makes a queen move that leaves the queen en prise to a direct or short-tactic capture (Bxd5, Nxg4, Bxg3, fork), though two boards are actually missed wins and one is a tempo/positional error rather than an outright hang.

1513.label: From a winning (occasionally equal) position, the player throws away the advantage by failing to grab a clear win—most often a hanging/free enemy piece, sometimes by merely threatening a piece instead of capturing it—with a couple of boards instead hanging the player's own material.

1522.label: In winning endgames the player plays a passive or imprecise move (usually a king move) that fails to make the one decisive play—typically capturing or neutralizing a passed pawn—squandering the win rather than losing any of its own material.

1518.label: The feature fires on impulsive 'patzer' checks (≈9/10 are checks) that throw away a forced mate or winning advantage — sometimes by outright hanging the checking piece and sometimes just by missing the faster win — and since the material that falls varies (bishop, rook, queen), no single piece can be named.

1514.label: The player holds a winning or drawn position and squanders it, most often (7/10) by grabbing material with a capture—frequently a rook or bishop—instead of playing the available forcing win/mate/perpetual; the remaining three boards miss the forcing line via a quiet move, and the grabbed/hung piece varies (rook, bishop, pawn) so no single piece is decisive.

1521.label: In a winning position the player plays a quiet (usually king) move that ignores a free capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away the win.

1524.label: In a roughly equal position the player makes a move that loses their own material — most often leaving the queen hanging, though a couple of cases instead miss a winning capture.

1519.label: A premature queen check in the opening that wastes tempo by inviting a developing interposition that attacks the queen — frequently dropping material (forks/hanging pieces) and once even missing forced mate.

1530.label: The queen makes a greedy pawn grab deep in enemy territory (b7/b2/g2/g7), ignoring development or a stronger capture/mate and frequently leaving the queen stranded or trapped.

1523.chip: Wastes critical tempo, misses decisive move

1525.label: Fires on simplifying captures (most often a rook recapture) while already winning an endgame; the moves range from optimal/top-engine-choice to occasional win-throwing trades, so it detects the conversion-by-simplification situation rather than a single recurring error.

1531.label: An opening pawn push that leaves a central pawn (e4/e5/d5) undefended, dropping it to a free capture.

1537.label: The player leaves their own queen undefended on g4/g5 in the opening, allowing it to be captured by the enemy bishop along the open long diagonal.

1529.label: In every position it's an endgame with exactly one good move — almost always a capture (queen, pawn, or rook) that wins or holds the draw — and the player instead makes a passive king/knight move that ignores it, turning a draw or holdable position into a loss.

1526.label: A passive or misjudged move that mishandles flank pawn tension, letting the opponent's favorable pawn break (axb5/hxg6/gxh4 etc.) open lines and either win material or collapse the position.

1535.label: In every position the player overlooks an available capture of the opponent's undefended queen (Qxh1, Bxc7, Bxd6, Bxe4, Rxh8, Qxd6, Bxd8, Bxf7, Bxd2+, bxc2), playing a quiet move instead and throwing away winning material.

1533.label: A voluntary exchange (usually a queen or rook capture) that simplifies into a lost pawn endgame, throwing away a won or drawn position — with two boards being outright piece hangs rather than trades.

1541.label: In an already-winning position the player plays a slow or purposeless move that throws away a forced win — most often a concrete forced mate — rather than hanging any of their own material.

1497.label: Across all 10 boards the engine's best move is a knight capture (NxX) that the player declined in favor of a quiet or committal alternative, squandering the advantage or material; the capturing piece is always a knight but the target and the missed/hung direction vary.

1532.label: In the opening the player declines the correct central pawn capture and mishandles the d/e/c-file tension, dropping material in the refutation (usually a central pawn, sometimes a full piece or a forked piece); since the exact material lost varies and a couple boards are pure missed wins, confidence is low.

1536.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight move)
1536.label: A developing move in the opening—usually a knight jump—that loses the player's own material for nothing, with the hung piece varying (knight, bishop, or queen) across positions.

1545.label: Plays a pointless tempo-wasting queen check (the queen always checks) that the opponent easily blocks/sidesteps, squandering the winning or equal position instead of playing the strong consolidating or tactical move.

1542.label: The player relocates a rook and walks into a knight tactic (fork, check, or discovered attack) that wins material—usually the rook or the exchange (bishop once); the knight is the decisive piece in ~8/10 boards, while boards 6 and 10 are missed wins (skipped Rd7+/forced mate) rather than hangs.

1553.label: Player loses their own queen — either ignoring it being en prise or planting it on a square (often with a check) where it's immediately captured for little or nothing.

1540.label: From a winning position the player throws away the advantage — roughly 60% by playing a safe/inferior move that skips a winning tactic or forced mate, and 40% by hanging material (rook/queen/bishop) outright; no single piece or punishment pattern dominates.

1555.label: The player makes a quiet/passive move and overlooks a forcing check that would have won material or delivered mate (the best move is a check in all 10 positions).

1554.label: In the opening the player throws their bishop at the opponent's fianchettoed bishop (h6/h3/a6/a3) onto an undefended square, where it is simply captured for free, hanging the piece.

1548.label: A careless move loses the player's own material (queen, rook, bishop, or pawn) or allows mate by removing a defender or ignoring an existing threat — the hung piece varies, so it is 'a piece', not one specific type.

1557.label: A knight gives a flashy check but hangs itself (or its support) and is simply captured, throwing away material across all ten positions.

1558.label: An opening move that loses the player's own material to a simple capture, fork, or trap — the hung piece varies (rook, bishop, knight, queen, pawn), so it's 'a piece' rather than any single one.

1559.label: In every position the player had a materially-safe, decisive winning move available—usually a forced checkmate, occasionally a piece-winning tactic—but chose a lesser move that only preserved a winning (not winning-by-force) position.

1546.chip: Missed stronger move, squanders advantage (often central break)
1546.label: Plays a slow/passive move that squanders a winning or better position by overlooking a stronger, materially-safe continuation (frequently a central pawn break) — nothing of the player's own is hung.

1552.label: Across the boards the player ignores an opponent piece sitting en prise (most often the queen, sometimes a rook) and plays an unrelated move instead of the simple winning capture, throwing away a winning position.

1556.label: In the opening the player greedily grabs material (usually a pawn, often with a knight) and squanders a large/winning advantage, the capture backfiring by either hanging a piece or fatally exposing the king.

1561.label: A knight move that abandons a key defensive duty (h7/h2/a pawn) or walks into a capture, letting the opponent win material or launch a decisive (often Greek Gift) attack and flipping a holding position into a loss.

1565.label: The player delivers a worthless desperation/spite check that the enemy king simply sidesteps, either sacrificing the checking piece or pulling a defender off its post, converting a lost-but-playable position into forced mate.

1568.chip: Hangs own material via pawn move
1568.label: A pawn move (usually a capture, often hxg6) opens a file or diagonal and hangs the player's own material — most often the rook/exchange to Qxh8 or a check, but sometimes a knight or pawn via fork — so the specific piece varies.

1569.label: In the opening the player repeatedly misses a free capture of the opponent's undefended queen, instead playing a reflexive pawn-chase or developing move.

1566.label: From an equal-or-better middlegame the player fires an aggressive check — most often a queen to h5 captured along the open 5th rank — that hangs the queen, though several boards instead throw the game away via a losing trade, a tempo-wasting check, or a back-rank blunder rather than a clean queen-hang.

1583.label: Promotes a pawn to a minor/non-queen piece (knight or rook) instead of a queen in a won endgame, converting a winning position into a draw or loss.

1575.label: A move that leaves the player's own piece undefended or trapped—most often a bishop—handing the opponent a free piece and a losing position.

1573.label: Player voluntarily trades a strong, active bishop (usually Bxf6/Bxd5) for a knight via an even recapture — not a hang but a poor trade — surrendering the bishop pair and attacking chances (and sometimes a concrete win) to throw away a clear advantage.

1576.label: In each position the player skips an available forcing move—usually a winning check (capture or mate)—and plays a natural but inferior move, though in about half the boards that move also outright loses, so the hung-vs-missed direction and the piece involved are not uniform.
